quests.trigger: A group of refugees reaches your shelter gate with nothing but the clothes they fled in.
quests.discovery: Three families — eleven people, four of them children — stand at the gate in the rain. They have nothing. No food, no tools, no names you recognize. The shelter is at capacity. The rations are counted. The rain is getting worse.

choices.label: Open the gate and share rations
choices.outcome_text: You open the gate. Eleven people file in, soaked, silent, grateful in a way that has no words. The rations stretch thinner. Nobody complains — not tonight. Tomorrow is tomorrow's arithmetic.
choices.epitaph: Opened the gate to eleven strangers in the rain. The rations stretched thinner. Nobody complained.

choices.label: Offer temporary shelter for one night
choices.outcome_text: One night. You make it clear. They nod, understanding the economy of mercy. By dawn they're gone, and the floor is cleaner than before they came.
choices.epitaph: Gave them one night. They left before dawn and cleaned the floor behind them.

choices.label: Give food but not entry
choices.outcome_text: You pass rations through the gate slot. Hands take them. Eyes meet yours through the bars. The rain keeps falling on their side.
choices.epitaph: Passed food through the gate. Kept the gate closed. The rain didn't stop.

choices.label: Turn them away
choices.outcome_text: You tell them the shelter is full. It isn't — not quite. But the lie is easier than the math. They turn away, the children last, and the smallest one looks back once.
choices.epitaph: Told them we were full. We weren't. The smallest child looked back once.

quests.trigger: A man who once robbed you returns, dying, asking for help.
quests.discovery: You know this face. Three weeks ago, on the east road, he took your water and your spare knife at gunpoint. Now he lies in the dirt outside your perimeter, gut-shot, blood soaking into ash. 'I know,' he says. 'I know I don't deserve it. But I'm dying.'

choices.label: Treat his wound despite everything
choices.outcome_text: You stitch him up with hands that remember what he took. He doesn't apologize with words. He apologizes by surviving, and by the cache location he whispers before the painkillers take him under.
choices.epitaph: Stitched up the man who robbed me. He paid me back with a cache location and the look on his face.

choices.label: Give painkillers but no treatment
choices.outcome_text: You ease the dying. That's all. No surgery, no stitches. Just the chemicals that soften the last hours. He thanks you with his eyes closed.
choices.epitaph: Gave him painkillers. Didn't save him. Made the dying gentler.

choices.label: Demand he return what he stole first
choices.outcome_text: He tells you where the knife is. The water is long gone. You treat him after. The sequence matters to you; you're not sure why.
choices.epitaph: Made him return the knife before treating the wound. The order mattered to me.

choices.label: Leave him where he lies
choices.outcome_text: You walk away. He doesn't call after you. He doesn't have the right, and he knows it. By morning, the spot where he lay is empty. You don't check which direction.
choices.epitaph: Left the robber where he fell. He had it coming. I didn't watch him go.

quests.trigger: Your shelter's food stores are raided because you helped someone who reported your location.
quests.discovery: The storage room is half-empty. Boot prints in the dust. The lock wasn't forced — someone had the combination. The family you sheltered last week knew where you kept it. They told someone. Your people are hungry now, and they're looking at you like you caused it.

choices.label: Accept responsibility and ration what remains
choices.outcome_text: You stand in front of them and say: 'I made a choice. This is the cost. We ration what's left. I take less.' Nobody argues. Nobody agrees either. But they follow.
choices.epitaph: Took responsibility for the theft. Rationed what remained. Took less than my share.

choices.label: Track down the family and demand restitution
choices.outcome_text: You find them two days east. They have nothing — the raiders took from them too. They give back what little they have. It isn't enough. It was never going to be enough.
choices.epitaph: Found the family. They had nothing left to give. The restitution was symbolic.

choices.label: Blame the family publicly and close the gate permanently
choices.outcome_text: You name them at the gathering. People nod. The gate closes. No more strangers. It feels like safety and tastes like something else.
choices.epitaph: Named the family. Closed the gate. Safety tastes different than I expected.

choices.label: Hunt the raiders who actually took the food
choices.outcome_text: You follow the boot prints east. Three raiders, poorly armed. You recover half the stores. The other half is gone — eaten, traded, lost. Half is better than blame.
choices.epitaph: Tracked the raiders. Recovered half. The other half feeds a lesson.

quests.trigger: A neighboring camp offers protection in exchange for a percentage of your supplies — or you can protect the weak camps between you.
quests.discovery: Harrow Camp sends a runner. They'll extend their patrol to cover your eastern flank — for twenty percent of your weekly stores. Alternatively, three small camps between you have no protection at all. You could extend your own patrol to cover them, at cost to your reserves. Or you do nothing, and the wasteland remains the wasteland.

choices.label: Extend your patrol to protect the weak camps
choices.outcome_text: You stretch your people thin. Three small camps sleep safer. Your reserves drop. But the corridor between you fills with traffic — people who walk because the road is watched. That traffic brings trade. Eventually.
choices.epitaph: Extended patrol to cover three camps. Stretched thin. But the road filled with people who walk because it's safe.

choices.label: Accept Harrow's deal — pay for protection
choices.outcome_text: Twenty percent leaves your stores every seven days. Harrow's patrol covers your flank. The weak camps remain unprotected. It's arithmetic, not morality. You tell yourself that.
choices.epitaph: Paid Harrow their twenty percent. My flank is covered. The three camps are not.

choices.label: Refuse both and strengthen your own walls
choices.outcome_text: You build higher and dig deeper. Your shelter hardens. The three camps between you go dark one by one over the following weeks. You hear it happen. The walls are thick enough not to feel it.
choices.epitaph: Built higher walls. The three camps went dark. I heard it through the stone.

choices.label: Organize all camps into a mutual defense pact
choices.outcome_text: It takes six days of talking. Everyone gives a little. Everyone gets a little. The pact holds through the first test — barely. But it holds.
choices.epitaph: Built a pact across four camps. Everyone gave a little. It held.

quests.trigger: A young woman asks to join your shelter specifically because she heard you help people.
quests.discovery: She walked four days to reach your gate. 'I heard what you did,' she says. 'The family in the rain. The man who robbed you. The patrol you run for the small camps.' She has medical training — field surgery, triage. She wants to work. She wants to be somewhere that matters.

choices.label: Welcome her and assign her to the infirmary
choices.outcome_text: She unpacks her kit the same hour. Within a week the infirmary runs smoother than it has since the exchange. Your reputation brought her here. Her skill keeps people alive.
choices.epitaph: Accepted the volunteer. She heard what I did and walked four days to help. The infirmary runs better now.

choices.label: Welcome her with a probation period
choices.outcome_text: Thirty days. She agrees without argument. By day twelve she's saved a man's hand. By day twenty the probation feels like an insult you're both too polite to name.
choices.epitaph: Put her on probation. By day twelve she'd saved a hand. The probation was a formality after that.

choices.label: Ask what she expects in return
choices.outcome_text: 'Food, shelter, purpose,' she says. 'Same as everyone.' It's honest. You let her in. The transaction is clean.
choices.epitaph: Asked what she wanted. Food, shelter, purpose. Same as everyone. Clean deal.

choices.label: Turn her away — the shelter can't support more people
choices.outcome_text: She nods. She doesn't argue. She walks back the way she came, four days into nothing. A week later, a camp to the south advertises a new medic. Her.
choices.epitaph: Turned away the medic. She walked four days back. Another camp gained what I refused.

quests.trigger: A convoy of plague-sick refugees approaches. Letting them in risks your shelter. Turning them away is a death sentence.
quests.discovery: Fourteen people, seven of them showing symptoms — the wet cough, the spotted hands. Your medic says it's containable if you isolate them. Your council says it's a death risk if you're wrong. The convoy is an hour out. The children are coughing.

choices.label: Accept them into quarantine and treat them
choices.outcome_text: You build the quarantine in four hours. Sheets for walls, bleach for everything else. The medic works through the night. Two die. Twelve survive. The cough doesn't spread. This time.
choices.epitaph: Built quarantine in four hours. Two died. Twelve survived. The cough stayed contained. This time.

choices.label: Set up treatment outside the walls
choices.outcome_text: You treat them at arm's length. Supplies passed through the fence, instructions shouted over it. It works — mostly. Three die without the hands-on care that might have saved them.
choices.epitaph: Treated them outside the walls. Three died who might have lived with closer care.

choices.label: Give them supplies and directions to the southern clinic
choices.outcome_text: You load them with what you can spare and point south. The clinic is three days' walk. Whether they make it is between them and the road.
choices.epitaph: Gave supplies and directions south. Three days' walk to the clinic. Their road, not mine.

choices.label: Turn them away — protect your own
choices.outcome_text: You close the gate. The convoy stands there for an hour, then turns south. Not all of them make it to the clinic. You hear the numbers later. You don't write them down.
choices.epitaph: Closed the gate on fourteen sick people. Heard the numbers later. Didn't write them.

quests.trigger: The child of someone who betrayed you arrives at your gate, alone and starving.
quests.discovery: You know this face — she has her father's jaw, the man who sold your supply route to raiders three months ago. She's eight, alone, and hasn't eaten in days. Her father is dead. She doesn't know you know. She just knows the gate and the hunger.

choices.label: Take her in without hesitation
choices.outcome_text: You don't mention her father. You give her food, a bed, a name on the roster. She's eight. She didn't choose her blood. By the second week, she's helping in the greenhouse, talking to the plants the way children do.
choices.epitaph: Took in the betrayer's daughter. Didn't mention her father. She talks to the greenhouse plants now.

choices.label: Take her in but keep her identity quiet
choices.outcome_text: You tell no one whose daughter she is. She sleeps in the children's quarters. Eats at the common table. If anyone notices the jaw, they don't say.
choices.epitaph: Kept her identity quiet. She eats at the common table. Nobody asks about the jaw.

choices.label: Feed her and send her to another camp
choices.outcome_text: You feed her, clean her up, and write a note to the camp south. They'll take a child. Everyone takes a child. You just can't take this particular one.
choices.epitaph: Fed the child and sent her south. Couldn't keep the betrayer's blood in my shelter. Couldn't starve it either.

choices.label: Turn her away — her father's debt is not paid
choices.outcome_text: You tell her the shelter is full. She nods the way children nod when adults lie to them — accepting the shape without believing the content. She walks east. You never learn where she ends up.
choices.epitaph: Turned away an eight-year-old for her father's crime. She walked east. I never asked where.

quests.trigger: Raiders poison a shared water source. You have clean water. Three camps don't.
quests.discovery: The eastern well tests positive for contamination — deliberate, chemical, unmistakable. Three camps relied on it exclusively. They have maybe two days of stored water. You have the filtration system, the clean reserve. Sharing means your own buffer drops to five days. Refusing means watching three camps die of thirst.

choices.label: Share your clean water until the well is decontaminated
choices.outcome_text: For eleven days your people carry water to three camps. Your buffer drops to nothing twice. But nobody dies of thirst. The well comes back online on day twelve. Three camps remember what you did when it mattered.
choices.epitaph: Shared water for eleven days. Buffer hit zero twice. Nobody died. Three camps remember.

choices.label: Share half — you can't risk your own reserve entirely
choices.outcome_text: Half measures. One camp gets enough. Two camps ration hard. Nobody dies, but it's close — closer than you'd admit to your own people.
choices.epitaph: Shared half the water. Nobody died. It was closer than I'll admit.

choices.label: Sell water at cost — not profiteering, just sustainability
choices.outcome_text: You sell at production cost. No profit. No charity. The camps pay in labor credits and stored goods. It's fair. It feels like less than fair, but it's fair.
choices.epitaph: Sold water at cost. Fair deal. Felt like less than fair.

choices.label: Keep your water — they should have had reserves
choices.outcome_text: You keep your reserve. One camp makes it to the decontamination date. One doesn't. The third relocates. You have clean water and the memory of what that silence sounded like from three camps over.
choices.epitaph: Kept the water. One camp didn't make it. I had clean water the whole time.

quests.trigger: Someone you helped months ago returns with a group — and a demand.
quests.discovery: The man whose leg you splinted on the east road stands at your gate with twelve armed followers. He's not threatening — not exactly. 'You built something here,' he says. 'Something good. I want in. Not as a guest. As a partner. Equal say, equal share.' His twelve are capable, well-fed, and watching your response carefully.

choices.label: Welcome them as partners — strength in numbers
choices.outcome_text: You share the table. His twelve integrate over the following month — slowly, carefully, watching each other learn the rhythms. The shelter doubles in capability. The politics double too.
choices.epitaph: Shared the table with twelve new partners. Doubled the capability. Doubled the politics.

choices.label: Offer residency but not equal governance
choices.outcome_text: You make the terms clear: shelter, food, work — but governance stays as it is. He considers it. His twelve discuss it. Half stay. Half move on. Six capable people is still six capable people.
choices.epitaph: Offered residency without governance. Six stayed. Six moved on. Six is plenty.

choices.label: Decline — ask them to build their own camp under your patrol umbrella
choices.outcome_text: You point them to cleared ground a kilometer south. Under your patrol. Separate governance. He nods — it's fair, and he knows it. Within a month there's a new camp in the corridor. Allied, not absorbed.
choices.epitaph: Pointed them south to build their own. Under my patrol, their own rules. A new camp in the corridor.

choices.label: Turn them away — twelve armed strangers is too many
choices.outcome_text: You close the gate. He doesn't argue. He looks at you the way someone looks at a promise that wasn't made but was understood. His twelve turn east. Another camp gets what you refused.
choices.epitaph: Closed the gate on twelve capable people. He looked at me like a broken promise. They went east.

quests.trigger: A dying raider begs you to take a message to his daughter — who lives in the camp that raided you.
quests.discovery: He's bleeding out from a patrol encounter — your patrol, your bullet, your responsibility in some arithmetic. 'My daughter,' he gasps. 'In Harrow Camp. Tell her... tell her I'm sorry I wasn't better.' Harrow Camp is the one that robbed your stores. His daughter is there. The message is all he has left to give.

choices.label: Promise to deliver the message — and keep the promise
choices.outcome_text: You find his daughter at Harrow Camp. She's sixteen, hard-faced, and cries when you say the words. She asks who you are. You tell her. She asks why. You don't have an answer good enough. She nods anyway.
choices.epitaph: Carried a dead raider's message to his daughter in the camp that robbed me. She cried. She asked why. I had no answer.

choices.label: Promise — but deliver the message through an intermediary
choices.outcome_text: You send the message with a trader headed to Harrow. Secondhand mercy. It arrives. Whether it arrives whole is between the trader and the girl.
choices.epitaph: Sent the message through a trader. Secondhand mercy. I hope it arrived whole.

choices.label: Stay with him until the end, but don't promise the message
choices.outcome_text: You hold his hand while he goes. The message stays undelivered. His daughter never knows the words. But he didn't die alone. That's what you gave instead.
choices.epitaph: Held his hand while he went. Didn't promise the message. Gave him company instead of delivery.

choices.label: Walk away — he's a raider, his people robbed you
choices.outcome_text: You leave him on the road. His blood is still warm when you walk away. The message dies with him. His daughter will wonder, for years, what the end looked like.
choices.epitaph: Left the raider on the road with his message unspoken. His daughter will wonder forever.

quests.trigger: Your shelter votes to expel a family accused of hoarding. You have the deciding vote.
quests.discovery: The Brennan family — father, mother, teenage son — stands accused of hiding food in their quarters. The evidence is circumstantial: extra weight, closed doors, a neighbor's suspicion. The vote is split. Yours is the deciding voice. Expulsion means the wasteland. Staying means doubt infects the shelter.

choices.label: Vote to keep them — investigate properly first
choices.outcome_text: You buy them time. The investigation finds a jar of preserved peaches — not hoarding, grief. The mother preserved them on her daughter's birthday. The daughter didn't survive the exchange. The jar is shared at the next meal. Nobody mentions it again.
choices.epitaph: Voted to investigate before expelling. Found a jar of peaches. Grief, not hoarding. Shared at the next meal.

choices.label: Vote to keep them with strict monitoring
choices.outcome_text: They stay, under watch. The suspicion fades when no evidence surfaces. The family never quite trusts the shelter again. But they survive.
choices.epitaph: Kept the family under monitoring. Suspicion faded. Trust didn't fully return.

choices.label: Abstain — refuse to cast the deciding vote
choices.outcome_text: You abstain. The vote fails by default — they stay. But everyone knows you dodged it. The family stays. The trust doesn't.
choices.epitaph: Abstained from the vote. They stayed by default. Everyone noticed the dodge.

choices.label: Vote to expel — the shelter's trust must be maintained
choices.outcome_text: You vote out. The Brennan family packs in silence. The son looks at you once — a look that files itself away for later. They walk into the wasteland with a jar of peaches nobody searched for.
choices.epitaph: Voted to expel the family. They left carrying a jar of peaches. I didn't know what it was until later.

quests.trigger: Your medic contracts the sickness from the quarantine patients. She asks you not to tell anyone.
quests.discovery: She shows you her hands — the spots, unmistakable. 'I was careful,' she says. 'It wasn't enough.' She wants to keep working. Says she has weeks before it gets bad. Says the shelter needs her more than it needs the truth. Her eyes say: don't take this from me.

choices.label: Keep her secret and let her work
choices.outcome_text: You say nothing. She works another eighteen days before the cough gives her away. By then, three people she treated have been exposed. Two survive. One doesn't. She survives. The cost lives in her face.
choices.epitaph: Kept the medic's secret. She worked eighteen more days. The cost came due. She carries it.

choices.label: Tell the shelter but advocate for her to keep working in isolation
choices.outcome_text: You tell them. The fear flashes through camp like voltage. But you stand for her — isolated work, masked, limited contact. She saves two more lives from behind a sheet wall. The shelter learns that mercy has logistics.
choices.epitaph: Told the shelter the truth. Advocated for isolated work. She saved two more lives from behind a sheet wall.

choices.label: Quarantine her immediately — no exceptions
choices.outcome_text: You quarantine her. By the book. She doesn't argue. The infirmary runs worse without her, and two people die of things she would have caught. She recovers. Returns. Doesn't quite look at you the same.
choices.epitaph: Quarantined the medic by the book. Two people died of things she would have caught. She recovered. Doesn't look at me the same.

choices.label: Expel her — the risk is too high
choices.outcome_text: You tell her to leave. She packs her kit in silence. The infirmary door closes behind her. She walks south. The shelter is safe. The shelter is also poorer, meaner, smaller.
choices.epitaph: Expelled the medic who caught the plague treating patients I brought in. The shelter is safer. And smaller.

quests.trigger: The three camps you protected send a delegation with a gift — their last working generator.
quests.discovery: Three people stand at your gate with a generator on a cart. 'You protected us,' the eldest says. 'You shared water when the well was poisoned. This is what we have.' It's their last working power source. Taking it strengthens you. Refusing it insults them. The gift has weight beyond watts.

choices.label: Accept graciously and offer shared access to the power
choices.outcome_text: You accept the generator and immediately offer a power-sharing schedule — your shelter charges their batteries every third day. The gift becomes a bridge. The bridge carries more than electricity.
choices.epitaph: Accepted the generator. Offered power-sharing every third day. The gift became a bridge.

choices.label: Refuse — they need it more than you do
choices.outcome_text: You push the cart back gently. 'Keep it. I didn't help you for payment.' The eldest tears up. They wheel it home. Your shelter stays dark. But the relationship deepens beyond transaction.
choices.epitaph: Refused the generator. Told them help isn't payment. They wheeled it home. The relationship grew.

choices.label: Accept but give them your spare solar panel in exchange
choices.outcome_text: You take the generator and give the panel. Even trade, no obligation. Clean. They nod, satisfied. Commerce, not charity — and both of you stronger.
choices.epitaph: Traded generator for solar panel. Even exchange. Both stronger. No debt.

choices.label: Accept without reciprocation — you earned it
choices.outcome_text: You take the generator. Thank them. Close the gate. They leave lighter and you leave brighter. It was earned. The arithmetic is clean. But something in the eldest's eyes wanted more than arithmetic.
choices.epitaph: Took the generator. Thanked them. Closed the gate. Earned is earned.

quests.trigger: Your medic has one dose of anti-radiation chelation. Two people need it. One is your scout. One is a stranger's child.
quests.discovery: One dose. Your scout — loyal, skilled, thirty-two years old, exposed on patrol three days ago. A stranger's daughter — seven, exposed when her camp's shielding failed. The medic says both will develop acute syndrome without treatment. One dose. Two bodies. The math breaks before you reach the answer.

choices.label: Give it to the child — children first, always
choices.outcome_text: The child receives the dose. Your scout watches, nods once, and says: 'Right choice.' He manages his symptoms with rest and clean water. He lives, diminished. She lives, whole. He never holds it against you.
choices.epitaph: Gave the chelation to the child. The scout nodded and said 'right choice.' He lived, diminished. She lived, whole.

choices.label: Give it to the scout — he serves the shelter
choices.outcome_text: Your scout recovers fully. The child's father carries her south to the clinic. Whether she makes it is between the road and her blood. Your scout patrols the next morning. The math was correct. The feeling wasn't.
choices.epitaph: Gave the dose to my scout. The child went south. The math was correct. The feeling wasn't.

choices.label: Split the dose — half efficacy for both
choices.outcome_text: The medic splits it against protocol. Half-dose for each. Both survive with moderate symptoms. Neither is whole. Neither is dead. The medic doesn't recommend it again.
choices.epitaph: Split the dose. Both survived with symptoms. Neither whole, neither dead. The medic won't do it again.

choices.label: Let the medic decide — it's not your call
choices.outcome_text: You step back. The medic gives it to the child without hesitation. 'Children first,' she says. 'That's not a debate.' Your scout nods. You wonder what it means that you couldn't decide.
choices.epitaph: Let the medic choose. She chose the child without hesitation. My scout nodded. I wonder about my hesitation.

quests.trigger: A faction you've never met offers an alliance — based entirely on the stories about you.
quests.discovery: A delegation from the Crossroads Collective arrives. You've never met them. They've heard of you — the open gate, the water sharing, the patrol pact, the plague quarantine. 'We want to be part of what you're building,' their leader says. 'Not above it. Part of it.' They control a trade route you desperately need.

choices.label: Accept the alliance on equal terms
choices.outcome_text: The Crossroads Collective joins the pact. Their trade route opens. Your corridor stretches from the ridge to the southern water. For the first time, what you built feels like it might be called a community.
choices.epitaph: Allied with the Crossroads Collective. Their trade route opened. What I built might be a community now.

choices.label: Accept with verification — trust but verify
choices.outcome_text: You accept pending a thirty-day trial. They agree without offense. By day fifteen, their caravans run your route. By day thirty, the trial is a formality.
choices.epitaph: Trial alliance for thirty days. By day fifteen, it was already real.

choices.label: Decline — alliances based on reputation are fragile
choices.outcome_text: You decline politely. They leave without rancor. The trade route stays closed. Your corridor stays what it is. Sometimes refusing growth is a kind of honesty.
choices.epitaph: Declined the Collective's offer. Reputation isn't the same as knowing someone. The route stays closed.

choices.label: Exploit the opportunity — demand favorable trade terms
choices.outcome_text: You leverage your reputation into a lopsided deal. They agree — barely. The alliance starts with a taste of resentment that never quite fades. You got the route. You lost the equal footing.
choices.epitaph: Leveraged my reputation into a better deal. Got the route. Lost the equity.

quests.trigger: A raider captain defects and asks to join your community — with intelligence about a planned attack on your corridor.
quests.discovery: He arrives alone, unarmed, hands visible. Former raider captain — you recognize the scars. 'I'm done with it,' he says. 'And I know what they're planning for your eastern corridor. I'll tell you everything. But I want a place here. A real place. Not a cell.'

choices.label: Accept him — everyone deserves a second chance
choices.outcome_text: He tells you everything. The attack is planned for next Thursday, eastern approach, twenty raiders. You prepare. The attack comes and breaks against your foreknowledge like water on stone. He earns his place in the weeks after — slowly, watching his own hands for the old habits.
choices.epitaph: Accepted the defector. His intelligence saved the corridor. He watches his own hands for old habits.

choices.label: Take the intelligence but house him outside the walls
choices.outcome_text: He talks. You listen. The attack fails. He lives outside the walls in a small structure. Close enough to see the community. Far enough that the community can pretend not to see him. Liminal. Earned, but unfinished.
choices.epitaph: Took his intelligence. Housed him outside the walls. Close enough to see us. Far enough to not quite belong.

choices.label: Take the intelligence and send him away
choices.outcome_text: He talks. You use it. You send him east with supplies and thanks. The attack fails. He vanishes into the wasteland with good information and no home. The transaction is complete.
choices.epitaph: Used his intelligence. Sent him away. Transaction complete. No home for him in any of it.

choices.label: Refuse — it's a trap
choices.outcome_text: You turn him away. The attack comes Thursday as he warned. You're unprepared. Three people die on the eastern wall. You'll wonder, for months, whether the paranoia was worth three lives.
choices.epitaph: Turned away the defector. The attack came Thursday. Three died. Paranoia cost three lives.

quests.trigger: Winter closes in. You have enough food for your people — barely. Three allied camps are short.
quests.discovery: The count is precise: sixty-three days of food for your shelter at current population. Winter will last seventy. The three allied camps are worse — forty days, maybe less. You can stretch yours to cover the gap. Or you can protect your own and hope the thaw comes early.

choices.label: Redistribute evenly across all camps — everyone makes it or nobody does
choices.outcome_text: You level the stores. Everyone goes to half-rations for the last two weeks. Everyone makes it. The hunger is shared, and shared hunger builds something that full bellies never do.
choices.epitaph: Leveled the stores across all camps. Half-rations for two weeks. Everyone made it. Shared hunger built something.

choices.label: Share your surplus but keep your safety margin
choices.outcome_text: You share the gap between sixty-three and seventy — seven days of food. The camps stretch it. One comes close to the edge. But everyone lives.
choices.epitaph: Shared seven days of surplus. Everyone lived. One camp came close to the edge.

choices.label: Organize a joint hunting/foraging expedition
choices.outcome_text: You gather hunters from all four camps. The winter forest gives reluctantly, but it gives. Enough to close the gap for the weakest camp. Not charity — cooperation.
choices.epitaph: Organized a joint hunt. The winter forest gave reluctantly. Enough to close the gap.

choices.label: Keep your stores — they should have planned better
choices.outcome_text: You keep your sixty-three days intact. One allied camp doesn't make it to thaw. The other two barely survive. The alliance survives on paper. The trust doesn't survive the memory.
choices.epitaph: Kept my stores. One camp didn't make it to thaw. The alliance survived on paper. Trust didn't.

quests.trigger: An ally offers to sacrifice themselves to draw raiders away from your community during an assault.
quests.discovery: Joss — the scout whose leg you treated, the man who brought twelve people to your gate — stands in front of you with a plan. 'I go east, loud, fast. They follow me. You hit them from behind.' He knows what 'they follow me' means. He's not asking permission. He's asking if you'll let him.

choices.label: Refuse — find another way
choices.outcome_text: You refuse. It takes six more hours to plan a flanking approach that doesn't require bait. It's messier. Two people are injured. Nobody dies. Joss looks at you afterward like you gave him something he didn't know he needed.
choices.epitaph: Refused the sacrifice. Found another way. Messier, longer, two injured. Nobody died. Joss looked at me like I gave him something.

choices.label: Accept — his choice, his right
choices.outcome_text: He goes east. They follow. You hit from behind. The assault breaks. Joss makes it back — barely, bleeding, crawling the last hundred meters. He lives. This time. The next plan like this might not end the same.
choices.epitaph: Let Joss run the decoy. He made it back. Barely. This time.

choices.label: Go yourself instead — you won't ask others to die for you
choices.outcome_text: You take the decoy run. East, loud, fast. They follow. Your people hit from behind. You run until your lungs burn, then you run further. You make it back at dawn, and Joss is waiting at the gate with water and the look of a man whose faith was just confirmed.
choices.epitaph: Ran the decoy myself. East, loud, fast. Made it back at dawn. Joss was waiting with water.

choices.label: Negotiate with the raiders instead — maybe there's a deal
choices.outcome_text: You send a runner with terms. The raiders consider it. They want twenty percent of your next harvest. You agree. The assault never comes. The cost is measured in grain, not blood. Joss is relieved. You feel the chain of the deal every time you look at the fields.
choices.epitaph: Negotiated with the raiders. Twenty percent of the harvest. No blood. The chain of the deal hangs in the fields.

quests.trigger: Your community asks you to judge a murder case — a man killed a raider who surrendered.
quests.discovery: Tomas killed a raider who had dropped his weapon. The raider was on his knees. Tomas put a bullet in him anyway. 'He killed my brother,' Tomas says. 'Last winter. On the east road.' The community wants justice. Some want blood. Some want mercy. They all want you to decide.

choices.label: Exile, not execution — we don't kill surrendered people
choices.outcome_text: You exile Tomas. He accepts it — barely. The community exhales. A line has been drawn: we don't kill the helpless, even when we understand why someone would. Tomas walks east. He doesn't look back.
choices.epitaph: Exiled Tomas for killing a surrendered man. The community drew a line. We don't kill the helpless.

choices.label: Community service — he works off the debt to community trust
choices.outcome_text: Six months of heavy labor: wall repair, latrine duty, the jobs nobody wants. Tomas accepts. The community watches. By month four, most have forgiven. The raider's friends haven't. But the line holds.
choices.epitaph: Sentenced Tomas to six months of hard community labor. Most forgave by month four. The line held.

choices.label: Acquit — the raider killed his brother, it was justice
choices.outcome_text: You acquit him. Half the community nods. The other half goes quiet. The line — whatever it was — blurs. The next time a surrendered enemy appears, the hesitation is gone from people's hands.
choices.epitaph: Acquitted Tomas. Called it justice. Half the community nodded. The other half noticed the line blur.

choices.label: Execute Tomas — murder is murder regardless of motive
choices.outcome_text: You order the execution. It happens at dawn. Half the community watches. Half doesn't. The line is drawn in the hardest ink possible. Nobody kills a surrendered person again. Nobody quite trusts the judge's seat again either.
choices.epitaph: Executed Tomas at dawn. Nobody kills a surrendered person here anymore. Nobody trusts the judge's seat either.

quests.trigger: A delegation arrives asking you to mediate a dispute between two warring camps — because of who you've become.
quests.discovery: Two camps — Ridgeline and Hollow Creek — have been shooting at each other for three weeks over a water access dispute. Fourteen dead. They ask you to mediate because your name carries weight. If you fail, both camps blame you. If you refuse, the shooting continues.

choices.label: Mediate — sit between them until they find words instead of bullets
choices.outcome_text: Four days of talking. Two of silence. On the seventh day, a water-sharing schedule that neither loves and both can live with. The shooting stops. Fourteen graves stay fresh. But no fifteenth.
choices.epitaph: Mediated for seven days. Found a water schedule nobody loved and everyone lived with. The shooting stopped.

choices.label: Mediate with force — bring your patrol as enforcement
choices.outcome_text: Your patrol stands between them while you talk. The guns are real and so is the authority. The deal happens in two days — faster, cleaner, backed by the implicit threat of a third party that won't take sides. Peace through strength. It holds.
choices.epitaph: Brought the patrol. Peace in two days. Backed by guns. It holds.

choices.label: Offer to mediate but set strict terms — both sides disarm first
choices.outcome_text: Both sides disarm. It takes a day of arguing just to get the guns stacked. Then the talking starts. Without weapons, the words come differently. The deal takes five days and holds better than anything built at gunpoint.
choices.epitaph: Made them disarm first. The talking changed without weapons. Five days. Solid deal.

choices.label: Refuse to mediate — not your fight
choices.outcome_text: You decline. The shooting continues for two more weeks. Twenty-three dead total when one camp finally breaks and relocates. Your name loses weight in the corridor. The delegation looks at you differently after.
choices.epitaph: Refused to mediate. Twenty-three dead when it finally ended. My name lost weight.

quests.trigger: A young man you mentored commits a terrible act — and comes to you for absolution.
quests.discovery: Darin — the teenager you took in years ago, taught to scout, gave purpose — stands in your doorway with blood on his shirt. Not his blood. 'I killed someone,' he says. 'They were begging me to stop and I didn't stop.' He looks at you the way children look at the one person whose judgment matters.

choices.label: Hold him accountable — the same rules apply to everyone you love
choices.outcome_text: You hold him to the same standard you held Tomas. He accepts it. He cries. You cry too, later, where nobody sees. The community watches you judge your own, and the line holds harder than ever.
choices.epitaph: Held Darin to the same standard. Judged my own. Cried later where nobody saw. The line held.

choices.label: Protect him — send him away quietly before anyone knows
choices.outcome_text: You give him supplies and a direction. Nobody asks where Darin went. But the blood on the shirt, the missing person in the corridor — someone will connect it eventually. The mercy you gave him costs the mercy others gave you.
choices.epitaph: Sent Darin away quietly. Protected my own. The blood will connect eventually.

choices.label: Listen to the full story before deciding
choices.outcome_text: You sit him down. You hear it — all of it. The context changes the shape but not the core. He killed someone who was surrendering. The motive was fear, not cruelty. You judge accordingly: exile with the right to earn return. He walks out knowing the door isn't permanently closed.
choices.epitaph: Heard the full story. Exiled with the right to earn return. The door isn't closed. But he has to find it again.

choices.label: Disown him — you will not be responsible for what he became
choices.outcome_text: You tell him he's not your responsibility anymore. The words break something in his face that was yours to build. He leaves. The community doesn't know the details. You do. That's enough weight for one lifetime.
choices.epitaph: Disowned Darin. The words broke something in his face. I built that thing. I broke it.

quests.trigger: The second winter is worse. The coalition you built faces collapse unless someone takes less.
quests.discovery: The harvest failed in two of four camps. The coalition is three months from starvation unless someone takes less than their share. Your camp has the most stored. The math is simple: if you give away forty percent of your reserves, everyone survives. If you don't, two camps die. Your people are scared. They didn't build these reserves to give them away.

choices.label: Give the forty percent — the coalition survives together or not at all
choices.outcome_text: You stand in front of your people and tell them what the math says. Some cry. Some curse. But you've built enough trust that they follow. The winter is brutal. The rations are thin. But in spring, four camps stand. And four camps remember who held them up.
choices.epitaph: Gave away forty percent. The winter was brutal. In spring, four camps stood. They remember who held them up.

choices.label: Give thirty percent and organize emergency foraging
choices.outcome_text: Thirty percent plus organized foraging. It's not enough — barely — but combined with strict rationing across all camps, it closes the gap. One camp loses four people to weakness-related illness. But the coalition holds.
choices.epitaph: Thirty percent plus foraging. One camp lost four people. The coalition held. Barely.

choices.label: Propose each camp sacrifices equally — proportional sharing
choices.outcome_text: Equal sacrifice sounds fair. In practice, it means the weakest camp gives what it can't afford. Two people die there. Your contribution is smaller than it should be. The math was proportional. The outcome wasn't.
choices.epitaph: Proposed proportional sharing. Sounded fair. The weakest camp paid the highest price.

choices.label: Keep your reserves — your people come first
choices.outcome_text: You keep the reserves. Two camps collapse before spring. The coalition dissolves. The survivors scatter to your shelter and the Collective — broken, hungry, blaming. Your stores last the winter. The coalition doesn't.
choices.epitaph: Kept my reserves. Two camps collapsed. The coalition died. My stores lasted. My name didn't.

quests.trigger: The coalition asks you to formalize the rules you've been living by — to write a code for all camps.
quests.discovery: The leaders of six camps sit in your meeting room. They want a written code — the rules that held the corridor together through plague, famine, and war. They want it in your words. They want it binding. This is the moment where instinct becomes law, where kindness becomes obligation, where mercy becomes doctrine.

choices.label: Write the code — mercy as obligation, help as law
choices.outcome_text: You write it in three nights. Seven articles. No camp turns away children. No camp hoards beyond sixty days of reserves. Shared water in crisis. Shared patrol in threat. Medical aid crosses all boundaries. It's imperfect. It's binding. It's more than existed before.
choices.epitaph: Wrote the code in three nights. Seven articles. Imperfect, binding, more than existed before.

choices.label: Suggest guiding principles instead of rigid law
choices.outcome_text: You refuse to write rules. Instead: principles. 'Help when you can. Share when it costs you something. Defend what cannot defend itself.' Looser. More fragile. But less likely to become the weapon that rigid law always becomes.
choices.epitaph: Offered principles instead of law. Looser, more fragile, less likely to become a weapon.

choices.label: Agree to write it but include enforcement mechanisms
choices.outcome_text: You write the code with teeth: violations mean expulsion from the coalition, loss of patrol protection, trade embargo. It's effective. It's also the first time mercy carries a threat. Something in the room changes when you read the enforcement clause.
choices.epitaph: Wrote the code with enforcement teeth. Effective. The first time mercy carried a threat.

choices.label: Decline — codes become cages
choices.outcome_text: You refuse. 'What we've built works because people choose it,' you say. 'The moment it's law, it's no longer mercy — it's compliance.' Some nod. Some look disappointed. The coalition continues without a code. It works. Until the day it doesn't.
choices.epitaph: Refused to write the code. Mercy chosen is different from mercy compelled. The coalition continues. For now.

quests.trigger: You're injured badly on patrol. The community needs to know who leads if you can't.
quests.discovery: The bullet took a piece of your shoulder that doesn't grow back. You'll recover — mostly. But the corridor held its breath when you fell, and the breath told everyone the same thing: there's no second you. The community needs a succession plan. Someone to carry what you built.

choices.label: Name the medic — she understands mercy better than anyone
choices.outcome_text: You name her in front of the community. She doesn't want it. She accepts it. The corridor exhales. The line of succession is clear, and it runs through the one person who chose to come here because of what you built.
choices.epitaph: Named the medic as successor. She didn't want it. She accepted it. The corridor exhaled.

choices.label: Name the defector Joss — redemption made complete
choices.outcome_text: You name Joss. The room goes quiet. A former raider captain, leading the mercy corridor. He stands, and you see in his face that he understands what this is: the full circle. Not everyone approves. But enough do.
choices.epitaph: Named Joss as successor. A former raider captain leading the mercy corridor. Full circle.

choices.label: Propose community elections — no single leader
choices.outcome_text: You abolish the single-leader model. Elections every six months. A council of three. It's messier. Slower. More resilient. The corridor becomes something that doesn't need you to hold its shape.
choices.epitaph: Proposed elections. A council of three. Messier, slower, more resilient. Doesn't need me.

choices.label: Say nothing — the community will figure it out when the time comes
choices.outcome_text: You say nothing. Recovery fills the silence. But the question hangs in the air, and when you walk the corridor afterward, people look at you differently — as a problem they'll have to solve someday, not just a leader.
choices.epitaph: Said nothing about succession. They look at me differently now. A problem they'll have to solve.

quests.trigger: A year has passed. The corridor is stable. You sit at the fire and someone asks: 'Was it worth it?'
quests.discovery: The fire burns low. The corridor stretches from ridge to water — six camps, two hundred people, a code that mostly works. Your shoulder aches where the bullet lives. Your stores are always thinner than you'd like. But children run between camps without fear. The road is walked, not avoided. A young man sits beside you and asks: 'You gave up a lot for this. Was it worth it?'

choices.label: 'Yes. Every time.'
choices.outcome_text: You say it without hesitation. The young man nods. The fire crackles. Somewhere in the corridor, a child laughs at something you can't hear. You didn't build this for the gratitude. You built it because the alternative was the road you walked before — alone, hard, empty. This is better. Not perfect. Better.
choices.epitaph: Was it worth it? Yes. Every time. A child laughed somewhere in the corridor. This is better.

choices.label: 'I don't know. But I'd do it again.'
choices.outcome_text: Honesty. You don't know if it was worth it. The bullet, the hunger, the betrayals, the weight. But you'd do it again because the alternative — watching and doing nothing — was never an option your body would accept.
choices.epitaph: Was it worth it? I don't know. But I'd do it again. The alternative was never in me.

choices.label: 'Ask me in another year.'
choices.outcome_text: You defer. Not because you don't know. Because the answer changes with the season, with the rations, with the faces at the gate. Today, yes. Tomorrow is tomorrow's question.
choices.epitaph: Was it worth it? Ask me in another year. The answer changes with the season.

choices.label: 'No. But it was necessary.'
choices.outcome_text: You say it flat. Not worth it — not for you. The cost was real, permanent, personal. But necessary. The corridor needed building. You were the one in position to build it. Worth and necessity aren't the same word.
choices.epitaph: Was it worth it? No. But it was necessary. Worth and necessity aren't the same word.

quests.trigger: You discover an elderly survivor has been hoarding water filters while the shelter's common supply runs dry.
quests.discovery: Maren's hands shake when she unlocks the cellar door. Behind the canned peaches and moth-eaten blankets, you count eleven ceramic filters — enough for a family for a year. She watches you count them. Her grandson coughs in the next room, a wet sound that doesn't stop. She says nothing. She doesn't have to.

choices.label: Take the filters. Tell her you'll distribute them fairly through the shelter.
choices.outcome_text: You carry them out in your pack. Maren doesn't argue. That night, you hand out filters to twelve families — including your own. The shelter council thanks you. Maren's grandson drinks unfiltered water. He stops coughing three days later. Not because he's better.
choices.epitaph: I told myself it was for the many. The math was clean. The boy wasn't.

choices.label: Offer to trade — your labor for a fair split. Keep her dignity intact.
choices.outcome_text: You spend two days fixing her roof in exchange for three filters. She wraps them in cloth and hands them to you herself. The shelter gets three more filters than it had yesterday. Maren's grandson drinks clean water. You drink clean water. Nobody owes anyone anything. It feels like a luxury.
choices.epitaph: Three filters. Two days of work. One old woman who still looked me in the eye.

choices.label: Report her to the shelter council. Let them decide what's 'fair.'
choices.outcome_text: The council votes. Seven filters confiscated, four left to Maren. She complies quietly. Her grandson gets two of the four. You watch the vote from the back of the room and notice nobody looked at you while it happened. The council chair shakes your hand afterward. Her grip is damp.
choices.epitaph: I let seven people decide for one. Easier than deciding myself, I told myself.

choices.label: Say nothing. Her resources are her business.
choices.outcome_text: You close the cellar door. Maren watches you walk away and something in her shoulders drops — not relief exactly, but the absence of a different kind of tension. The shelter's water problem continues. You drink your ration and taste the rust. Other people's grandchildren drink the same.
choices.epitaph: I walked past eleven filters and a dying child. I still sleep. Mostly.

quests.trigger: A wounded stranger collapses at your perimeter. They're carrying a map marked with supply caches.
quests.discovery: He bleeds out against the concrete barrier, a through-and-through in the abdomen that you can see breathing. His fingers keep pressing at the wound as if he could push himself back together. With his other hand, he holds a folded map — you can see the edges, marked in red pencil. Supply caches. At least four of them. His name is Dex. He doesn't offer it. He asks for water.

choices.label: Give him water. Take the map. Let him go.
choices.outcome_text: You uncork your canteen and hold it while he drinks. His hands are steady enough for that much. When he's done, you take the map from his lap. He doesn't resist — he doesn't have the strength or the leverage. You bandage the wound poorly and point him east. He walks for twenty meters before he sits down. You have the map. He has a chance. Neither of you believes it's a fair trade.
choices.epitaph: He drank. I took. He walked. I don't know if he made it. I don't go back to check.

choices.label: Tend the wound properly. Earn his trust. Learn where the caches really are.
choices.outcome_text: You clean the wound with boiled water and pack it with the last of your antibiotic paste. Dex talks because you gave him a reason to. The map has four caches marked, but he tells you about a fifth — one he didn't draw, kept for emergencies. You take him to the shelter. He recovers slowly. The fifth cache is real.
choices.epitaph: Antibiotic paste costs more than water. So does trust. Both were worth it.

choices.label: Take the map. He won't need it where he's going.
choices.outcome_text: You slide the map from under his fingers while he's drinking. He's too far gone to stop you and too dehydrated to shout. You leave him the rest of your canteen — not out of mercy, but because a corpse at your perimeter draws attention. He dies around midnight. You're already at the first cache by dawn. The red pencil marks are precise. He knew this terrain.
choices.epitaph: Four caches by sunrise. One body by moonrise. The math doesn't keep me up. The silence does.

quests.trigger: A family of four arrives at the shelter gate. They have nothing. They're asking for work.
quests.discovery: The father speaks. The mother doesn't look up — she's counting the children with her eyes, the way parents do when they're making sure the number hasn't changed. They've walked three days from a collapsed settlement to the south. They have no tools, no trade goods, no skills beyond farming and the father's half-trained knowledge of basic carpentry. The shelter has work. The shelter also has forty mouths already and a grain bin that shows the bottom some mornings.

choices.label: Take them in. Full rations. They'll earn their keep.
choices.outcome_text: You assign the father to repairs, the mother to the kitchen. The children — eight and eleven — carry water. Within a week, the father has reinforced the east wall with scrap lumber. The mother stretches every ration by a tenth. The grain bin still shows the bottom, but now there are hands to scrape it cleaner. You eat the same amount. Everyone else eats slightly more. Nobody mentions the arithmetic.
choices.epitaph: Four more mouths. Six more hands. The math worked this time. It won't always.

choices.label: Offer work — but half rations until they've proven themselves.
choices.outcome_text: The father's jaw tightens but he nods. The mother finally looks up. She asks if the children get full rations. You say yes. She nods too. They work. The father builds. The mother cooks. After two weeks, you raise them to full rations. The children have gotten thinner in the interim. The mother notices everything. She says nothing about it. That's worse than if she'd shouted.
choices.epitaph: Two weeks of half rations. The children didn't complain. Parents notice that kind of thing.

choices.label: Tell them you can't help. Point them toward the eastern road.
choices.outcome_text: You close the gate. Through the gap, you watch the father pick up the youngest and the mother take the oldest's hand. They walk east. The mother doesn't look back. The father does, once, at the bend. Three days later, you hear that the eastern road leads to a settlement that's been raiding caravans. You don't know if that's the family you turned away. You don't go looking to find out.
choices.epitaph: I pointed east. I don't know what's east. I chose not to know.

choices.label: Take only the father. He has useful skills. The rest can wait outside.
choices.outcome_text: The father looks at you for a long time. Then he looks at his wife. She gives the smallest nod — the kind that means go, not the kind that means it's alright. He comes inside. You hear the children asking questions as the gate closes. The father builds you a proper workshop in three days. He doesn't speak unless spoken to. On the fifth morning, he asks if his family can come in. You say you'll consider it. He doesn't ask again.
choices.epitaph: A carpenter without a family builds faster. He also builds nothing worth coming home to.

quests.trigger: A member of a rival settlement approaches you with information — and a price.
quests.discovery: Her name is Sable. She sits across from you in the neutral ground between the two settlements, a burnt-out convenience store with no roof and one wall still standing. She says she can tell you when the Kessler group moves their supplies, where their watch schedule has gaps, which of their people are growing restless. She wants antibiotics for her sister. She wants them tomorrow. She says the information is worth more than medicine because information doesn't run out. You notice she hasn't blinked in a while.

choices.label: Pay her price. Full antibiotics course. Information is power.
choices.outcome_text: You hand over the pills — half your remaining stock. Sable counts them before she pockets them. Over the next week, she delivers: supply movements, guard rotations, three names of people in Kessler's group who might flip. The intelligence is good. You restructure your own patrols around it. Kessler loses two trade caravans to 'bad luck' on the eastern road. He doesn't know you know his schedule. Sable's sister improves. Sable keeps talking.
choices.epitaph: I bought a spy with medicine. Her sister lived. Kessler didn't notice the holes until they were too big to patch.

choices.label: Counter-offer: partial payment, ongoing arrangement. Make her dependent.
choices.outcome_text: You give her three pills — enough for two days. Tell her the rest comes with each delivery. Sable's eyes go flat. She understands the arrangement. Over the following weeks, she brings you intelligence regularly. Her sister's condition stabilizes but doesn't improve. Sable starts bringing you information about her own group's internal disputes — things she wasn't asked for, things that suggest she's trying to prove her value. You've created a dependency and then exploited it. She knows this. You both know this.
choices.epitaph: Three pills at a time. Enough to keep hope alive, not enough to close the deal. She hates me. She needs me. That's the same thing now.

choices.label: Refuse. Using her would make you no better than the people she's betraying.
choices.outcome_text: You stand up. Tell her you don't trade in people's secrets for their sister's life. Sable stares at you. Then she laughs — one short bark that echoes off the remaining wall. She says nobody's offered to help without a price in four months. You don't have antibiotics to spare, but you have a contact at the water station who trades in medical supplies. You write down a name and a location. Sable looks at the paper like it might bite her. She walks out. You never learn what she knew about Kessler. You sleep well.
choices.epitaph: I gave her a name instead of taking hers. The water station contact came through. I don't know what Sable did with the medicine. I hope her sister is breathing.

quests.trigger: You discover a rival group's supply route runs through territory you can control.
quests.discovery: The trail is obvious once you know to look — boot prints worn into the same deer path, broken branches at head height, a cigarette butt crushed into the mud every forty meters like breadcrumbs. The Kessler group has been running supplies from the military outpost to their main camp through a narrow ravine that sits just inside your effective range. Three trips a week. Predictable. Undefended. You could end their supply line in an afternoon. Or you could do something more interesting with the information.

choices.label: Ambush the next run. Take the supplies. Send a message.
choices.outcome_text: You wait in the ravine with two people you trust. The Kessler supply team arrives at dawn — four people, two pack animals, armed but not expecting trouble. The confrontation lasts eleven seconds. You take everything: medical supplies, tools, three boxes of canned goods. You leave them with their clothes and one knife between them. The message arrives at Kessler's camp by nightfall. He doubles his guard. He also starts looking for a new route. You've made an enemy more careful, which is worse than an enemy who's merely angry.
choices.epitaph: Four people. Two pack animals. Three boxes of peaches. One knife shared between them. I counted everything. I don't count their faces.

choices.label: Block the route quietly. Force them to come to you for passage.
choices.outcome_text: You don't ambush anyone. Instead, you collapse two sections of the ravine path with carefully placed debris and dig a trench across the flat approach. It takes three days of work. On the fourth day, a Kessler scout appears at your perimeter and asks — politely — about 'temporary passage arrangements.' You charge them twenty percent of every load. They pay. They pay every week after that. Kessler knows who's doing it. He can't prove it's you, and even if he could, the alternative is a longer route through the burn zone. You've built a toll road. The money is clean. The method isn't.
choices.epitaph: Twenty percent. Every week. They call it a passage fee. I call it a business. The ravine doesn't call it anything. The ravine just has a trench now.

choices.label: Sell the route information to a third party — let someone else profit from the chaos.
choices.outcome_text: The peacekeepers at the outpost have been looking for reasons to expand their patrol zone. You sell them the route details — timing, numbers, armaments — framed as a 'security concern.' They intercept the next Kessler supply run with a show of force. No one dies, but Kessler loses two days of supplies to 'inspection.' Kessler blames the peacekeepers. The peacekeepers think they're doing good work. You're three steps removed and completely deniable. The peacekeepers pay you in trade credits. Kessler never suspects you.
choices.epitaph: I sold a road to the people who patrol roads. Everyone got what they wanted except Kessler. That was the point.

choices.label: Leave the route alone. Knowledge is leverage — use it later.
choices.outcome_text: You memorize the pattern and walk away. The information sits in your head like a loaded weapon you haven't pointed at anyone yet. Three weeks later, when Kessler makes an aggressive move at the water station, you remind him — quietly, privately — that you know exactly how his supplies move. He goes very still. Then he makes a concession at the negotiating table that he wouldn't have made otherwise. No one had to bleed. The route was worth more unspent than spent. You keep the knowledge. It appreciates.
choices.epitaph: A bullet is worth one use. A secret is worth every use. I kept the secret. Kessler kept his supplies. We both kept our people.

quests.trigger: A traveling merchant offers you an exclusive trade deal — if you cut off a competing settlement.
quests.discovery: The merchant's name is Voss. He trades out of a reinforced cart pulled by two mules that look better fed than most people in the valley. He has tools, medicine, ammunition, and a smile that suggests he's already calculated your margin. The deal is simple: exclusive trading rights through your territory, favorable prices, priority access to new stock. The condition is equally simple — you stop the Aldric settlement from accessing the eastern trade road. 'They're undercutting me,' Voss says. 'I'd rather do business with someone who understands monopoly.' He doesn't say the word monopoly. He says 'exclusive partnership.'

choices.label: Accept. Block the Aldric settlement's access. Take the exclusive deal.
choices.outcome_text: You station people at the two access points along the eastern road. Aldric's traders arrive, find the road 'closed for safety repairs,' and are directed to a longer alternative that adds two days to their journey. Voss's carts pass through without delay. His prices to you drop fifteen percent. Aldric's people start paying more for everything within a month. Their leader sends a messenger asking what's happened. You send back a polite note about 'temporary security measures.' The messenger doesn't mention your name in his report. He doesn't have to.
choices.epitaph: Fifteen percent cheaper tools. Two extra days for Aldric. The math was simple. The morality wasn't. I chose the math.

choices.label: Counter-propose: you'll take the deal, but Aldric keeps access. You mediate.
choices.outcome_text: Voss doesn't like it. You can see the calculation behind his eyes — he wanted a weapon, not a diplomat. But he agrees to a trial period. You arrange a meeting between Voss and Aldric. The negotiation takes six hours. Aldric agrees to buy certain categories exclusively through Voss in exchange for reduced prices on staples. Voss gets market control. Aldric gets cheaper goods. You get a cut of every transaction as 'facilitation fee.' Everyone benefits. Voss respects you more. Aldric trusts you more. Neither of them realizes you've positioned yourself as the only person both sides need.
choices.epitaph: I didn't build a wall. I built a bridge and charged tolls on both sides. Everyone called it fair. Maybe it was.

choices.label: Refuse. You don't strangle neighbors for a discount.
choices.outcome_text: Voss's smile doesn't change, but something behind it does. He says he understands. He says there are other partners in the valley. He moves his cart through your territory without buying or selling anything. Three days later, you hear he's set up a trading post near Aldric's settlement. Your people start making the longer journey to reach him because his prices are better than anything you can offer. You refused to hurt Aldric. Aldric is now better supplied than you. The moral choice has a moral cost. You pay it.
choices.epitaph: I said no to a monopoly. Voss said no to me. Aldric got the medicine. I got the lesson.

quests.trigger: You learn someone in your group has been sharing information with outsiders.
quests.discovery: It's not a spy — not exactly. It's Callum, one of your scouts, who's been talking to his sister. His sister lives in the Aldric settlement. They trade news the way families do — how he's eating, whether he's safe, what the weather's been like. Except some of what he's shared is operational: your patrol routes, your water rationing schedule, the fact that your grain bin is running low. He doesn't think it's sensitive. His sister doesn't think it's intelligence. But the Aldric leader is observant, and patterns are patterns. Callum is sitting by the fire when you confront him. He doesn't deny it. He says he didn't think it mattered.

choices.label: Expel him. Make it public. Set an example.
choices.outcome_text: You do it at the morning assembly. Callum's face goes through several colors before settling on white. You lay out what he shared, what it could cost, what the precedent means. He's gone within the hour — pack on his back, heading for a settlement that may or may not take him. The message lands: information security is not optional. Three people who were close to Callum stop meeting your eyes. They don't disagree. They're afraid. Fear and loyalty look identical from a distance. You'll take what you can get.
choices.epitaph: He talked to his sister. I made an example of him. The group is quieter now. Quiet isn't the same as loyal.

choices.label: Handle it privately. Reassign him to a role with less access.
choices.outcome_text: You pull Callum aside. Explain what his 'family updates' actually reveal. His face changes when he understands. He didn't think — that's the problem, not malice. You move him to interior maintenance. No patrols, no route knowledge, no access to supply counts. He accepts it quietly. His sister writes to him and he writes back, but the letters go through your mail now. You read them. They're just family news. You tell yourself that's why you stopped checking after the third week. You almost believe it.
choices.epitaph: He didn't mean it. That's what makes it dangerous. I moved him sideways and started reading his mail. I tell myself it's temporary.

choices.label: Use it. Feed Callum false information to pass to his sister — and through her, to Aldric.
choices.outcome_text: You sit down with Callum and explain the situation calmly. Then you explain the alternative: he can continue talking to his sister, but the information flows both ways now. You give him a version of your patrol schedule that's two days offset from reality. You tell him your grain reserves are higher than they are. Callum passes it along because he believes it — he has no reason not to. Three weeks later, Aldric makes a trade offer based on the false supply data. They overestimate your position. You get better terms. Callum never knows he's a conduit. His sister never knows either. The lie travels through love like a virus through blood.
choices.epitaph: I turned a brother into a broadcast tower. He talks to his sister. I talk through him. Aldric hears what I want them to hear. Nobody lied. That's the worst part.

choices.label: Let it continue. Family bonds aren't espionage. Adjust your operational security instead.
choices.outcome_text: You change the things that matter — rotate patrol schedules more frequently, move sensitive supply counts to a need-to-know basis, stop discussing strategy where family members might overhear. Callum keeps writing to his sister. You don't read the letters. The Aldric leader is still observant, but there's less to observe. It costs you efficiency — more compartmentalization means slower decisions — but it costs you less than expelling a good scout over a conversation with his sister. Callum's sister writes back about their mother's garden. Nothing in the letter is intelligence. You're fairly sure.
choices.epitaph: I changed the locks instead of changing the man. His sister's letters are probably just letters. Probably.

quests.trigger: A small settlement asks you to protect them from raiders — for a price.
quests.discovery: The settlement is called Lowfield. Fourteen people, mostly farmers who've turned a collapsed gas station into something resembling a home. They have crops — actual growing crops — a rarity in the contaminated soil of the valley. They also have a problem: a raider group has been hitting them every ten days or so, taking what they want, leaving bruises and threats. Lowfield's leader, a woman named Tess, sits across from you with dirt under her fingernails and exhaustion in her voice. She's offering forty percent of their next harvest in exchange for protection. Permanent protection. She says the word 'permanent' like it costs her something.

choices.label: Accept. Forty percent is steep, but the crops are valuable. Protect them completely.
choices.outcome_text: You station three people at Lowfield permanently. The raiders come on schedule and find armed guards who know the terrain. The confrontation is brief — two raiders down, the rest running. Lowfield's crops are safe. Your people eat better for the next three months. Tess pays the forty percent without complaint the first time. The second time, she asks if there's been any discussion about reducing the rate. You explain that the threat hasn't decreased. She doesn't ask again. Lowfield grows. Your share grows with it. The farmers work harder. Some of them stop making eye contact with your guards.
choices.epitaph: Forty percent. Every harvest. They grow the food. I grow the guards. Nobody calls it a racket. We all know what it is.

choices.label: Accept — but negotiate down to twenty-five percent. They need to stay viable.
choices.outcome_text: Tess blinks when you say twenty-five. She was clearly prepared to agree to forty. You explain that a starving farm doesn't produce much of anything. She agrees quickly — too quickly, as if she's afraid you'll change your mind. Your guards protect Lowfield. The raiders don't come back after the second attempt. The harvest comes in at twenty-five percent, which is still a lot of grain. Tess's people eat. Your people eat. The arrangement holds. After six months, Tess brings you a jar of preserved tomatoes as a 'bonus.' They're the first tomatoes you've seen in a year. They taste like something from before.
choices.epitaph: Twenty-five percent and a jar of tomatoes. The tomatoes weren't part of the deal. That's what made them worth more.

choices.label: Decline. Their problem isn't your problem. You're not running a charity.
choices.outcome_text: Tess leaves without arguing. She expected this, maybe. Three weeks later, the raiders hit Lowfield hard. They take the standing crop and burn what they can't carry. Your scouts report smoke for two days. You don't send anyone. Lowfield's survivors scatter — some head east, some south, a few show up at your perimeter looking hollow. You take in three of them. They work. They don't talk about Lowfield. Neither do you.
choices.epitaph: Fourteen people. One gas station. A field of crops I'll never eat. I said it wasn't my problem. It became three more mouths. The math changed.

choices.label: Offer to help eliminate the raiders — then absorb Lowfield into your group entirely.
choices.outcome_text: You present it as partnership. Your people handle the raider threat. Lowfield joins your settlement — shared resources, shared labor, shared protection. Tess listens. She's smart enough to see what's happening. She asks what happens if she says no. You say you'll understand completely. She says yes. The raiders are eliminated within a week — your people are motivated. Lowfield's crops become your crops. Lowfield's people become your people. They have full rations, real security, and no autonomy. Tess farms. She doesn't lead anymore. Some nights, she sits on the gas station roof and looks south. You don't know what she's looking at. You don't ask.
choices.epitaph: I didn't conquer Lowfield. I invited it in. Tess said yes. She always had a choice. It just wasn't a good one.

quests.trigger: Someone in your group has been stealing — small amounts, but consistently.
quests.discovery: The inventory doesn't lie, even when people do. Three cans of beans missing here. A knife that wasn't where it should be there. A half-roll of medical tape that everyone said was 'probably just misplaced.' The pattern takes two weeks to become clear. The thief is Harlan — one of your original group, someone who helped build the shelter's east wall, who shared his last cigarette during the first winter. He's been taking small amounts and distributing them to a family that isn't part of your settlement: his daughter, her husband, two grandchildren. They live six kilometers south. They're struggling. Harlan hasn't asked for help because asking means admitting the group can't take care of its own. So he's been stealing instead.

choices.label: Confront him publicly. Make the theft known. Let the group decide.
choices.outcome_text: You lay it out at the evening meal. The cans, the knife, the tape. Harlan's face goes through surprise, then shame, then something harder — the expression of a man who's been found out and has decided he doesn't care. He explains about his daughter. Some people nod. Some don't. You put it to a vote. The group decides: expulsion, with a warning that return means worse. Harlan leaves that night. His daughter's family never gets the supplies. Three people who voted for expulsion don't meet your eyes the next morning. The thefts stop. The resentment doesn't.
choices.epitaph: He stole for his grandchildren. I made his theft public. The group voted. The math worked. The feeling didn't.

choices.label: Handle it privately. Offer to help his family through official channels.
choices.outcome_text: You find Harlan alone. You don't accuse — you ask. He breaks before you finish the first question. His daughter's family is down to one meal a day. Her husband can't work after a fall. Harlan couldn't ask because the group's resources are tight and he knew the answer would be no. You tell him the answer is still no — the group can't support an outside family. But you can arrange a trade: Harlan's daughter can come to the settlement two days a week to work in exchange for a separate ration allocation. It's not charity. It's a program. Harlan stops stealing. His daughter comes. The grandchildren eat. The precedent is messy but humane.
choices.epitaph: He stole because he couldn't ask. I listened because I could. His grandchildren eat now. The system bent. It didn't break.

choices.label: Let it continue. He's stealing for family. You'd do the same.
choices.outcome_text: You close the inventory ledger and put it back on the shelf. The missing cans are a rounding error. The knife is replaceable. Harlan's grandchildren are eating because their grandfather is willing to risk expulsion for them. You've done worse for less. The thefts continue at the same small rate. Your inventory shrinks by a percent or two each month. Nobody else notices, or if they do, they don't say anything. You tell yourself it's compassion. Some of it is. Some of it is the knowledge that Harlan would do the same for you.
choices.epitaph: Three cans a week. A knife. Half a roll of tape. I called it compassion. I also called it insurance.

quests.trigger: A respected member of your group is questioning your leadership — openly, loudly, and with supporters.
quests.discovery: Her name is Petra. She was a teacher before the exchange. She still has the voice — the one that carries to the back of a room without shouting. She's been saying things at meetings: that your decisions are getting harder to justify, that the group's morale is dropping, that you've become more interested in control than survival. She's not wrong about all of it. She has six or seven people who nod when she speaks. Not a faction yet. But the architecture of one. She's talking to you now, after a meeting, in front of the others. She's giving you a chance to respond. Her tone is calm. Her eyes aren't.

choices.label: Challenge her to a formal leadership vote. Let the group decide.
choices.outcome_text: You call the vote that evening. Petra is surprised — she expected resistance, not a referendum. The results are clear: fourteen for you, six for Petra, two abstentions. You win. Petra accepts it gracefully. Her supporters accept it less gracefully. Over the following weeks, Petra stops speaking at meetings. Two of her supporters ask to be reassigned to exterior work — anything that keeps them out of the main shelter. You've won the vote. You've also mapped exactly who wasn't with you. The map is more valuable than the victory.
choices.epitaph: Fourteen to six. I won. I also learned exactly who wasn't with me. The vote was the point. The result was just the excuse.

choices.label: Acknowledge her concerns publicly. Adjust course. Bring her into the decision-making.
choices.outcome_text: You tell the group Petra has a point. You name specific decisions that could have been handled better — the Lowfield arrangement, the information security protocols, the ration adjustments. You propose a council: three elected members who review major decisions before implementation. Petra's expression shifts from adversarial to cautious to something like respect. She agrees to serve on the council. The first decision she reviews is one she would have voted against — and she votes for it, with amendments. It's better than your original plan. The group notices. Your authority is slightly diminished. The group's decisions are slightly improved. You learn to live with the trade.
choices.epitaph: I gave up absolute authority and got better decisions. Petra gave up opposition and got a seat at the table. We both lost something. We both gained more.
