choices.label: Undermine her quietly. Question her loyalty. Let her supporters drift away.
choices.outcome_text: You don't confront her. You don't need to. Over the next two weeks, you have private conversations with each of her supporters. You don't lie — you just ask questions. 'Have you noticed Petra hasn't volunteered for exterior duty?' 'Did you know Petra was considering leaving last month?' 'Do you think Petra has the group's interests first, or her own reputation?' By the time Petra speaks at the next meeting, three of her seven supporters are looking at the floor. She makes her points. Fewer people nod. She feels the shift but can't identify its source. Within a month, she stops speaking at meetings entirely. She's still in the group. She's just... quiet. You've neutralized a threat without a single public confrontation. The method was clean. The morality isn't.
choices.epitaph: I didn't fight her. I asked questions. Seven supporters became four, then two, then none. Petra is still here. She's just quiet now. I made her quiet.

quests.trigger: Your workers are demanding better conditions — more food, shorter shifts, rest days.
quests.discovery: It starts with the carpentry team. Then the kitchen staff. Then the water collectors. By the third day, you have a list of demands written on a piece of cardboard and signed by nineteen people. The demands aren't unreasonable: one rest day per ten-day cycle, an extra half-ration for exterior workers, and a review of the medical supply allocation. The problem isn't the demands. The problem is the precedent. You've never had a collective negotiation before. The list is being presented by a man named Dex — not the Dex from the map, a different one, a former mechanic who's become the de facto representative for the labor force. He's calm, organized, and completely serious. He says they'll continue working while negotiations proceed. He doesn't say they won't.

choices.label: Accept all demands. The workers have a point.
choices.outcome_text: You agree to the rest day, the extra rations, the medical review. Dex looks surprised — he was clearly prepared for a fight. The changes take effect immediately. Exterior workers get an extra half-ration. The rest day is awkward at first — people don't know what to do with unstructured time — but within a week, morale improves measurably. Productivity on working days goes up. The medical review finds three people who needed treatment they hadn't requested. Your resource margins shrink by about eight percent. The group is healthier, better rested, and slightly more loyal. The precedent is also set: collective negotiation works. You'll face it again.
choices.epitaph: Nineteen signatures. Three demands. I said yes to all of them. The margins shrank. The people didn't. That's the math I chose.

choices.label: Negotiate. Accept some demands, reject others. Find the middle.
choices.outcome_text: You sit down with Dex and the three team representatives. The negotiation takes four hours. You agree to the rest day and the medical review. You reject the extra rations but offer a different concession: exterior workers get first choice of shelter assignments when space opens up. Dex pushes back on the rations. You hold firm — the food supply can't support it. He accepts it with visible reluctance. The agreement is signed. It's not perfect. Nobody got everything. But the process itself is the precedent: negotiation, not confrontation, is how this group resolves disputes. The rest day feels earned. The ration denial feels fair. Mostly.
choices.epitaph: Four hours. Three demands. I said yes to two. The third became something else. Nobody was happy. Everyone accepted it. That's governance.

choices.label: Reject the demands. Remind them that survival isn't a negotiation.
choices.outcome_text: You tear the cardboard in half. You say the words: 'This isn't a democracy. We survive because we work. If you can't work, there are people outside who will.' The room goes very quiet. Dex's face doesn't change, but his hands do — they clench, then release, then clench again. The workers go back to work. Nobody strikes. Nobody complains. Three people leave within the week — two to the eastern road, one to join Aldric. They take their skills with them. The carpentry team is short-handed for two months. The water collection schedule slips. The people who stayed are more obedient. They're also more resentful. You've won the argument. You've lost some of your best workers.
choices.epitaph: I tore the cardboard. I said the words. Three people left. The carpentry team is short-handed. The people who stayed are quieter. Quiet isn't loyal.

quests.trigger: Your second-in-command questions a decision that hurt someone. They're having second thoughts.
quests.discovery: Reeves has been with you since the beginning. He helped you secure the shelter, organize the first rationing system, and make the hard calls that kept people alive. He's the person you trust most. Which is why it matters when he sits across from you, hands wrapped around a cup of water he's not drinking, and says: 'The Lowfield arrangement — Tess's people, they're not thriving. They're surviving for us. There's a difference.' He's not challenging your authority. He's questioning your methods. He says he's been thinking about the Harlan situation too, and the way you handled Petra. He's not accusing you of cruelty. He's asking if you've noticed the cost. He looks tired. Not physically — tired in the way that people get when they've been carrying something heavy for too long and finally admit it.

choices.label: Listen. Really listen. Acknowledge that he might be right.
choices.outcome_text: You don't defend. You don't explain. You listen. Reeves talks for twenty minutes about specific people, specific moments, specific costs that you didn't see because you were looking at the bigger picture. He's right about most of it. You admit that. He looks relieved — not because you agreed, but because you heard him. You agree to review the Lowfield arrangement and the medical allocation. Reeves stays. He's still your second-in-command. But something has shifted — he speaks more freely now, and you listen more carefully. The group's decisions improve incrementally. The cost is that you have to admit you were wrong sometimes. That turns out to be survivable.
choices.epitaph: Reeves talked. I listened. He was right about most of it. I admitted it. The group got better decisions. I got a harder mirror.

choices.label: Explain your reasoning. Help him see the larger picture.
choices.outcome_text: You walk him through the logic: the Lowfield arrangement secured food for sixty people. Harlan's theft, if unchecked, would have set a precedent. Petra's opposition, if empowered, would have fractured the group at a vulnerable moment. Every decision had costs. Every decision also had benefits that outweighed them. Reeves listens. He nods at some points. He pushes back on others. By the end, he says he understands the reasoning even if he doesn't love the outcomes. You agree to be more transparent about the trade-offs. Reeves stays. He's still your second-in-command. But he's also still carrying the weight. You've lightened it slightly by sharing the burden of explanation. It's not the same as sharing the burden of doubt.
choices.epitaph: I explained the logic. He understood it. He still doesn't love the outcomes. Neither do I. But now he carries it with me instead of alone.

choices.label: Dismiss his concerns. He's getting soft. The group needs strength, not doubt.
choices.outcome_text: You tell Reeves that survival isn't a popularity contest. You say the words: 'If you can't make the hard calls, say so now and I'll find someone who can.' Reeves goes quiet. Something in his face closes — not anger, not sadness, but the expression of a man who's decided not to bother anymore. He nods. He stays. He does his job. But he stops bringing you information he thinks you don't want to hear. He stops questioning decisions. He stops being the person who tells you when you're wrong. You've kept your second-in-command. You've lost your conscience. The group doesn't notice immediately. You will.
choices.epitaph: I told him to get hard or get out. He stayed. He also stopped telling me when I was wrong. I didn't notice the difference at first. Everyone does eventually.

quests.trigger: Someone from before the exchange finds you. They need help. Helping them would cost your group.
quests.discovery: His name is Mako. You knew him before — not close, but well enough that you shared meals and talked about the kind of world you'd build after the crisis passed. He looks like the crisis passed him first. He's lost weight, his hands are scarred, and he has a cough that sounds like it's been there for months. He found out you were leading a settlement. He walked two days to get here. He's asking for shelter, medical attention, and a place to stay. He doesn't have anything to trade. He says he doesn't have anyone else. Your medical supplies are limited. Your shelter is full. Your group has a policy about resource allocation that you helped write. Mako is looking at you with the expression of someone who remembers who you used to be.

choices.label: Take him in. Full support. The policy can bend for someone you knew before.
choices.outcome_text: You assign Mako a bunk, get him to the medical station, and make sure he eats a full meal that night. The cough is bad but treatable. Over the next two weeks, he recovers enough to work — light duty at first, then regular shifts. He's a good worker. He doesn't talk about the past much. He doesn't thank you, either, which you appreciate more than if he had. Your group notices the exception. Some people understand. Some don't. One person asks if the policy applies to everyone or just people you know. You don't have a good answer. Mako stays. He earns his place. The precedent is messy but human.
choices.epitaph: Mako walked two days. I said yes. The policy bent. Someone asked if it applies to everyone. I didn't answer. Mako earned his place. The question didn't.

choices.label: Offer limited help — medical treatment and three days of food. Then he's on his own.
choices.outcome_text: You treat the cough. You give him three days of rations and a place to sleep in the common area. Mako understands the limits. He doesn't argue. On the fourth morning, he packs the food you gave him and walks out. You watch him go through the gate. He doesn't look back. You don't know where he goes. Your group doesn't say anything about it, but the mood is heavier for a day. You helped someone. You also turned someone away. Both things are true. You live with both of them.
choices.epitaph: Three days. A treated cough. Food for the road. He didn't argue. That's what I remember — not the yes or the no, but that he didn't argue.

choices.label: Turn him away. The group comes first. Always.
choices.outcome_text: You tell him the shelter is full. You tell him the policy doesn't allow exceptions. You tell him you're sorry. Mako nods. He expected this, maybe. He turns and walks back the way he came. You watch him until he's out of sight. The cough gets quieter as he gets farther away. Your group doesn't know what happened — you handled it at the gate, privately. You eat dinner that night. The food tastes like nothing. You sleep. You dream about someone walking down a road with a cough and three days of food. You don't tell anyone about the dream.
choices.epitaph: I said no to someone I knew before. He walked away. The cough got quieter. The food tasted like nothing. I still don't talk about it.

quests.trigger: Your informant in a rival group wants out. They know too much — including things about you.
quests.discovery: Sable appears at your perimeter at dusk. She looks worse than the last time you saw her — thinner, more watchful, the kind of tired that comes from sleeping with one eye open. She says she wants out. She says she's given you what you needed and now she wants her name removed from every arrangement, every record, every conversation. She says she wants to disappear. The problem is that Sable knows things: the routes your people patrol, the weaknesses in your defenses, the fact that you've been using false information through intermediaries. She knows because you told her. If she goes to the wrong person — or if the wrong person finds her — everything you've built becomes vulnerable. She says she understands. She just wants out.

choices.label: Let her go. She's earned it. Trust her to disappear.
choices.outcome_text: You give her two days of rations and a clean direction — south, toward the coastal settlements where nobody knows her face. Sable takes the supplies. She looks at you for a long moment, as if she's trying to decide whether to say something. She doesn't. She walks south. You rotate your patrol routes within the week, just in case. The Kessler group doesn't show any new knowledge of your operations. Sable kept her word, or she's very good at waiting. You change the routes anyway. Trust is a luxury when the cost of being wrong is this high.
choices.epitaph: I let her walk south. Two days of food. A clean direction. I changed my patrol routes the next week. Trust is expensive. I paid it.

choices.label: Let her go — but follow her. Make sure she actually disappears.
choices.outcome_text: You give her the supplies and the direction. You also send one of your best scouts to track her for three days. The scout reports back: Sable walked south, exactly as directed. She didn't stop to talk to anyone. She didn't leave messages. She reached the coastal road on the second day and kept going. The scout lost her in a crowd of refugees near the river crossing. She disappeared. You're fairly confident she's gone. The surveillance cost you three days of scout time and the knowledge that you don't trust people who've worked for you. Sable is free. You know she's free. You also know you checked. Both things are true. You live with both.
choices.epitaph: I let her go. I also followed her. She disappeared. I know she disappeared. I also know I checked. That's the part I don't like.

choices.label: She can't leave. She knows too much. Find her a role where the knowledge is contained.
choices.outcome_text: You tell Sable she can't leave — not because you're cruel, but because the information she carries is too dangerous to let walk free. You offer her a position in the interior: storage management, no outside contact, no access to current operational details. She'll be fed, housed, and safe. She'll also never leave the shelter again. Sable's face goes through several expressions before settling on something blank. She accepts. She has no leverage. You've turned an informant into a prisoner with a job. She works in storage. She doesn't speak to anyone who isn't assigned to inventory. She's safe. She's also trapped. You tell yourself it's necessary. The math supports it. The morality doesn't.
choices.epitaph: She wanted out. I said no. She works in storage now. She's fed, housed, safe. She's also never leaving. I call it containment. She calls it something else.

quests.trigger: An ally asks you to help them eliminate a rival — permanently. This is the line.
quests.discovery: The ally is Kessler. That's the first surprise. After months of tension, raids, and proxy conflicts, Kessler's people are sitting across from yours in the neutral ground of the burnt-out convenience store. Kessler himself is there — older than you expected, scarred, with the calm voice of someone who's made peace with violence. The second surprise is the request. He wants your help removing a rival leader named Varek — not defeating him in a trade dispute, not outmaneuvering him politically, but removing him. Permanently. Kessler says Varek is 'bad for the valley.' He says Varek has been raiding settlements that should be under 'protection.' He says removing Varek would 'stabilize everything.' He doesn't say 'for both of us.' He says 'for the valley.' You notice the distinction.

choices.label: Agree. Varek is a problem. This solves it for both of you.
choices.outcome_text: The operation takes four days. Your people provide the intelligence — Varek's schedule, his guard rotation, the layout of his compound. Kessler's people provide the muscle. Varek dies in his sleep. His group fractures within a week — half scatter, half join Kessler, a handful come to you asking for work. The valley is more stable. Kessler owes you. You owe yourself an explanation for why you said yes. The operation was clean. The bodies were messy. You don't sleep well for a month. You tell yourself it was necessary. Kessler tells you it was necessary. You're not sure either of you believes it.
choices.epitaph: Varek died in his sleep. I provided the intelligence. Kessler provided the muscle. The valley is quieter. I'm not.

choices.label: Refuse. You don't do assassinations. Find another way to handle Varek.
choices.outcome_text: You tell Kessler no. He doesn't argue — he just looks at you with an expression that's either respect or disappointment, and you can't tell which. You spend the next three weeks building a coalition against Varek through legitimate means: trade embargoes, diplomatic pressure, and a public accounting of his raids. Varek loses support. His group shrinks. He's eventually forced to leave the valley entirely. It takes longer than assassination. It costs more in trade concessions. It also doesn't require you to become the kind of person who plans killings in a burnt-out convenience store. Varek is gone. You're still yourself. The valley is stable. The method was harder. The cost was higher. The morality was cleaner.
choices.epitaph: I said no to a killing. It took three weeks and cost more. Varek left the valley alive. I left the conversation alive. Both mattered.

choices.label: Counter-offer: you'll help isolate Varek economically, but no violence.
choices.outcome_text: Kessler doesn't love it, but he accepts the alternative. You cut Varek off from trade routes, convince two other settlements to stop dealing with him, and create economic pressure that makes his position untenable. Varek's group starts shrinking within a month. He tries to raid your allies and finds them better defended than expected. He leaves the valley after six weeks — not dead, just gone. Kessler gets what he wanted. You didn't have to plan a killing. The method was slower and less certain. Varek might come back. He might not. You've solved the problem without crossing a line. The line is still there. You can see it. You haven't stepped over it.
choices.epitaph: No killing. Just pressure. Varek left. He might come back. The line is still there. I can see it. That's enough for now.

quests.trigger: A new leader is gaining followers by being everything you're not — open, generous, trusted.
quests.discovery: Her name is Calla. She appeared in the valley three months ago and has been building something at the old water treatment plant — a settlement that runs on consensus, shared resources, and the kind of transparency that makes your own arrangements look calculated. People are leaving your group to join hers. Not many — four in the last month — but the trend is clear. Calla doesn't criticize you publicly. She doesn't have to. Her existence is the criticism. She's offering something you stopped offering: the belief that survival doesn't require the kind of choices you've been making. Your scouts report that her settlement is well-organized, well-fed, and genuinely democratic. It's also smaller than yours and less defensible. She's built something good. She's also built something vulnerable.

choices.label: Propose an alliance. Combine strengths. Her legitimacy, your infrastructure.
choices.outcome_text: You approach Calla directly. She's cautious but willing to talk. The negotiation takes two meetings and a lot of honest conversation. The alliance is structured as a partnership: your settlement handles defense and infrastructure, hers handles food production and community governance. Decisions are made jointly. Your group is larger and more established, so you have more weight — but Calla has a vote and a veto on community issues. The merger works better than expected. Calla's people bring organizational skills your group lacks. Your people bring resources and security. The valley is more stable. You've also diluted your authority. Calla has equal standing now. The decisions are better. The power is shared. You're not sure if that's a success or a surrender. Calla seems to think it's both.
choices.epitaph: I proposed an alliance. Calla accepted. The decisions are better. The power is shared. I'm not sure if I won or lost. Calla says both.

choices.label: Undermine her. Expose the weaknesses in her settlement. Let her fail on her own.
choices.outcome_text: You don't attack Calla directly. Instead, you wait. Her settlement is principled but fragile — one bad harvest, one raid, one internal dispute and the consensus model will fracture. You make sure the bad harvest happens: you buy up seed stock from traders before Calla's people can reach them. You make sure the raid happens: you don't warn her when your scouts report raider movement near her settlement. The settlement survives both, but barely. People start leaving. Calla's consensus model requires time for decisions, and time is a resource they don't have. Within two months, her group has shrunk by a third. She's still there. She's still principled. She's also struggling. You've proven that idealism has a cost. Calla is paying it.
choices.epitaph: I didn't attack her. I just didn't help. The harvest failed. The raiders came. Her group shrank. Idealism has a cost. I made sure she paid it.

choices.label: Absorb her settlement. Offer to merge — on your terms.
choices.outcome_text: You approach Calla with a merger proposal: her people join your settlement, keeping their governance model internally but deferring to your leadership on external matters. Calla listens. She asks questions. She negotiates. She gets concessions — autonomy on internal decisions, representation in your council, protection for her community's practices. The merger happens. Calla's people join yours. Her consensus model operates within your larger structure. You've absorbed her legitimacy without absorbing her power. Calla has autonomy, but you have authority. Her people are fed, housed, and protected. They're also part of your settlement now. Calla knows what happened. You know what happened. The valley calls it a merger. The reality is more complicated.
choices.epitaph: I offered a merger. Calla negotiated. She got autonomy. I got authority. Her people are safer. They're also mine now. We both know the difference.

quests.trigger: Calla's people rescue someone you punished. It makes you look weak. Or merciful. Depending on who's telling the story.
quests.discovery: The person is Dex — not the informant Dex, a different one, a young man who was expelled from your settlement two weeks ago after a dispute over resource allocation. He was angry, he said things, he was given the choice between leaving quietly or being forced out. He chose to leave. Calla's people found him on the road, half-sick, and brought him to their settlement. They treated him. They gave him a place. They didn't ask many questions. Now Dex is telling anyone who'll listen that Calla's settlement is better than yours — not because it's richer or safer, but because they took him in when you cast him out. The story is spreading. Your group is hearing it. Some people are starting to wonder.

choices.label: Publicly acknowledge the expulsion was harsh. Offer to renegotiate Dex's return.
choices.outcome_text: You stand up at the next meeting and say the words: 'Dex was expelled under circumstances that could have been handled better.' The room goes quiet. You offer to invite him back under revised terms. The invitation reaches Calla's settlement within two days. Dex doesn't come back — he's found a place with Calla's people. But the gesture lands. Your group sees that you can admit mistakes. Calla sees that you're willing to adjust. The story changes from 'they cast him out' to 'they tried to bring him back.' Your authority isn't weakened. It's more complicated than that. You've shown flexibility. In a world this hard, flexibility is a kind of strength. Most people don't see it that way. Some do.
choices.epitaph: I admitted the expulsion was harsh. Dex didn't come back. The story changed. Flexibility is strength. Most people don't see it. Some do.

choices.label: Ignore it. Dex made his choice. Calla can have him.
choices.outcome_text: You don't respond to the story. You don't criticize Calla. You don't try to retrieve Dex. He left. He found somewhere else. That's his business. Your group continues working. The story circulates for a week, then gets replaced by newer news — a supply delivery, a perimeter repair, a birth in the settlement. Dex becomes a footnote. Calla's settlement continues existing. Your settlement continues existing. The valley has two options now instead of one. Some people prefer one. Some prefer the other. You don't lose anyone else that month. The story didn't matter as much as it seemed to. Or it mattered in ways you can't measure. You choose not to calculate which.
choices.epitaph: I ignored the story. Dex stayed with Calla. The valley has two options now. Some people prefer hers. Some prefer mine. I stopped counting.

choices.label: Respond publicly. Explain why Dex was expelled. Let the facts speak.
choices.outcome_text: You release a statement — not angry, just factual. Dex was expelled because he violated the resource allocation agreement, because he disrupted work assignments, because he was given alternatives and chose confrontation. The facts are accurate. They're also incomplete — they don't include the context, the stress, the reasons Dex was angry. The statement circulates. Some people in your group feel vindicated. Some people in Calla's settlement feel attacked. Calla doesn't respond. She doesn't need to. The facts are accurate. The full story is more complicated. You've won the argument on paper. You've also made yourself look defensive. The valley notices both things.
choices.epitaph: I released the facts. They were accurate. They were also incomplete. I won the argument. I also looked defensive. The valley notices both.

quests.trigger: Calla makes a mistake. You can exploit it — or warn her. This is the endgame.
quests.discovery: Calla's settlement has overextended. They've taken in too many refugees, their food reserves are lower than they realize, and a coming winter will force them to either ask for help or start turning people away. Your scouts have the numbers. You know exactly how tight their situation is. Calla doesn't know that you know. You could warn her — share the data, offer a trade arrangement that would stabilize her settlement through the winter. Or you could wait. Let the winter do the work. Let her settlement fracture under the pressure. Let the people who left you come back because there's nowhere else to go. The choice is simple. The morality isn't.

choices.label: Warn her. Share the data. Offer help — with conditions.
choices.outcome_text: You send the data to Calla. You also send an offer: your settlement will provide grain through the winter in exchange for a formal trade agreement that benefits both groups. Calla reads the data. She reads the offer. She accepts both. The trade arrangement is structured as a partnership, not a bailout. Calla's settlement survives the winter. Your settlement gets reliable food imports. The valley is more stable. You've also proven that you're willing to help a competitor survive. Calla respects you more. Your group respects you more. The morality is clean. The strategy is also sound. Both things are true.
choices.epitaph: I warned her. I helped her. The valley is more stable. Calla respects me. The morality is clean. The strategy is sound. Both matter.

choices.label: Say nothing. Let the winter handle it. Her failure is your opportunity.
choices.outcome_text: You don't warn Calla. You don't exploit her situation directly — you just don't prevent the natural consequences. The winter is hard. Calla's food reserves run out by mid-season. She starts turning people away. Her settlement shrinks. Some of her people come to you. You take them in. They bring skills, labor, and the quiet shame of people who've lost their idealistic experiment. Calla's settlement survives, but barely. She's still there, still principled, still democratic. She's also smaller, poorer, and more cautious. You've proven that idealism has a cost. Calla paid it. You didn't have to lift a finger. The valley is more stable. Your settlement is larger. Calla is still a rival. She's just a weaker one.
choices.epitaph: I said nothing. The winter did the work. Calla's settlement shrank. Mine grew. I didn't lift a finger. The valley is quieter. Calla is poorer. I won without fighting.

choices.label: Offer help — but publicly. Make your generosity visible. Make her dependence clear.
choices.outcome_text: You make a public offer of assistance — grain, tools, medical supplies. The offer is genuine. The presentation is calculated. You announce it at a joint meeting, in front of both settlements. Calla can't refuse without her people going hungry. She accepts. The aid arrives. Your settlement is framed as the benefactor. Calla's settlement is framed as the recipient. The power dynamic shifts visibly. Calla's people see your settlement as the stronger partner. Your people see your settlement as the generous one. The reality is more complicated. You've helped. You've also established dominance. Calla knows it. You know it. The valley sees the generosity. Only the two of you see the calculation.
choices.epitaph: I helped publicly. The aid was real. The presentation was calculated. Calla's people see us as stronger. Mine see us as generous. Only Calla and I see the calculation.

quests.trigger: Calla's settlement collapses. She comes to you. This is the final confrontation.
quests.discovery: Calla walks into your settlement alone. She's thinner than when you last saw her. Her clothes are worn. She doesn't have weapons visible, but she has the posture of someone who's decided that violence isn't the point anymore. She asks to speak with you. Privately. You go to the meeting room. She sits down. She says her settlement can't survive the winter. She says she's tried everything — consensus, shared labor, democratic resource allocation. She says the model doesn't work at scale. She says she was wrong. She looks at you. She says: 'What happens now?' The question isn't about logistics. It's about what kind of person you are when you've won.

choices.label: Offer her a place. Full integration. Her people are welcome. She keeps her dignity.
choices.outcome_text: You tell Calla her people are welcome — full rations, full membership, no second-class status. You offer her a position on your council. She'll have a voice. She won't have authority, but she'll have influence. Calla listens. She asks if you're doing this out of strength or guilt. You say you're doing it because it's the right thing. She doesn't believe you entirely. She accepts anyway. Her people integrate over the following weeks. Some of them thrive. Some of them never quite adjust to your settlement's structure. Calla stays. She speaks at meetings. She questions decisions. She's still principled. She's also pragmatic now. The valley is unified. The cost was Calla's idealism. The benefit was her survival. Both are real.
choices.epitaph: I offered her a place. She accepted. Her people integrated. Calla still questions decisions. She's also alive. The valley is unified. The cost was her idealism. The benefit was her survival.

choices.label: Offer her a place — but no leadership role. She's a member, not a partner.
choices.outcome_text: You tell Calla her people are welcome. You don't offer her a council position. She's a member now, not a leader. Calla's face goes through several expressions before settling on acceptance. She agrees. Her people integrate. Calla works. She doesn't speak at meetings. She doesn't question decisions. She's quiet in the way that people get when they've lost their platform. Her people notice. Some of them adjust. Some of them never quite settle. You've absorbed her settlement. You've also neutralized her influence. The valley is unified. Calla is alive. She's also diminished. You tell yourself it was necessary. The math supports it. The morality is more complicated.
choices.epitaph: I offered her a place. Not a role. Calla works. She's quiet now. The valley is unified. She's diminished. I tell myself it was necessary.

choices.label: Turn her away. Her experiment failed. She can find somewhere else.
choices.outcome_text: You tell Calla no. Her people can come — individually, as workers. She can come too. But the settlement as a unit, the democratic model, the alternative you've been competing with — that's over. Calla stares at you. She says she understands. She leaves. You don't know where she goes. Some of her people come to your settlement over the following weeks. They work. They don't talk about Calla. You don't ask about her. The valley is unified under your leadership. The alternative is gone. You've won. The victory is complete. It's also lonely. You sit in the meeting room sometimes and think about the question Calla asked: 'What happens now?' You're still answering it.
choices.epitaph: I said no. Calla left. Her people came. The valley is mine. The alternative is gone. I won. I also sit in the meeting room thinking about her question. I'm still answering it.

quests.trigger: You control the valley's food supply. Winter is coming. The math is brutal.
quests.discovery: The grain inventory is clear: you have enough to feed your settlement through the winter at current ration levels. You don't have enough to feed the entire valley. The outlying settlements — Lowfield, the remnants of Calla's group, a handful of independent families — will face shortages. They'll come to you for help. You can share, which means your own people eat less. You can hoard, which means they go hungry. Or you can trade, which means they work for food they used to gather themselves. The math is simple. The morality isn't. Your council is divided. Reeves — if he's still with you — has an opinion. The rest of the group is watching to see what you do when the choice is this clear and this costly.

choices.label: Share. Reduce your own rations. Nobody in the valley starves.
choices.outcome_text: You cut your settlement's rations by fifteen percent. The grain is distributed across the valley. Lowfield gets enough to supplement their own stores. The independent families get through the worst weeks. Your people are hungrier. Morale dips. Work output drops slightly. The valley survives. Your settlement is seen as the provider — the group that didn't let neighbors starve. The cost is real: three people in your settlement develop mild malnutrition. One child gets sick. The child recovers. The cost was real. The morality was also real. You fed people. Your people ate less. Both things are true.
choices.epitaph: I cut rations fifteen percent. The valley survived. Three of my people got sick. One was a child. The child recovered. I fed people. My people ate less. Both things are true.

choices.label: Trade. They work for food. Labor in exchange for grain.
choices.outcome_text: You offer grain at a price: labor. The outlying settlements send workers to your settlement — road repair, perimeter maintenance, storage organization. In exchange, they take home enough grain to supplement their own stores. The arrangement is structured, predictable, and fundamentally unequal. Your settlement gets the labor. They get the food. The work is real. The food is real. The power dynamic is also real. Lowfield's leader calls it a 'partnership.' You call it a 'trade arrangement.' The workers call it something else — they call it 'working for food.' The valley survives. Your settlement is stronger. The outlying settlements are dependent. The morality is pragmatic. The reality is hierarchy.
choices.epitaph: They worked for food. We got the labor. They got the grain. The valley survived. My settlement is stronger. They're dependent. I call it trade. They call it working for food.

choices.label: Hoard. Your people come first. The rest of the valley can figure it out.
choices.outcome_text: You keep the grain. Your settlement eats well through the winter. The outlying settlements struggle. Lowfield manages — barely — on their own stores. Two independent families don't. You hear about it in spring: one family lost a grandparent to exposure and malnutrition. The other family scattered — three people went east, two went south. You don't investigate. You don't offer explanations. Your settlement survived intact. Your people are healthy. The valley is smaller. The cost was real. The morality was also real. You chose your own. Others chose survival elsewhere. The math worked. The people didn't.
choices.epitaph: I kept the grain. My people ate. Two families didn't survive. One lost a grandparent. The other scattered. The math worked. The people didn't.

quests.trigger: A child comes to the gate. Their parent is in your storage room — imprisoned for theft.
quests.discovery: The child is nine years old. Maybe ten. Hard to tell when they're this thin. They're standing at the gate with the kind of stillness that comes from being scared and trying not to show it. They say their name is Finn. They say their mother is in the storage room. They say they haven't eaten since yesterday. The mother — you know the case. She was caught stealing medical supplies. Not for resale. For her brother, who lives outside the settlement and has an infected wound. The theft was real. The punishment was real: three days in the storage room, then expulsion. The child doesn't know about the expulsion. The child just knows their mother isn't home and they're hungry. The guard at the gate is looking at you. This wasn't supposed to be your problem.

choices.label: Feed the child. Bring them inside. Sort out the mother's situation separately.
choices.outcome_text: You take Finn inside. You get them food — a full meal, not a ration. You find out where they've been sleeping. You arrange temporary care while you review the mother's case. The theft was real. The punishment was also real. You reduce it: the mother is released with a warning and a requirement to work off the value of the stolen supplies. She's not expelled. She's not thanked. She's given a choice: work or leave. She chooses work. Finn eats. The mother works. The settlement sees that the system can bend without breaking. The precedent is messy but humane. You've shown that the rules have flexibility. You've also shown that the rules still exist.
choices.epitaph: The child was hungry. I fed them. The mother stole. I reduced the punishment. The system bent. It didn't break. Finn ate. The mother worked. Both things are true.

choices.label: Follow the rules. The mother's punishment stands. Offer the child temporary care.
choices.outcome_text: You tell the guard to bring Finn inside for a meal. You don't intervene in the mother's case. The theft was real. The punishment was applied fairly. The child eats. The mother serves her three days and is expelled as scheduled. Finn goes with her. You don't know where they go. You've followed the rules. The rules were clear. The child was hungry. The child ate. The mother was expelled. The child went with her. The system worked. The outcome was harsh. Both things are true. You sleep. You dream about a child standing at a gate with the kind of stillness that comes from being scared.
choices.epitaph: I followed the rules. The child ate. The mother was expelled. The child went with her. The system worked. The outcome was harsh. I dream about the stillness.

choices.label: Make an exception. Release the mother. The child needs her.
choices.outcome_text: You release the mother immediately. You explain the decision to the council: the child's welfare takes precedence over the punishment. The mother is released. She's also given a work assignment to repay the value of the stolen supplies. She accepts without argument. Finn is with their mother. The settlement sees that the system can bend for children. The precedent is specific — it's about kids, not about theft generally. The mother works. Finn eats. The settlement understands the distinction. You've shown mercy without abandoning principle. The balance is delicate. It holds.
choices.epitaph: I released the mother. The child needed her. The system bent for children. The mother worked. Finn ate. The balance held.

quests.trigger: Your rules caused a death. You can admit it or bury it.
quests.discovery: The man's name was Corin. He was expelled from your settlement six weeks ago for 'disruptive behavior' — which meant he questioned a decision at a meeting and didn't stop when asked. He left. He tried to join Lowfield. Lowfield turned him away — they were following your 'guidance' about not accepting people you'd expelled. Corin tried to survive on his own. He didn't make it. A scavenging trip went wrong — he fell in a collapsed building, broke his leg, couldn't get back. He died of exposure three days later. Your scouts found the body. They also found his pack, which had a notebook. The notebook had a single entry from two days before he died: 'Nobody coming. Nobody cares.' The scouts brought you the notebook. They're looking at you. They know what happened. The question is what you do with it.

choices.label: Admit it. Publicly. Tell the settlement what happened and why.
choices.outcome_text: You stand up at the next meeting. You tell them about Corin. You tell them about the expulsion, the guidance to Lowfield, the notebook entry. You say the words: 'Our rules contributed to his death.' The room is very quiet. Some people look angry. Some look sad. Some look like they already knew. You announce a policy review: expulsion decisions will now require council approval, and settlements under your influence will be instructed to accept expelled individuals rather than turn them away. The policy change is real. The cost was real. Corin is still dead. The settlement sees that you can admit mistakes. They also see that the mistakes were serious. Your authority is shaken. It's also more legitimate now. Legitimacy has a cost. You're paying it.
choices.epitaph: I told them about Corin. I admitted the rules contributed to his death. The policy changed. Corin is still dead. My authority is shaken. It's also more legitimate. The cost was real.

choices.label: Bury it. The notebook disappears. Corin's death is a tragedy, not a policy failure.
choices.outcome_text: You tell the scouts the notebook is 'inconclusive' and file it away. Corin's death is recorded as a scavenging accident. No policy changes. No public discussion. The scouts who found the body know the truth. You know the truth. The settlement doesn't. Life continues. The expulsion policy remains unchanged. Lowfield continues following your guidance. Nobody else dies — this time. The notebook sits in a drawer. The entry reads: 'Nobody coming. Nobody cares.' You close the drawer. You tell yourself it was necessary. The math supports it. The morality doesn't. You sleep. You dream about a man in a collapsed building writing in a notebook. You don't tell anyone about the dream.
choices.epitaph: I buried it. The notebook disappeared. Corin's death was an accident. The policy didn't change. The scouts know. I know. The settlement doesn't. I close the drawer. I dream about the notebook.

choices.label: Acknowledge it privately to your council. Adjust the policy quietly.
choices.outcome_text: You bring the notebook to the council. You explain the situation. You don't make it public, but you do change the policy: expulsion decisions now require council approval, and settlements are no longer instructed to refuse expelled individuals. The changes are framed as 'routine updates' rather than responses to a specific death. The council understands. The settlement doesn't know about Corin. The policy is better. The accountability is incomplete. You've improved the system without admitting the system killed someone. The council respects the discretion. The morality is pragmatic. The full truth is buried. The policy is still better than it was. Both things are true.
choices.epitaph: I told the council. I changed the policy quietly. The settlement doesn't know about Corin. The policy is better. The accountability is incomplete. Both things are true.

quests.trigger: One settlement remains independent. They refuse to join your coalition. They must be dealt with.
quests.discovery: The settlement is called Ridge. It's small — maybe twenty people — but they're positioned well: high ground, defensible, with access to a clean water source. They've refused every offer to join your coalition. They've refused trade agreements. They've refused diplomatic visits. Their leader, a woman named Ash, sent a single message: 'We're fine on our own.' That was three months ago. Since then, Ridge has remained stubbornly independent. They don't raid your people. They don't interfere with your operations. They just... exist. Separately. Your council is asking why you haven't 'dealt with them' yet. The question implies that independent settlements are a problem. You're not sure they are. But the question is being asked openly now.

choices.label: Leave them alone. Independence isn't a threat.
choices.outcome_text: You tell the council that Ridge isn't a problem. They don't raid. They don't interfere. They just want to be left alone. You can respect that. The council doesn't entirely agree, but they accept the decision. Ridge continues existing. Ash continues leading. The valley has one independent settlement. It's a reminder that not everyone wants to be part of your coalition. That's their choice. You let them make it. The valley is mostly unified. Ridge is the exception. The exception proves that the rule isn't absolute. Some people value that. Some people find it irritating. You let Ridge exist. The morality is clean. The strategy is also sound — forcing the issue would cost more than leaving it alone.
choices.epitaph: I left them alone. Ridge exists. Ash leads. The valley is mostly unified. Ridge is the exception. The exception proves the rule isn't absolute. I let them choose.

choices.label: Apply pressure. Cut off their trade. Make independence expensive.
choices.outcome_text: You instruct your trade partners to stop dealing with Ridge. The settlement loses access to tools, medical supplies, and manufactured goods. They can still grow food. They can still access water. But their quality of life drops noticeably. Ash sends a message: 'This is petty.' You don't respond. Three months later, Ridge sends a delegation. They're not asking to join the coalition. They're asking for a trade agreement. You agree — on terms that favor your settlement. Ridge gets access to supplies. You get leverage. Ash signs the agreement. She doesn't look happy. She looks like someone who's learned that independence has a cost. You've taught her the lesson. The method was harsh. The outcome is stable.
choices.epitaph: I cut off their trade. Ridge suffered. Ash signed the agreement. She's not happy. She learned independence has a cost. I taught her. The method was harsh. The outcome is stable.

choices.label: Absorb them. Offer integration — or face consequences.
choices.outcome_text: You send Ash an ultimatum: join the coalition or face isolation. The message is polite but clear. Ash reads it. She looks at her settlement — twenty people, high ground, clean water. She looks at your settlement — hundreds of people, unified valley, overwhelming resources. She makes the calculation. Ridge joins the coalition. Ash keeps her leadership role internally, but external decisions defer to your authority. The settlement is absorbed. The independence is over. Ash leads Ridge within your structure. She doesn't lead Ridge apart from it. You've unified the valley. The cost was Ridge's autonomy. The benefit was stability. Both are real. Ash knows it. You know it. The valley calls it unity. Ridge calls it something else.
choices.epitaph: I gave Ash an ultimatum. She chose integration. Ridge joined. The independence ended. The valley is unified. The cost was Ridge's autonomy. Ash knows it. I know it.

quests.trigger: Someone tries to kill you. They fail. The question is: was any of it worth it?
quests.discovery: The assassin is young — maybe twenty. They get past the outer perimeter before being stopped. They have a knife and a look of absolute conviction. They don't make it to you. Your guards handle it. The assassin is restrained, questioned, and held. The motivation is clear: the assassin's family was among the people expelled from your settlement months ago. The father died on the road. The mother and younger sibling are somewhere in the valley, struggling. The assassin blames you. They're not entirely wrong. The assassin is sitting in a storage room, staring at the wall. Your council is asking what to do with them. The guards are asking the same question with different emphasis. You're asking yourself a different question entirely: was the path that led here — the choices, the consolidations, the enforcement — worth this moment?

choices.label: Show mercy. Release the assassin. Offer their family help.
choices.outcome_text: You go to the storage room. You talk to the assassin. You listen. Then you release them. You also send people to find their mother and sibling. You offer them shelter, food, medical care. The assassin stares at you. They don't understand. You explain: their father died because of decisions you made. You can't bring him back. You can help the rest of the family. The assassin leaves. They don't thank you. They don't forgive you. They take their family's offer and disappear into the settlement. You've shown mercy. You've also admitted — publicly, implicitly — that the expulsion policy had costs. The council is divided. The settlement is divided. You've done the right thing. The right thing is complicated.
choices.epitaph: I released the assassin. I helped their family. The father died because of me. The rest survive because of me. The assassin doesn't forgive me. I don't expect it. I did the right thing. The right thing is complicated.

choices.label: Follow the rules. The assassin attacked leadership. Expel them.
choices.outcome_text: The policy is clear: attempted violence against leadership results in expulsion. The assassin is released outside the perimeter with three days of rations. They walk away. You don't know where they go. The family — the mother and sibling — remain in the settlement. They're not punished for the assassin's actions. They work. They don't speak about the assassination attempt. The settlement continues. The policy was applied consistently. The outcome is harsh. The assassin tried to kill you. You expelled them. The family stays. The morality is procedural. The reality is that a young person with a knife and a grudge is now outside your walls with nowhere to go. You followed the rules. The rules don't keep you up at night. The person does.
choices.epitaph: I expelled the assassin. The policy was clear. The family stays. The assassin walks. I followed the rules. The rules don't keep me up. The person does.

choices.label: Make an example. Public trial. Public punishment. Send a message.
choices.outcome_text: You hold a public trial. The assassin is found guilty of attempted violence. The punishment is expulsion and a permanent ban from returning. The trial is conducted properly — evidence, testimony, verdict. The punishment is applied consistently. The message is clear: violence against leadership will not be tolerated. The settlement understands. The council supports the decision. The assassin's family remains in the settlement. They work. They don't speak about it. You've sent a message. The message was received. The cost was a young person with a knife and a conviction that you were responsible for their father's death. They weren't entirely wrong. You expelled them anyway. The valley is unified. The unity has a cost. You're paying it.
choices.epitaph: I made an example. The trial was proper. The punishment was applied. The message was received. The assassin wasn't entirely wrong. I expelled them anyway. The valley is unified. The unity has a cost.

quests.trigger: You've won. The valley is yours. Everyone fears you. Was it worth it?
quests.discovery: You sit in the meeting room. It's quiet. The council meeting ended an hour ago. Every decision was approved. Every policy was implemented. The valley is unified under your leadership. Lowfield produces food. The water station operates under your authority. The military outpost is garrisoned with your people. The settlements are connected, supplied, protected. You control the trade routes. You control the resource allocation. You control the justice system. You sit in the meeting room and look at the wall. There's a map drawn on it — the valley, the settlements, the routes, the resources. It's all there. It's all yours. The room is quiet. Nobody is arguing. Nobody is questioning. Nobody is challenging. You've won. You're alone in the room. The question is sitting across from you, even though there's nobody there: was it worth it?

choices.label: Yes. The valley is stable. People are fed. The system works.
choices.outcome_text: You answer the question: yes. The valley is stable. People are fed. The system works. You think about the cost — the expulsions, the cover-ups, the assassin, the child at the gate. You think about the benefits — the unified valley, the reliable food supply, the protection from external threats. The benefits outweigh the costs. The math works. You sit in the meeting room and feel something that might be satisfaction. It might also be exhaustion. It might also be the absence of something else — something that used to be there before the choices stacked up. You stand up. You leave the room. The valley is yours. You've won. The question is still there. You've answered it. You're not sure the answer is complete.
choices.epitaph: I said yes. The valley is stable. The system works. The cost was real. The benefit was real. I sat in the room. I was alone. I've won. I'm not sure the answer is complete.

choices.label: No. The cost was too high. The valley is unified but the people are diminished.
choices.outcome_text: You answer the question: no. The valley is stable, but the stability has a cost. People are fed, but they're also cautious. The system works, but it works because people are afraid to challenge it. You think about Calla, about Corin, about the assassin, about Finn at the gate. You think about the choices that led here — each one rational, each one defensible, each one adding a layer of something that wasn't there before. The valley is unified. The unity is built on control. You sit in the meeting room and feel something that might be regret. It might also be clarity. You stand up. You leave the room. The valley is yours. You've won. The cost was too high. You know it now.
choices.epitaph: I said no. The cost was too high. The valley is unified but diminished. I think about Calla, Corin, the assassin, Finn. Each choice was rational. Each choice added a layer. I've won. The cost was too high. I know it now.

choices.label: I don't know. The question doesn't have an answer. The valley is what it is.
choices.outcome_text: You don't answer the question. You sit in the meeting room and look at the map. The valley is unified. The system works. People are fed. People are also cautious, controlled, diminished in ways that aren't visible on the map. You think about the choices — each one rational, each one defensible, each one leading to this moment. You don't know if it was worth it. You're not sure anyone in your position would know. The question doesn't have an answer. It only has the asking. You stand up. You leave the room. The valley is yours. You've won. The question is still there. You'll keep carrying it. That's the cost. That's the victory. Both things are true.
choices.epitaph: I didn't answer. The question doesn't have an answer. The valley is what it is. I've won. I've also lost something. I don't know what. I'll keep carrying the question. That's the cost. That's the victory. Both things are true.

quests.trigger: A stranger sits near the shelter gate, turning a dog tag over in their fingers. They haven't spoken to anyone in three days.
quests.discovery: The stranger doesn't look up when you approach. Their thumb traces the engraved letters on a dog tag — the same letters, over and over, wearing the metal smooth. A canteen sits beside them, half-full. They push it toward you without a word, then stop mid-motion, as if remembering they're allowed to speak.

choices.label: Sit down. Say nothing. Let the silence do the work.
choices.outcome_text: You lower yourself onto the concrete beside them. Minutes pass. The wind carries grit across the gate. Finally, they speak — not to you, exactly, but to the air between you. A name. Their sister's. The tag belonged to someone who didn't come back from the eastern road. They tell you about the last letter, the one that arrived two weeks after the burial. You listen. That's all. But when they stand, they leave the tag on the ground between you. Not a gift. A witness mark.
choices.epitaph: I sat with a stranger until the silence broke open. Their sister's name tasted like copper and rain.

choices.label: Ask who the tag belonged to.
choices.outcome_text: They flinch at the question, then loosen. A name. A sister. The eastern road. The story comes out in fragments — a supply run gone wrong, a bridge that wasn't there, a radio that stopped answering. You piece it together from the gaps. When they finish, they look at you for the first time. 'You're the first one who asked,' they say. Not grateful. Just stating a fact.
choices.epitaph: Asked a question. Got a whole life in return. Didn't know that was possible anymore.

choices.label: Offer them food in exchange for the story.
choices.outcome_text: They look at the food, then at you. Something closes behind their eyes. They take the food — of course they take the food — but the story stays locked. 'Some things aren't for trade,' they say, and turn away. You've learned nothing except that hunger and grief don't share the same currency.
choices.epitaph: Tried to buy a story. Got nothing. Some doors only open from the inside.

choices.label: You don't have time for this. Walk on.
choices.outcome_text: You pass them without a word. Their thumb keeps tracing the tag. You hear nothing — no plea, no curse, just the soft metal-on-skin sound fading behind you. The gate closes. Somewhere inside the shelter, someone else is carrying a story you'll never hear.
choices.epitaph: Walked past. The sound of that tag rubbing metal followed me for three days.

quests.trigger: An old scavenger at a fire near the eastern road keeps glancing at you. When you approach, they gesture to the seat across the flames.
quests.discovery: The fire is small — careful, almost. The scavenger sits cross-legged on a piece of cracked asphalt, a tin cup of something warm between their knees. They're old in the way the wasteland makes old: not wrinkles but erosion. When you sit, they don't offer the cup. Instead, they point at the sky. 'You know what color it was? Before?' They're not asking about the weather. They're asking if you remember a world that had blue.

choices.label: "Tell me about it."
choices.outcome_text: They talk for an hour. Not about the before — about the in-between. The weeks after the first exchange when everyone still thought it would end. They were a teacher. They kept showing up to the school building even after the roof collapsed, setting up chairs in the rubble, waiting for students who never came. 'The habit of it,' they say. 'That's what almost killed me. The habit of expecting things to work.' You listen to the fire. The cup goes cold. The story doesn't end — it just runs out of air, like everything else.
choices.epitaph: An old teacher kept setting up chairs in a collapsed school. I understand that now. I think.

choices.label: Share what you remember of the before, too.
choices.outcome_text: You trade memories like ration cards. They had a garden. You had... something. The exchange is uneven — theirs are vivid, yours are fading at the edges — but the act of sharing builds a bridge neither of you expected. They nod slowly when you finish. 'Good,' they say. 'Someone else carries it now. One more person.' The fire dies. They stand, stiffly, and walk east. You realize they were giving you something. Not a story. A responsibility.
choices.epitaph: Traded memories by a fire. Left lighter and heavier at the same time.

choices.label: "I don't have time for nostalgia."
choices.outcome_text: The scavenger's face doesn't change. They just pick up their cup, drink, and set it down. 'Nostalgia,' they repeat, as if tasting a word from a dead language. 'That's what the young ones call it.' They turn back to the fire. You've been dismissed — not with anger, but with something worse. Pity.
choices.epitaph: Called remembering a waste of time. The old woman's pity was worse than any raider's threat.

quests.trigger: A child at the water station is drawing in the dirt with a stick. The drawing looks like a map — or a warning.
quests.discovery: The child is maybe eight, maybe ten — hard to tell in the wasteland. They're drawing concentric circles in the dust, with lines radiating outward like a sun that fell to earth. When you crouch beside them, they don't stop. 'This is where the water goes,' they say, pointing to the center. 'And this is where it comes from. But nobody listens to the where.' They look up at you with the unflinching seriousness that only children and the dying possess.

choices.label: Ask them to explain the map. Take it seriously.
choices.outcome_text: The child traces the lines with a dirty finger. The water comes from underground — they've been watching where the seepage appears after rain, marking it with stones no one else notices. It's not a child's game. It's observation, patient and methodical, from someone who's learned that adults stop looking at the ground. You kneel in the dirt and listen to a ten-year-old explain hydrology through drawings. The map is crude. The knowledge is real.
choices.epitaph: A child drew me a map of water. Adults had walked past it for weeks.

choices.label: Give them a real pencil and paper to draw it properly.
choices.outcome_text: Their eyes widen — not at the pencil, but at the paper. They draw carefully, labeling things in a child's uneven hand. The map that emerges is more detailed than the dirt version: three source points, a contamination zone marked with an X, and a path to clean water that no one at the station has found. They hand it to you like it's nothing. Like they didn't just solve a problem the adults gave up on.
choices.epitaph: Gave a child a pencil. Got a map that might save lives. The world rewards the wrong people.

choices.label: Tell them to be careful — the dust might be contaminated.
choices.outcome_text: The child looks at their hands, then back at the drawing. 'I know,' they say. 'But someone has to write it down.' They smooth over the drawing with their foot and walk away. The map is gone. Whatever they saw in the water's patterns is gone too. You protected their health and lost something you can't name.
choices.epitaph: Protected a child. Lost a map. Sometimes the safe choice costs more than the risky one.

choices.label: Children don't understand water tables. Walk on.
choices.outcome_text: You walk past. The child doesn't watch you go — they're already drawing again, a new map, a new set of lines that another adult will ignore. The water station creaks and pumps. Somewhere beneath it, the water follows paths that a child understands and you don't.
choices.epitaph: Ignored a child. Ignored a map. The water kept flowing. I kept not knowing.

quests.trigger: A doctor at the knowledge keeper camp has been writing by lamplight for three nights straight. Tonight, they finally look up and beckon you over.
quests.discovery: The doctor's desk is a door balanced on two crates. Papers cover every surface — not notes, but diagrams. Cross-sections of the human lung, annotated in a cramped hand. They push a sheet toward you. 'Tell me if this makes sense,' they say. Their eyes are red-rimmed. They haven't slept. The diagram shows radiation damage patterns that don't match any published research you've seen — because it was never published. It was never meant to be seen.

choices.label: Study the diagrams carefully. Ask what they've found.
choices.outcome_text: The doctor talks for two hours. Their research — conducted on the dead, on the dying, on themselves — shows that low-dose chronic exposure creates a pattern distinct from acute radiation sickness. A slow fibrosis. They've been tracking it in survivors for months, mapping the progression. 'Nobody wants to hear that the air is killing them slowly,' the doctor says. 'But if they knew the signs, they could slow it. Filter the air. Boil the water twice. Small things.' You listen. You memorize. The doctor's hands stop shaking for the first time in days.
choices.epitaph: A doctor showed me the shape of slow death. I carried it out so others might live longer.

choices.label: Offer to help them organize the research.
choices.outcome_text: You sort the papers while they talk. The research is meticulous — sample counts, exposure durations, symptom timelines. It would have been a career-defining paper in the before. Now it's a survival guide written in a dead woman's handwriting. Together, you arrange it into something readable. The doctor watches you work and says, quietly, 'I thought I'd die with this on my desk. Now it might outlive me.'
choices.epitaph: Helped a doctor organize her life's work. She called it survival. I called it the least I could do.

choices.label: "This is above my head. But good work."
choices.outcome_text: The doctor nods, but something dims. They pull the papers back, stack them neatly, and return to the lamplight. You've been polite. You've been honest. And you've left a room where knowledge was being born and walked away from it. The doctor writes alone again.
choices.epitaph: Said it was above me. It wasn't. It was just uncomfortable.

choices.label: "People don't want bad news right now."
choices.outcome_text: The doctor's pen stops. They look at you the way a surgeon looks at a tumor. 'People don't want a lot of things,' they say. 'That doesn't change what's true.' They turn back to the papers. The conversation is over. You've confused comfort with cowardice and called it kindness.
choices.epitaph: Told a doctor to hide the truth. She didn't argue. That was worse.

quests.display_name: The Last Broadcast of Settlement Nine
quests.trigger: A radio operator at the abandoned home is replaying the same recording over and over. The signal is from a settlement that no longer exists.
quests.discovery: The radio crackles in the dark room like a heartbeat. The operator sits with headphones pressed tight, eyes closed. The recording loops: a woman's voice, calm and precise, reading a supply manifest. Then static. Then the voice again. The operator opens one eye when you enter. 'They were the last ones to fall back from the burn zone,' they say. 'This is everything that's left of them. Forty-three names on a manifest. A voice saying what they had. What they needed. What they were.'

choices.label: Listen to the full recording. Memorize the names.
choices.outcome_text: The recording runs eleven minutes. Forty-three names. Supply quantities down to the individual bandage. A voice that doesn't waver even when the static swells. You sit in the dark and commit each name to memory — not because anyone will call a roll, but because forgetting is the second death. When it ends, the operator looks at you. 'You heard them,' they say. Not a question. A confirmation. 'Now you carry them too.'
choices.epitaph: Forty-three names. I can still hear the thirty-first. She had a cough between words.

choices.label: Ask the operator how they got the recording.
choices.outcome_text: The story unfolds slowly. The operator was at Settlement Nine. They were the radio tech. When the burn zone expanded, they were sent out with the recording — the last manifest, the last proof that forty-three people existed. 'I was the one who got away,' they say. 'So I'm the one who has to remember.' The weight of survival sits between you like a third person in the room.
choices.epitaph: The radio operator was the one who escaped. Carrying ghosts is a kind of survival.

choices.label: "We need to focus on the living, not the dead."
choices.outcome_text: The operator removes the headphones and sets them on the radio. 'The living were the dead once,' they say. 'And the dead were the living. You're drawing a line that doesn't exist.' They put the headphones back on. The recording resumes. You've been told something important, but you're not sure you're ready to understand it yet.
choices.epitaph: Told a mourner to move on. She didn't argue. The dead don't argue. That's the point.

quests.trigger: A coded message comes through the radio at the military outpost. The operator says it's been repeating for six days. Nobody can crack it.
quests.discovery: The military outpost smells of rust and old batteries. The radio operator — a former signals technician, by their bearing — slides a sheet of paper across the table. Groups of five characters. Repeating every forty-seven seconds. 'It's not military cipher,' they say. 'I'd know those. This is something else. Personal.' They've been staring at it for six days. The pattern is there — you can feel it — but the key is missing. The operator pushes a second sheet toward you. 'I found this in the dead drop where the signal originates. It's a grocery list. From before.'

choices.label: Compare the grocery list to the cipher. Look for a personal key.
choices.outcome_text: It takes an hour. The key is the grocery list — not the items, but the quantities. Each number maps to a letter shift. The decoded message is not tactical. It's a father telling his daughter where he buried her mother's jewelry box. Coordinates. A description of the oak tree. 'I'm sorry I couldn't save more,' the message ends. The operator reads it and puts their head in their hands. 'A father,' they whisper. 'All this time. A father.'
choices.epitaph: Cracked a six-day cipher. It was a father's apology. Some messages aren't meant for armies.

choices.label: Help the operator decode it systematically.
choices.outcome_text: You work through it together — frequency analysis, pattern matching, dead ends. Three hours in, the operator finds the key: a personal memory encoded in the grocery list. The decoded message is coordinates and a name. A burial site. The operator stares at the decoded text. 'Someone loved someone enough to broadcast their location to the world,' they say. 'Even after the world ended.'
choices.epitaph: Spent three hours on a cipher. Found a love story. The war didn't erase everything.

choices.label: "It's probably nothing. Just noise."
choices.outcome_text: The operator's jaw tightens. 'Noise doesn't repeat every forty-seven seconds for six days.' They turn back to the radio. You've dismissed something that clearly matters to someone, and the operator will remember that. Not the dismissal — the fact that you didn't even try.
choices.epitaph: Called a message noise. The operator didn't forgive me. Neither would the father behind the cipher.

quests.trigger: A trader at the water station keeps a second ledger — one they don't show customers. Tonight, they leave it open on their table.
quests.discovery: The trader is packing up for the night. Their trade ledger is locked in a case, but a smaller book lies open on the table — a personal account. Not of money. Of debts. Names and dates and small annotations: 'owed three filters — lost daughter to fever, couldn't charge,' 'gave away last antibiotics — mother, same cough as his,' 'accepted a drawing instead of payment — child, needed to feel useful.' The trader sees you reading and doesn't close the book.

choices.label: Read the ledger. Ask about the people in it.
choices.outcome_text: The trader sits back down. Each name has a story. The mother who traded her wedding ring for clean water — the trader gave it back. The child who brought a drawing — the trader still has it, pinned inside the ledger's back cover. The soldier who owed everything and died before paying — the trader crossed out the debt the day they heard. 'A ledger isn't about money,' the trader says. 'It's about who owed what to whom, and who forgave what when it didn't matter anymore.' You close the book gently. The trader nods.
choices.epitaph: Read a trader's secret ledger. Every debt was a person. Every forgiveness was a choice.

choices.label: "You could have gone broke doing this."
choices.outcome_text: The trader laughs — a dry, cracked sound. 'Went broke on day twelve. This is day four hundred and something.' They tap the ledger. 'This is the real accounting. The other one is just... keeping score with people who don't remember the rules.' They close the book and slide it into their pack. 'You're the first one who noticed,' they add, almost as an afterthought.
choices.epitaph: A trader went broke on day twelve. Kept going anyway. The real currency was always people.

choices.label: "You should hide that. Someone could use it against you."
choices.outcome_text: The trader considers this. Then they close the book and lock it away. 'Maybe,' they say. 'But if I start hiding who I am, what am I trading for?' The practical advice lands, but something else closes with the book. You've been useful. You've also been a reminder that the world is still dangerous, even at a water station, even at night, even to kindness.
choices.epitaph: Gave practical advice. It was correct. It was also the least important thing in the room.

choices.label: "Sentiment doesn't keep you alive."
choices.outcome_text: The trader closes the ledger slowly. 'No,' they say. 'It doesn't. But it's what I'm alive for.' They pack up in silence. The conversation is over. You've drawn a line between survival and living, and the trader has chosen a side you don't understand yet.
choices.epitaph: Told a kind man sentiment was weakness. He pitied me for it.

quests.trigger: A former soldier at the military outpost has started talking in their sleep. The other refugees are frightened. You're asked to intervene.
quests.discovery: The soldier sleeps on a cot in the corner of the outpost's barracks. Even from across the room, you can hear the fragments — place names, numbers, a repeated phrase in a language you don't recognize. The other refugees have backed away. The soldier's hands move in their sleep: checking a magazine, cradling something that isn't there, digging. When you sit beside them, their eyes open — not awake, not asleep — and they say, clearly, 'The bridge is gone. Tell them the bridge is gone.'

choices.label: Stay with them. Wake them gently. Ask what they need to tell.
choices.outcome_text: They wake shaking. The story comes in pieces over the next hour. They were part of a retreat — the last column out of the eastern corridor. They carried a message: the bridge at sector seven was compromised, and anyone using it would fall into irradiated water. The message was delivered. But the column that received it didn't make it. Forty soldiers walked onto a bridge that the soldier's unit knew was gone. 'I carry it home every night,' they say. 'The bridge is gone. I keep telling people. But the people I need to tell are already dead.'
choices.epitaph: A soldier's war followed them home. The bridge was gone. The dead couldn't hear. I could.

choices.label: Write down what they say in their sleep. Give it to them in the morning.
choices.outcome_text: You sit with paper and pencil through the night. The soldier talks for three hours. You write everything — names, coordinates, the repeated phrase (it's a unit motto: 'No one walks alone'). In the morning, you hand them the pages. They read them in silence. Then they fold the papers carefully and put them in their pocket. 'Now it's not just in my head,' they say. 'Thank you for taking it out.'
choices.epitaph: Wrote down a soldier's nightmares. Gave them back in the morning. Lighter, they said. Both of us.

choices.label: Move them to a separate room so others can sleep.
choices.outcome_text: You carry the soldier's things to a storage room. They sleep more peacefully there — alone. The other refugees relax. But the soldier's story stays locked in their sleeping mind, unspoken, unrecorded. You've solved a practical problem. You've also ensured that whatever the bridge was, whatever message it carried, dies with the soldier. Eventually.
choices.epitaph: Solved the noise problem. Lost the story. Some practical solutions have impractical costs.

choices.label: "They need to get over it. We all do."
choices.outcome_text: The refugee who asked you to intervene nods. The soldier sleeps on, carrying their bridge, their dead, their unspoken message. You've sided with the living against the haunted. It's understandable. It's also the kind of thing that makes survivors into strangers.
choices.epitaph: Said a soldier should get over it. Easier said. The bridge was still gone in their dreams.

quests.display_name: The Prophet of the Burn Zone
quests.trigger: A figure at the burn zone's edge claims to have seen something in the ash storms. Others call them mad. They're asking for one person to listen.
quests.discovery: The prophet — if that's what they are — stands at the edge of the burn zone where the ash falls thickest. Their skin is scarred, their eyes clear. They don't preach. They describe. 'The storms have a pattern,' they say. 'Three days calm, then a wall of ash from the northwest. Then two days of red dust. Then calm again. I've tracked it for forty cycles.' They show you marks scratched into a flat stone — a calendar, crude but consistent. 'People call it prophecy. It's just paying attention.'

choices.label: Study the stone calendar. Ask how they learned to track the storms.
choices.outcome_text: The prophet — the observer, the weather-reader, whatever you call them — explains. They were a meteorologist before the exchange. The instruments are gone, but the patterns remain. Forty cycles of watching, scratching, counting. The prediction is simple: the next ash wall comes in two days. Anyone in the open will be buried. 'I'm not a prophet,' they say. 'I'm just the one who didn't stop looking.' You copy the pattern into your own notes. The next storm arrives exactly when they said it would.
choices.epitaph: Called a prophet. They were a scientist with a rock and patience. The storm came on time.

choices.label: Help them warn the settlement before the next storm.
choices.outcome_text: Together, you walk back to the nearest shelter. The observer presents their stone calendar. Some listen. Some don't.
