You vouch for them — not because you understand the science, but because you've seen the marks, counted the cycles, watched the last storm arrive on schedule. Half the shelter moves to interior rooms. The ash wall comes. The ones who moved are alive. The observer doesn't gloat. 'Next one's in three days,' they say. 'Start earlier.'
choices.epitaph: Helped a weather-reader save people who called them mad. The ash doesn't care about opinions.

choices.label: "Even if you're right, people won't listen to a burn-zone hermit."
choices.outcome_text: The observer nods slowly. 'That's what I was afraid of.' They return to the burn zone's edge. The storm comes. People shelter — some by luck, some by chance. The observer survives too, scratched into their stone calendar. You were right about people not listening. You were wrong to use it as an excuse not to try.
choices.epitaph: Was right about people. Wrong to let it stop me. The observer kept counting anyway.

choices.label: "This is superstition. Ash storms are random."
choices.outcome_text: The observer doesn't argue. They just turn back to the burn zone and resume their counting. You walk away confident in your rationality. Two days later, the ash wall comes. You survive. So does the observer. The difference is that they knew it was coming, and you got lucky. Luck runs out. Patterns don't.
choices.epitaph: Called science superstition. Got lucky once. The observer kept counting. I kept being wrong.

quests.trigger: A mediator at the peacekeeper outpost is trying to divide a single water filter between two settlements. Both claim it first. Both are dying without it.
quests.discovery: The mediator sits between two envoys who won't look at each other. The water filter sits on the table — a battered but functional unit, the only one within fifty kilometers. The mediator has been talking for six hours. They look at you with exhausted eyes. 'I need one more perspective,' they say. 'Not to decide. To understand what I'm deciding between.' The two settlements: one has children. The other has the engineers who can maintain the filter long-term. Both claims are legitimate. Both are desperate.

choices.label: Listen to both sides fully before speaking.
choices.outcome_text: You hear both cases. Settlement A: fourteen children under twelve, three adults with radiation sickness, no technical capacity. Settlement B: no children, but six engineers and a workshop. Losing the filter kills A slowly. Losing the filter kills B's ability to fix the next one. You listen. You ask questions. And then you say something neither side expected: 'What if the engineers go to Settlement A? The filter stays with the children, and the people who can maintain it go where it's needed.' Silence. Then, slowly, the impossible becomes discussable.
choices.epitaph: Listened to two dying settlements. Found a third option no one saw because everyone was defending.

choices.label: Propose a rotation schedule — the filter moves between settlements.
choices.outcome_text: The rotation plan is practical: two weeks at Settlement A, two weeks at B, with the engineers traveling to maintain it. Both envoys hate it. Both accept it. The mediator signs the agreement and looks at you. 'It won't last,' they say. 'But it lasts long enough for someone to find a second filter.' Sometimes the best solution is the one that buys time.
choices.epitaph: Proposed a compromise both sides hated. It lasted eleven days. That was eleven days of water.

choices.label: "Give it to the settlement with children. That's simple."
choices.outcome_text: The mediator nods. Settlement B's envoy stands and walks out. The filter goes to the children. The mediator pulls you aside. 'You chose the moral answer. Now Settlement B's engineers will let their filter break because they have no incentive to maintain someone else's equipment. In three months, both settlements will be without water. But the children will have lasted longer.' You helped. You also created a problem you can't see from here.
choices.epitaph: Chose the children. The math was cruel. The engineers let the second filter die. Morality has a half-life.

choices.label: "This isn't my problem. You're the mediator."
choices.outcome_text: The mediator stares at you. Then they turn back to the envoys and resume the negotiation alone. The filter stays on the table. The conversation continues for another three hours. You leave. Behind you, two settlements are still dying, and the mediator is still the only one trying to stop it. You've preserved your neutrality. You've also demonstrated that neutrality has a cost, and other people pay it.
choices.epitaph: Walked away from a mediation. The mediator didn't. Some distances are measured in conscience.

quests.trigger: A former raider at the raider camp wants to surrender intelligence about their old group. But they need someone to hear the full story first — to understand what they're leaving behind.
quests.discovery: The defector sits with their back to the wall, a packed bag at their feet. They've been with the raiders for two years. They want out — not because of guilt, but because they've seen what comes next. 'They're not just raiding anymore,' they say. 'They're building. A fort. A hierarchy. They're becoming the thing we survived.' They want to trade information: patrol routes, supply caches, the location of the new fort. But first, they need you to understand why they joined in the first place. 'Nobody starts as a raider,' they say. 'They start as someone who ran out of other options.'

choices.label: Listen to their full story before taking the intelligence.
choices.outcome_text: The story takes two hours. A family destroyed. A settlement burned. A choice between starving alone or eating with people who take. The defector describes the slow erosion — how the first theft felt like survival, the tenth felt like routine, the hundredth felt like nothing. 'That's the part I'm running from,' they say. 'Not the raiding. The nothing.' You listen. You take the intelligence. And you understand, without agreeing, how a person becomes a raider. The defector leaves through the back. You hope they find something to replace the nothing.
choices.epitaph: A raider told me how they became one. The scariest part was how it made sense.

choices.label: Take the intelligence and promise to advocate for their safety.
choices.outcome_text: The defector hands over a hand-drawn map — patrol routes, cache locations, the fort's weak points. In exchange, you promise to make sure the peacekeepers know they've left the group. 'I don't need forgiveness,' they say. 'I just need to not be hunted.' You nod. The map is detailed, accurate, valuable. The defector disappears into the night. You've gained intelligence and made a promise. Whether it's kept depends on people you can't control.
choices.epitaph: Took a raider's map. Promised their safety. Promises are expensive currency now.

choices.label: "Just give me the information. We don't need the backstory."
choices.outcome_text: The defector's face hardens. They hand over the map — terse, functional, stripped of context. 'Patrol routes. Cache locations. That's what you want.' The intelligence is good. But you've missed the part that would have helped you understand not just where the raiders are, but why they do what they do. Information without context is just coordinates.
choices.epitaph: Got the map. Missed the meaning. Intelligence without understanding is just a list of places.

choices.label: "You're a raider. Why should I believe anything you say?"
choices.outcome_text: The defector stands. The bag stays at their feet. 'You shouldn't,' they say. 'That's why I needed someone to listen first. So they'd know whether the change was real.' They pick up the bag and walk out the other side. The intelligence is gone. The defector is gone. You've protected yourself from a possible lie and lost a possible truth. The raiders' fort is still being built. Someone else will find it. Someone else will listen.
choices.epitaph: Refused to listen. A defector walked back into the raiders. Maybe they deserved it. Maybe not.

quests.trigger: The knowledge keeper is packing books into waterproof cases. They've been collecting them from the ruins. They want someone to know what's being saved — and what's being lost.
quests.discovery: The knowledge keeper's collection fills three rooms of the camp. Books stacked floor to ceiling — not just technical manuals, but novels, poetry collections, children's picture books, histories. They're cataloging each one on index cards, cross-referencing by subject and condition. 'We're saving the knowledge,' they say. Then they pause. 'But I need someone to tell me: which parts of the knowledge matter? I can't save everything. The water's rising in the lower rooms. I have to choose.'

choices.label: Help them sort. Listen to what each book means to them.
choices.outcome_text: You spend the night sorting. The knowledge keeper tells you about each book as they decide. The medical textbook — essential. The farming guide — essential. The poetry collection — they hold it longest. 'This one has a poem about rain,' they say. 'Real rain, before the ash. If we lose the technical books, people die. If we lose this, people forget what they were surviving for.' They save both. The water rises. Some books get wet. The knowledge keeper carries the poetry collection on their head to keep it dry.
choices.epitaph: Saved books from rising water. A keeper chose poetry over comfort. I understood why.

choices.label: "Save the practical books first. Stories can wait."
choices.outcome_text: The knowledge keeper nods and starts with the medical texts. Efficient. Rational. The poetry collection goes into the last case, on top, where the water reaches it first. They don't notice until it's too late. The technical knowledge survives. The poem about rain dissolves into pulp. You were right about priorities. The knowledge keeper doesn't say so. They just carry the wet case out and set it in the sun, as if drying might restore something that wasn't just ink.
choices.epitaph: Saved the practical books. Lost a poem about rain. The keeper dried the pages. Nothing came back.

choices.label: Ask what they would save if they could only take one book.
choices.outcome_text: The question stops them. They walk through the collection, touching spines. Finally, they pull out a small, water-stained book. A children's story. 'This was my daughter's,' they say. 'It's not important to anyone else. But it's the book I read to her every night before the exchange.' They put it back. 'I can't choose one. That's the point. Knowledge isn't a single book. It's the whole shelf.' They start carrying cases to higher ground, one by one, saving everything they can.
choices.epitaph: Asked which book mattered most. The keeper couldn't choose. That was the right answer.

choices.label: "It's just paper. Focus on surviving."
choices.outcome_text: The knowledge keeper looks at you the way a doctor looks at someone who doesn't believe in germs. 'Paper,' they repeat. They return to their cataloging. You've drawn a line between survival and meaning, and the person who's dedicated their life to preserving meaning has decided you're on the wrong side of it. The water rises. The books get saved — or they don't. Either way, you're not part of it anymore.
choices.epitaph: Called books just paper. The keeper stopped talking to me. Some losses aren't measured in calories.

quests.trigger: A former teacher at the shelter meeting room has gathered three children for a lesson. They have no books, no chalk, no classroom. They want you to sit in.
quests.discovery: The teacher has arranged three crates as desks. The children sit on the floor. The lesson, you realize, is about memory. The teacher is teaching them to memorize — not facts, but structures. How to remember a sequence. How to build a memory palace from a place they've never seen. 'The world will try to take everything from you,' the teacher says. 'But it can't take what you've built inside your head.' They notice you at the door. 'Sit,' they say. 'This lesson is for anyone who wants to carry something forward.'

choices.label: Sit down. Learn the technique. Take it seriously.
choices.outcome_text: You sit on the floor between a seven-year-old and a ten-year-old. The teacher builds a memory palace out of the shelter — room by room, detail by detail. Each room holds a category: survival skills in the gate room, medical knowledge in the storage room, agricultural techniques in the meeting room. The children absorb it like water. You do too. The technique works — you can still recall the sequence hours later. The teacher watches you all with quiet satisfaction. 'Now it survives,' they say. 'Even if I don't.'
choices.epitaph: Sat on the floor and learned to remember. A teacher built a palace in my head. It still stands.

choices.label: Ask the teacher how long they've been doing this.
choices.outcome_text: Since the exchange. Every settlement they've passed through, they've gathered children and taught them. Not reading or math — those come and go. They teach the architecture of memory itself. 'Give a child a fact, it lasts a day. Teach them to build a palace, and they can carry a library.' They've done this in fourteen settlements. Three of those settlements no longer exist. 'But the children remember,' they say. 'So the knowledge moves.'
choices.epitaph: A teacher has been building memory palaces in children across fourteen settlements. Three settlements are gone. The palaces remain.

choices.label: "They need practical skills, not memory tricks."
choices.outcome_text: The teacher doesn't argue. 'Practical skills fade when the tools break,' they say. 'Memory is the tool that never breaks.' They return to the lesson. The children are listening — really listening — in a way that practical instruction rarely achieves. You've voiced a reasonable concern. You've also demonstrated that you don't understand what education means when there are no schools left.
choices.epitaph: Called memory tricks impractical. The children remembered everything. I remembered nothing.

quests.trigger: A woman at the abandoned home is humming a song she says she heard from her grandmother. She's forgotten the words but remembers the melody.
quests.discovery: The woman sits on the steps of a collapsed house, humming. The melody is unlike anything you've heard in the wasteland — not a work song, not a warning, not a prayer. It's something older. Something that was written for no purpose except beauty. She stops when she sees you. 'I know the tune,' she says. 'But the words are gone. My grandmother sang it in a language I never learned.' She hums it again. The melody fills the empty street like water filling a dry well.

choices.label: Ask her to hum it again. Try to write down the melody.
choices.outcome_text: She hums it three times. You sketch the notes on scrap paper — you're not a musician, but the intervals are clear. The melody is simple, repetitive, built for a voice that wanted to be remembered. When you show her the notation, she cries — not from sadness, but from relief. 'Now it's not just in my head,' she says. 'It exists somewhere else.' You fold the paper and give it back to her. 'It was always yours,' you say. She shakes her head. 'Now it's yours too.'
choices.epitaph: Wrote down a song with no words. A woman's grandmother lives in the melody. Now so do I.

choices.label: Sing along. Try to find harmony with what she remembers.
choices.outcome_text: Your voice is rough. Hers is clear. Together, the melody takes on a shape neither of you could make alone — a harmony that fills in the gaps where the words should be. She stops, listens to the echo between the walls, and says, 'That's it. That's what it sounded like when she sang it with my grandfather.' You've reconstructed something from memory and breath. The song doesn't need words. It has you.
choices.epitaph: Sang harmony with a stranger. A dead language filled the gap. The song didn't need words.

choices.label: "Songs don't matter now. People need food, not music."
choices.outcome_text: The woman stops humming. She looks at you with an expression that isn't anger — it's grief, but not for the song. For you. 'Food keeps the body,' she says. 'This keeps everything else.' She stands and walks away. The melody follows her, humming under her breath. You're left with the silence you asked for. It's exactly as nourishing as it sounds.
choices.epitaph: Told a woman songs don't matter. She pitied me. The silence she left was very loud.

quests.trigger: A cartographer at the eastern road is drawing a map of everything they remember. They say it's the last one they'll make — their eyes are failing.
quests.discovery: The cartographer works by candlelight, a magnifying glass pressed to one eye. The map covers an entire wall — every road, settlement, water source, and danger zone they can recall. But the edges are blurring. They hold the candle too close. They squint at distances that should be clear. 'Two more weeks,' they say, without looking up. 'Then I can't do this anymore. I need someone to copy the important parts.' They hand you a pencil. 'Start with the water sources. Everything else is secondary.'

choices.label: Copy the water sources. Ask about each one as you draw.
choices.outcome_text: You copy for six hours. Each water source has a story — the well that went salty after the second storm, the spring that appeared in a crater nobody remembers forming, the cistern under the old school that still collects rain. The cartographer dictates annotations in a steady voice, correcting your lines when they drift. 'Here,' they say, touching a spot on the map. 'This is where I grew up. It's not a water source. But I wanted it on the map anyway.' You draw it in. Some things belong on maps for reasons that have nothing to do with survival.
choices.epitaph: Copied a dying cartographer's map. Drew in their childhood home. Some places matter beyond water.

choices.label: Copy the entire map. Work through the night.
choices.outcome_text: You work until the candle burns down and the cartographer replaces it. By dawn, you've copied eighty percent. The cartographer reviews your work with the magnifying glass, making tiny corrections. 'You have good hands,' they say. 'The map will outlive both of us.' They roll your copy carefully and hand it to you. 'Take it somewhere it does good. I'll finish the original for the wall.' You carry a dead woman's memory of the world in your pack. It weighs almost nothing. It weighs everything.
choices.epitaph: Copied a map through the night. A cartographer's eyes are failing. The map will not.

choices.label: "I'll find someone with better eyes to help you."
choices.outcome_text: The cartographer nods but doesn't stop working. 'Do that,' they say. You leave and search. The nearest person with cartography skills is three days' walk away. By the time you return, the cartographer has finished the water sources but the roads are getting sloppy. 'You took too long,' they say, without blame. You help where you can. The map is incomplete. The cartographer's eyes are worse than they said.
choices.epitaph: Went to find help. Came back too late. The map is incomplete. So is everything else.

choices.label: "Maps are dangerous. Raiders could use this."
choices.outcome_text: The cartographer sets down the pencil. 'Maps are knowledge,' they say. 'Knowledge is dangerous. So is ignorance. So is everything, if you look at it that way.' They return to the wall. You've raised a valid concern. You've also told a dying woman that her life's work is a liability. The map stays on the wall. Whether it helps or harms depends on who finds it. That was always true.
choices.epitaph: Called a dying woman's map dangerous. She didn't argue. Maps don't argue. They just show what's there.

quests.trigger: A leader from a rival settlement is stranded at the raider camp after a supply run goes wrong. They expect hostility. Instead, they find you willing to listen.
quests.discovery: The rival leader sits with a bandaged arm, a broken supply cart beside them. They recognize you — or your settlement's mark — and tense. But the raiders aren't here, and the night is cold, and they're alone with a stranger who isn't reaching for a weapon. 'Your people took our southern water access,' they say. Not an accusation. A statement of fact. Then, quieter: 'We would have done the same.' The fire crackles. Neither of you moves toward your respective sides.

choices.label: "Tell me what happened from your side."
choices.outcome_text: They talk for an hour. The southern water access wasn't seized — it was abandoned by your settlement during the flood season, and theirs needed it. They didn't take it. They occupied it. The distinction matters to them. They describe their settlement — not as an enemy, but as a group of people making impossible choices with incomplete information. You recognize the description. It sounds like yours. When they finish, you share your side. The two stories overlap more than either settlement realized. The rival leader nods slowly. 'Maybe we should talk,' they say. 'Before the next misunderstanding.'
choices.epitaph: Listened to a rival's story. Heard my own settlement's reflection. We were more alike than we knew.

choices.label: Share water and bandage their arm. Talk about something else.
choices.outcome_text: You work on the bandage in silence. The rival leader winces but doesn't pull away. When the water passes between you, neither acknowledges what it means. You talk about the weather, the raiders, the quality of the firewood. Ordinary things. The enemy becomes a person complaining about smoke in their eyes. By morning, when their cart is fixed enough to roll, you've exchanged no intelligence, made no treaties, and accomplished nothing strategic. You've also ensured that the next encounter between your settlements won't start with weapons.
choices.epitaph: Bandaged a rival's arm. We talked about smoke and firewood. The next meeting won't start with weapons.

choices.label: "Your people started this. Don't pretend otherwise."
choices.outcome_text: The rival leader's jaw tightens. They don't argue — they've had this argument before, with people who weren't listening. 'Fine,' they say. 'We started it. You finished it. Are we done?' The fire burns lower. The night gets colder. You've won an argument with an injured person who was offering you a different kind of exchange. The victory tastes like ash.
choices.epitaph: Won an argument with an injured rival. The victory tasted like the ground I was sitting on.

choices.label: Say nothing. Wait for the raiders to deal with them.
choices.outcome_text: You sit in silence. The rival leader watches you, reading your intent. They stand, wincing, and begin repairing their cart one-handed. 'I see,' they say. The raiders don't come that night. In the morning, the rival leader is gone. You've done nothing — said nothing, helped nothing, risked nothing. You've also confirmed everything the rival settlement believes about yours. That you'll watch an enemy bleed and call it neutrality.
choices.epitaph: Watched a rival bleed and called it nothing. They'll remember. My settlement will pay for it.

quests.trigger: A person who betrayed your settlement months ago has returned. They say they owe you an explanation. Not an apology — an explanation.
quests.discovery: They stand at the edge of the peacekeeper outpost's common area, where the light is neutral and no one has a reason to shoot. The betrayer — they gave your settlement's supply locations to a rival group — looks older than you remember. Thinner. They don't approach. 'I'm not asking to come back,' they say. 'I'm asking you to understand why I did it. Not so you'll forgive me. So you'll know it could happen to anyone.' The peacekeeper outpost's neutral ground holds you both at equal distance.

choices.label: Listen. Not to forgive — to understand.
choices.outcome_text: The story is not heroic. Their sibling was held by the rival group. The trade was simple: information for a life. They made the calculation in a night. Your settlement's supplies were exposed; their sibling was returned alive. 'I'd do it again,' they say. 'That's what you need to understand. Not that I'm sorry. That I'd do it again.' You listen. The betrayal doesn't shrink. But it gains a shape — a human shape, ugly and comprehensible. You leave knowing something you wish you didn't: that anyone, given the same choice, might choose the same way.
choices.epitaph: Listened to a betrayer's reason. They'd do it again. So might I. That's the part that keeps me awake.

choices.label: "Tell me. But know that I'll share this with the settlement."
choices.outcome_text: The betrayer nods. 'That's why I came to neutral ground. I wanted it on the record.' They tell the story — the sibling, the trade, the calculation. You listen, then repeat it back to the settlement when you return. Some understand. Some don't. The betrayal is no longer a mystery; it's a fact with a reason attached. The settlement debates what to do. Nothing is resolved. But the unknown — the thing that breeds fear — has been replaced with something manageable. A reason. A human, terrible, understandable reason.
choices.epitaph: Brought a betrayer's reason home. The settlement didn't forgive. But they understood. That's different.

choices.label: "I don't owe you my attention."
choices.outcome_text: The betrayer nods. 'I know.' They turn and walk away. You've exercised your right to not listen. The reason stays unspoken. The betrayal remains a hole in your settlement's story — a gap where understanding should be. You'll fill it with assumptions. The betrayer will carry the truth alone. Both of you are poorer for the exchange you didn't have.
choices.epitaph: Refused to listen to a betrayer. The hole in our story stayed a hole. I filled it with guesses.

choices.label: "You betrayed us. There's nothing to explain."
choices.outcome_text: The betrayer's expression doesn't change. 'That's what I was afraid you'd say.' They leave. You've closed a door that was opened at personal cost. The betrayal is now a permanent story — the one where someone did something unforgivable and there was no reason, because no one asked. It's simpler. It's also less true.
choices.epitaph: Shut down a betrayer. Got simplicity instead of truth. They're not the same thing.

quests.trigger: A soldier from the opposing faction is found wounded near the military outpost. In their delirium, they keep calling for someone by name — the same name as someone you lost.
quests.discovery: The soldier is young, bleeding from shrapnel, and speaking in fragments. The name they keep saying is one you know — a name from your own settlement's casualty list. Your first thought is that this is a trick. Your second is that the name is spoken with a familiarity that goes beyond intelligence gathering. You crouch beside them. The soldier's eyes find yours. 'Tell Mara I found the... I found the place,' they say. Then they lose focus. The name sits in the air between you like a bridge neither of you built.

choices.label: Stay with them. Bandage the wound. Listen for more.
choices.outcome_text: You work on the shrapnel while the soldier drifts in and out of coherence. The story emerges in pieces: they and your settlement's Mara were siblings, separated before the exchange. They've been searching — not for tactical advantage, but for each other. The 'place' they found was the family home, reduced to rubble, but they'd marked the foundation stones so Mara would recognize them. You bandage the wound. The soldier stabilizes. You carry a message that no one asked for: that Mara's sibling is alive, and they've been looking. The war doesn't pause for this. But something does.
choices.epitaph: Bandaged an enemy. Found out they were family. The war didn't pause. Something did.

choices.label: Treat the wound, then ask about the connection to Mara.
choices.outcome_text: The soldier, stabilized enough to speak clearly, tells you the story. Siblings. Separated. The search. The foundation stones. You listen with the medical kit in one hand and a growing realization in your chest: the war has made enemies of people who were looking for the same thing you were. You write down the location of the foundation stones. You promise to tell Mara. The soldier grips your wrist. 'Don't let her come to the front,' they say. 'Just tell her I'm alive. That's enough.'
choices.epitaph: An enemy soldier was someone's sibling. Treated the wound. Carried the message. The war kept its shape.

choices.label: Treat the wound and hand them over to the peacekeepers.
choices.outcome_text: You patch the shrapnel and flag down a peacekeeper patrol. The soldier is taken to the outpost's medical station. The name — Mara's name, the sibling connection — stays with you. You could pass it along. You could also let it die in the bureaucracy of neutral ground. You write it down in your journal. Someday, maybe, the information will find the right person. Someday is a word that means a lot in a world with no calendars.
choices.epitaph: Handed an enemy to the peacekeepers. Wrote down a name. Someday might mean something. Maybe.

choices.label: "They're the enemy. Leave them."
choices.outcome_text: You stand and walk away. The soldier's voice follows you — the name, the fragments, the plea for someone named Mara. You don't look back. By morning, the soldier is dead or gone. The message dies with them. Mara never learns. Somewhere, a sibling searched across a war zone and got close enough to leave a message at your feet. You chose not to carry it. The name echoes less each day. That's how it works.
choices.epitaph: Left an enemy to die. A message died with them. Mara never knew. The name faded. That's how it works.

quests.display_name: The Stranger Who Knew Your Name
quests.trigger: A stranger at the shelter gate knows your name. They say they knew someone you used to be. They want to tell you what that person became.
quests.discovery: The stranger is leaning against the gate wall, arms crossed, watching you approach. They say your name — not the name you use now, but the one from before. The one you stopped using. 'You look different,' they say. 'Harder. I knew you when you were soft.' They're not threatening. They're not nostalgic. They're reporting, like a witness describing a scene. 'I'm not here to bring you back,' they say. 'I'm here because someone should tell you what you've lost. Even if you don't want to hear it.'

choices.label: Listen. Let them describe the person you were.
choices.outcome_text: They talk for twenty minutes. The person you were laughed easily. Trusted strangers. Cried at things that weren't dangerous. The stranger describes you with the precision of someone who paid attention. 'You used to stop for animals on the road,' they say. 'Now you walk past.' The description is accurate and unbearable. You listen because it's true. When they finish, you ask, 'Is that person still in here somewhere?' The stranger shrugs. 'I don't know. But they were worth mentioning.' They walk away. You stand at the gate for a long time.
choices.epitaph: A stranger described who I was. I stood at the gate for an hour. The person they described was worth knowing.

choices.label: Ask how they knew you. What happened between then and now.
choices.outcome_text: The stranger was in your first settlement — the one that fell. They watched you change. 'Day by day,' they say. 'Each loss made you more efficient and less... there.' The conversation is not an accusation. It's a timeline. You learn things about yourself you couldn't see from the inside: the moments when you stopped asking questions, stopped offering help, stopped looking up. The stranger has been carrying this observation for months. 'Someone should say it,' they told themselves. Now they have. You carry it forward. It's heavier than you expected.
choices.epitaph: Learned what I look like from the outside. The stranger carried the mirror for months. I carry it now.

choices.label: "That person is dead. I'm who I need to be now."
choices.outcome_text: The stranger nods. 'Probably,' they say. 'But dead people don't need to hear things. You do.' They leave. You've defended the person you've become. You've also refused to examine whether the becoming was a choice or just a survival reflex. The gate closes. The stranger's description stays in your ear like a song you can't quite remember.
choices.epitaph: Said the old me was dead. The stranger said dead people don't need mirrors. I wasn't sure they were wrong.

choices.label: "You don't know me. Walk away."
choices.outcome_text: The stranger holds your gaze for a moment. Then they push off the wall and walk away without another word. You've dismissed someone who carried a message you didn't ask for but might have needed. The gate is quiet. The person they described — the soft one, the one who stopped for animals — is quieter still. You've protected yourself. The cost is invisible. That's how these costs work.
choices.epitaph: Told a mirror to walk away. It did. The person it described stayed hidden. Safer. Smaller.

quests.trigger: A child in the shelter storage has drawn a picture and taped it to the wall. It shows a table with many chairs. Everyone is sitting. No one is fighting.
quests.discovery: The drawing is crude — crayon on scavenged paper — but the composition is deliberate. A long table, seen from above. Chairs around it. Figures in each chair, each a different color. No weapons. No walls. Just people sitting. A sun in the corner — not the ash-filtered yellow of the real sky, but a bright, impossible orange. The child is sitting nearby, watching you look. 'That's what it could be,' they say. 'If everyone listened.'

choices.label: Ask the child to explain each figure. Who are they?
choices.outcome_text: The child points to each figure. Blue is the water station people. Red is the raiders — 'but they're sitting down, so they're not raiding.' Green is the settlement you're from. Yellow is 'the ones across the river.' Each figure has a detail: the blue ones have cups, the green ones have bread, the red ones have... flowers. 'Even they can grow things,' the child says. You study the drawing. It's not naive. It's a proposal. A seven-year-old has drawn a peace treaty in crayon, and it's more detailed than anything the adults have produced.
choices.epitaph: A child drew peace in crayon. The raiders had flowers. I couldn't argue with the composition.

choices.label: Tell the child it's a good drawing. Ask if they want to add more.
choices.outcome_text: The child's face lights up. They pull out more crayons — stubs, mostly, salvaged from somewhere. They add details: a garden behind the table, a path leading to it, animals in the garden. 'They need food too,' the child says, drawing a deer. You watch the world expand on paper. When the child finishes, they step back and survey it. 'It's not finished,' they say. 'It's never finished. That's the point. You keep adding.' You nod. The drawing stays on the wall. It's the most optimistic thing in the shelter.
choices.epitaph: A child kept adding to a drawing. It was never finished. That was the point. I understood.

choices.label: "That's a nice picture. But the real world doesn't work like that."
choices.outcome_text: The child looks at the drawing, then at you. 'I know,' they say. 'That's why I drew it. So someone could see what it should look like before they decide it's impossible.' They peel the drawing off the wall and fold it carefully. You've been honest. You've also taken a vision of what could be and told a child it doesn't match your spreadsheet. The drawing disappears into the child's pack. The wall is bare again.
choices.epitaph: Told a child the real world doesn't work like their drawing. They said that's why they drew it. I had no answer.

choices.label: Ignore it. It's just a child's drawing.
choices.outcome_text: You walk past. The child watches you go. The drawing stays on the wall — the table, the chairs, the figures in different colors, the orange sun. Other people will see it. Some will stop. The child's proposal hangs in the shelter storage like a question no one answered. Eventually, someone will take it down. Or it will curl and fade. Either way, the table with all the chairs exists somewhere — on paper, in a child's mind — whether or not you look at it.
choices.epitaph: Walked past a child's drawing of peace. It stayed on the wall. I didn't. The drawing outlasted my attention.

quests.display_name: The Elder's Map to Nowhere Safe
quests.trigger: An elder at the eastern road has drawn a map to a place they call 'the quiet.' They admit it might not exist anymore. They need someone to hear why they're looking for it.
quests.discovery: The elder's map is hand-drawn on the back of a pre-war road atlas page. It shows a route through the burned zones, past the flooded areas, to a valley marked only with the word 'quiet.' 'It was a retreat center,' they say. 'Before. Meditation, silence, no signal. The world forgot about it. Maybe it forgot about the ash too.' They know the route might be blocked, the valley might be irradiated, the quiet might be a memory pretending to be a destination. 'But I need to try,' they say. 'And I need someone to know why.'

choices.label: Study the map. Ask what 'quiet' means to them.
choices.outcome_text: The elder describes the quiet — not as silence, but as the absence of having to explain yourself. 'Out here, everything is justification. Why you eat. Why you rest. Why you keep going. The quiet was a place where you didn't have to explain.' They trace the route with a trembling finger. You study the terrain — it's dangerous, possibly impassable. But you understand the destination. It's not a place on a map. It's a state of being. 'If you find it,' you say, 'tell me where it is.' The elder smiles. 'If I find it, I won't need to tell anyone. That's the point.'
choices.epitaph: An elder drew a map to quiet. I studied it. The destination wasn't a place. It was the absence of having to explain.

choices.label: Offer to go with them. Help them find it.
choices.outcome_text: The elder considers. Then they shake their head. 'You have your own quiet to find. Mine is mine to walk toward.' They fold the map and tuck it into their coat. 'But thank you for offering. That's the first kind thing anyone's said about the journey.' You watch them walk east, following a map to a place that might not exist. The walk itself is the point. You understand that now. Some destinations are just reasons to keep moving.
choices.epitaph: Offered to walk with an elder. They refused. The journey was the destination. I understood that finally.

choices.label: "The route is too dangerous. You'll die out there."
choices.outcome_text: The elder nods. 'Probably.' They fold the map and put it away. 'But I'd rather die walking toward quiet than sitting in noise.' They don't leave that day. But you've planted a doubt — or reinforced one that was already there. The map stays folded. The elder stays put. The quiet stays unfindable. You've kept them alive. Whether that's a gift or a sentence depends on how you define living.
choices.epitaph: Convinced an elder not to walk toward quiet. They stayed alive. I'm not sure they stayed living.

choices.label: "There's no such place. You're chasing a ghost."
choices.outcome_text: The elder looks at you with the patience of someone who has outlived most certainties. 'Maybe,' they say. 'But the map is good company.' They return to their seat by the road. You've been factual. You've also told an old person that their last hope is delusion. The map stays folded. The elder stays silent. You walk away carrying the weight of a truth that doesn't make anyone's life better.
choices.epitaph: Told an elder their hope was a ghost. They said the map was good company. I had nothing to offer instead.

quests.trigger: A dying person at the burn zone has asked for a listener. Not a priest, not a doctor — just someone to sit with them while they say what they need to say.
quests.discovery: They're lying on a cot in the burn zone's makeshift medical station. The radiation took hold weeks ago; there's nothing left to do but manage the pain. They've refused the priest. They've sent the doctor away. 'I just need someone to hear it,' they tell the attendant. 'Not to forgive. Not to fix. Just to hear.' You're the one they've chosen — a stranger. The attendant looks at you with something between hope and apology.

choices.label: Sit down. Take their hand. Listen to everything.
choices.outcome_text: The confession is not dramatic. It's a list. Names of people they hurt. Choices they made that cost others. A theft that someone else was blamed for. A lie that changed a family's trajectory. A moment of cowardice that got someone killed. They speak for an hour. You hold their hand. You don't forgive — that's not what they asked for. You witness. When they finish, they close their eyes. 'It's lighter,' they say. 'Knowing someone heard it.' They die three hours later. You carry the list. Not as burden. As testimony.
choices.epitaph: Held a dying person's hand while they listed their sins. It wasn't forgiveness. It was lighter anyway.

choices.label: Listen, and ask if there's anything they want done with the information.
choices.outcome_text: The dying person thinks. 'Tell the one I stole from. Not to forgive me. Just so they know it wasn't their fault.' You write down the name and the details. The confession becomes a task — not a burden, but a delivery. You'll carry this message to someone who deserves to hear it. The dying person watches you write. 'That's all,' they say. 'I just needed it to go somewhere. Not stay in here.' They gesture at their chest. You nod. The message has a destination now. The confession is no longer a secret. It's a delivery.
choices.epitaph: A dying person gave me a message to deliver. The confession found its destination. I was the courier.

choices.label: Sit with them, but tell the attendant to find a priest too.
choices.outcome_text: The attendant leaves. You sit. The dying person speaks, but their eyes keep drifting to the door, waiting for the priest who may or may not come. The confession is split between you and an anticipated absolution. When the priest arrives, they take over. You step back. You were present. You were also a placeholder. The dying person got what they needed — eventually. But the moment of being the sole listener, the one they chose, was something you shared with an empty chair.
choices.epitaph: Sat with a dying person but called for backup. They got their priest. I got the edge of the moment.

choices.label: "I'm not the right person for this. Find someone who knew them."
choices.outcome_text: The attendant looks at the dying person. The dying person shakes their head. 'You're the right person,' they say. 'Because you're not anyone I have to protect.' You leave anyway. The attendant finds someone else — a friend, a family member, someone with stakes. The confession happens. But it's tangled with relationship, with history, with the need to be forgiven. You were chosen for the opposite: the clarity of a stranger. You declined. The confession happened without that clarity.
choices.epitaph: Declined to hear a confession. They wanted a stranger. I said no. The truth went to someone who couldn't be neutral.

quests.trigger: The knowledge keeper has been watching you. They say you've been listening to the right things, in the right way. They want to know if you'll accept a responsibility.
quests.discovery: The knowledge keeper leads you to a back room of the camp — a room you didn't know existed. Inside are journals. Dozens of them. Each one is a record of someone's story, collected by a previous listener. 'We call them the Storykeepers,' the knowledge keeper says. 'People who listen not for information, not for advantage, but because the stories need to exist somewhere other than in the heads of the people who lived them.' They push a journal toward you. 'Read the last entry. Then decide.'

choices.label: Read the journal. Accept the responsibility.
choices.outcome_text: The last entry is from a woman who walked for three months to deliver a message to her daughter. She never arrived. But the message — carried by a Storykeeper who met her on the road — reached the daughter anyway. You read it twice. Then you look up. 'I'll do it,' you say. The knowledge keeper nods. They hand you a blank journal and a pencil. 'The first story is yours to choose,' they say. 'But choose carefully. The ones you listen to become the ones you carry.' You take the journal. The weight is not in the paper. It's in the promise.
choices.epitaph: Accepted a blank journal. Became a Storykeeper. The weight is in the promise, not the paper.

choices.label: Read the journal, but ask what the commitment involves.
choices.outcome_text: The knowledge keeper explains: you listen. You record. You carry the stories to the Long Table — a gathering, held when the moon is right, where Storykeepers share what they've collected. 'Not to change anything,' they say. 'Just so the stories are spoken aloud. So they're not secrets anymore.' You consider this. The commitment is real — time, attention, the emotional cost of carrying other people's truths. 'I need to think about it,' you say. The knowledge keeper nods. 'The journal will be here.'
choices.epitaph: Asked what it meant to carry stories. The answer was: everything. I needed to sit with that.

choices.label: "I've been listening, but I'm not a keeper. I'm a survivor."
choices.outcome_text: The knowledge keeper doesn't argue. 'Survivors listen too,' they say. 'The question is whether you listen and let it go, or listen and hold it.' They put the journal away. You've been honest about your limits. You've also declined a role that would have given your listening a structure, a purpose beyond survival. The stories you've heard stay with you — uncollected, unarchived, carried only in your memory. That's enough. It has to be.
choices.epitaph: Declined the journal. Said I was a survivor, not a keeper. The stories stayed with me anyway.

choices.label: "This sounds like a cult. I'm not joining anything."
choices.outcome_text: The knowledge keeper's expression doesn't change. 'Not everything that matters is a cult,' they say. 'And not every invitation is a trap.' They close the room. The journals stay inside. You've protected your independence. You've also refused to take seriously a tradition of preserving human experience in a world that's trying very hard to erase it. The door closes. The stories continue without you.
choices.epitaph: Called the Storykeepers a cult. The door closed. The stories continued. I didn't.

quests.trigger: You've been invited to the Long Table. The knowledge keeper says you've earned a seat. The gathering happens at the shelter meeting room, when the ash storms calm.
quests.discovery: The shelter meeting room has been rearranged. A long table — real wood, scavenged from somewhere — stretches the length of the room. Chairs surround it. At each chair sits a Storykeeper, their journals open, their faces lit by candles. The knowledge keeper stands at the head of the table. 'You've listened,' they say. 'Not because you were told to. Not because it was useful. Because the stories mattered.' They gesture to an empty chair. 'Sit. Your stories are part of this now.'

choices.label: Sit down. Open your journal. Share what you've carried.
choices.outcome_text: You sit. The candle flickers. You open your journal — the one that holds the stranger's dog tag, the child's water map, the doctor's diagrams, the soldier's bridge, the trader's ledger, the defector's confession, the rival's story, the betrayer's reason. You read the first entry aloud. The room is silent. Not the silence of emptiness — the silence of attention. When you finish, the Storykeeper to your left begins. Then the next. The stories move around the table like a shared meal. No one records. No one judges. The stories are spoken, and they exist in the air, and they are enough.
choices.epitaph: Sat at the Long Table. Read my stories aloud. The room held them. That was the whole point.

choices.label: Sit down, but listen first. Let others speak before you do.
choices.outcome_text: You sit and you do what you've always done: you listen. The Storykeepers speak in turns. A doctor's research. A child's map. A soldier's bridge. A trader's ledger. You hear stories you collected — spoken by other people, carried by other voices. The stories have traveled. They've changed slightly in the retelling. They're still true. When your turn comes, you speak. Your voice sounds different in this room — not louder, but more present. The stories you've carried are no longer just yours. They belong to the table now.
choices.epitaph: Listened at the Long Table before speaking. Heard my own stories in other voices. They'd traveled.

choices.label: Stand at the door. You're not sure you belong here.
choices.outcome_text: The knowledge keeper sees you hesitate. 'The chair is empty,' they say. 'That's all the qualification there is.' You step inside but don't sit. The gathering begins. You watch from the doorway as the stories move around the table. You hear fragments — enough to know they're real, not enough to carry them. The knowledge keeper catches your eye. 'Next time,' they say. There might be a next time. The table will be there. The chair will be empty. Whether you sit in it is a question for another day.
choices.epitaph: Stood at the door of the Long Table. Didn't sit. The chair stayed empty. Next time, maybe.

choices.label: "I don't need a ceremony. The stories are already with me."
choices.outcome_text: The knowledge keeper nods. 'Then you're already at the table,' they say. 'Wherever you are.' You leave. The gathering happens without you. The stories are spoken in a room you're not in. You carry your own stories in your own way — unshared, unspoken, held only in the architecture of your memory. It's valid. It's also lonely. The Long Table exists for a reason: stories are heavier when no one else is holding them.
choices.epitaph: Declined the Long Table. Said the stories were already with me. They were. They were also heavier alone.

quests.trigger: The Long Table has ended. The knowledge keeper asks you one final question: what happens to the stories now?
quests.discovery: The candles are burning low. The other Storykeepers have left, their journals closed, their stories spoken into the air of the shelter meeting room. The knowledge keeper remains. One question. 'The stories you've collected — what do you do with them now?' They're not testing you. They're asking because the answer matters. The stories can be archived, shared, sealed, scattered. Each choice has consequences. The room is quiet. The candles are almost gone. The answer is yours.

choices.label: "They go where they're needed. I carry them to whoever needs to hear them."
choices.outcome_text: The knowledge keeper smiles — the first time you've seen it. 'A walker,' they say. 'The best kind.' You close your journal and tuck it into your pack. The stories will travel — to the water station, where a child needs to know the water map is real. To the military outpost, where a soldier needs to hear the bridge story. To the peacekeeper outpost, where a mediator needs to know that enemies have siblings too. You are the carrier. The stories move because you move. The Long Table was not an ending. It was a starting line. You walk out into the ash-filtered dawn, and the world is full of people who need to hear what you know.
choices.epitaph: Became a walker. The stories move because I move. The Long Table was a starting line, not an end.

choices.label: "They stay at the Table. Archived. Safe. For when someone needs them."
choices.outcome_text: The knowledge keeper nods. 'A keeper,' they say. 'The archive needs those.' You place your journal on the shelf with the others — dozens of them, each one a life's worth of listening. The room becomes a library of human experience. Someday, someone will need the doctor's diagrams, or the soldier's bridge, or the child's water map. They'll find them here. You've built something that outlasts you. The candles go out. The archive remains. You walk into the dawn lighter than you've been in weeks.
choices.epitaph: Archived the stories. Built a library of human experience. It will outlast me. That's the point.

choices.label: "They stay with me. I'm not ready to let them go."
choices.outcome_text: The knowledge keeper doesn't judge. 'They're yours,' they say. 'You earned them.' You close the journal and hold it. The stories are part of you now — not just memories, but responsibilities. You'll carry them until you find the right moment, the right listener, the right table. Maybe that moment comes tomorrow. Maybe it comes in ten years. The stories are patient. They've been waiting in people's heads for months. They can wait in yours a while longer. You walk into the dawn carrying everything you've heard. It's heavy. It's yours.
choices.epitaph: Kept the stories. They're heavy. They're mine. Someday I'll find the right table. The stories are patient.

choices.label: "I don't know. I need to think about it."
choices.outcome_text: The knowledge keeper nods. 'That's an honest answer.' They blow out the last candle. The room goes dark. 'Take your time,' they say. 'The stories aren't going anywhere.' You walk out into the dawn with your journal and an unanswered question. The stories wait. The table waits. You walk. Somewhere ahead, the answer is forming — not in your mind, but in the next conversation, the next stranger, the next story that demands to be heard. You'll know what to do when you hear it. You always have.
choices.epitaph: Didn't have an answer. Walked into the dawn anyway. The stories waited. So did I.

quests.trigger: You promised to share medicine with a sick neighbor. The medicine is scarce now.
quests.discovery: Maren's boy has the lung-rot. You told her three days ago, standing at her door, that you'd bring antibiotics when your next ration cycle opened. Now the cycle opened. You have four pills. Your own people have two coughing. The shelter medic looked at you hard when you took them.

choices.label: Deliver the pills as promised
choices.outcome_text: You walk to Maren's door in the grey light. She doesn't cry — she's past that. She takes the pills and counts them against her palm. The boy will live. Your shelter's medic doesn't speak to you for two days.
choices.epitaph: Kept my word. Four pills for a child I barely know. The medic still won't look at me.

choices.label: Keep the pills for your own people
choices.outcome_text: You tell yourself the arithmetic: your people first. The coughing stops by morning. When Maren's boy dies three days later, you don't attend the burial. You were busy. You were always busy.
choices.epitaph: Kept the pills. The boy died on day three. I was busy. I was always busy.

choices.label: Trade the pills to the peacekeepers for favors
choices.outcome_text: The outpost commander takes the pills without counting. In return, you get a marked map — supply caches along the eastern road. Maren's boy dies. The map is worth more than one child. You tell yourself that at night, and almost believe it.
choices.epitaph: Traded antibiotics for a map. The commander didn't count them. I did.

choices.label: Give half — keep the rest
choices.outcome_text: Two pills. Maren looks at your hand and does the math. She takes them without a word. It's enough to slow the rot, not stop it. The boy survives another week. You've bought time for everyone and certainty for no one.
choices.epitaph: Gave her two. Kept two. Enough to slow it. Not enough to stop it.

quests.trigger: A desperate man tells you where he hid his family's emergency cache, trusting you to keep the secret.
quests.discovery: Doran pulls you behind the water tank, voice low. He found a cache before the second storm — canned goods, a hand drill, iodine tablets. He buried it under the collapsed overpass near the eastern road. 'Nobody knows,' he says. 'Not even my wife. I'm telling you because you're the only one I trust.' His eyes are red-rimmed. His youngest hasn't eaten in two days.

choices.label: Keep the secret as promised
choices.outcome_text: You nod and say nothing. Doran's youngest eats from his own rations that night — less, but enough. The cache stays buried. You carry the knowledge like a stone in your pocket, heavy and useless.
choices.epitaph: Kept Doran's secret. The knowledge sat in my pocket like a stone. Heavy and useless.

choices.label: Dig it up while Doran sleeps
choices.outcome_text: You go at third bell. The overpass concrete is cracked and easy to move. Canned peaches, a hand drill wrapped in oilcloth, three blister packs of iodine. You bury the evidence of the theft under fresh rubble. Doran never suspects. His youngest eats dust for another week.
choices.epitaph: Took Doran's cache while he slept. Canned peaches and iodine. His youngest kept eating dust.

choices.label: Sell the location to the raiders for protection
choices.outcome_text: The raider camp pays in safe passage — a marked flag for your patrol route. They dig the cache by noon. Doran goes to check on his insurance the next morning and finds the hole. He doesn't come to you for help. He leaves the shelter that night. You hear he headed south.
choices.epitaph: Sold Doran's secret to the raiders. Got safe passage. He left the shelter that night. Didn't say goodbye.

choices.label: Tell Doran you'll help him retrieve it together
choices.outcome_text: You go together at dawn. The cache is intact. Doran carries half; you carry half. He trusts you completely. The weight of that trust is heavier than the canned goods, and more difficult to set down.
choices.epitaph: Went with him. Carried half. His trust weighed more than the cans.

quests.trigger: A quiet engineer fixes the water recycler. You can claim the credit and the political capital that comes with it.
quests.discovery: The water recycler has been dead for eleven days. Rationing is brutal. Then Ise — quiet Ise, the former hydrologist who never speaks at meetings — fixes it overnight. She tells no one. By morning, the tanks are filling and people are weeping with relief. You saw her working. You know what she did. But nobody else does. The shelter is looking for a hero, and Ise is already back in her corner, invisible.

choices.label: Publicly credit Ise for the repair
choices.outcome_text: You find Ise at the morning briefing and say her name. The room turns. She flinches like she's been struck. They applaud. She doesn't smile. Later she tells you, quietly, that she preferred the invisibility. But her ration card gets upgraded, and that's real.
choices.epitaph: Said her name. She flinched at the applause. Preferred the invisible work. But the extra ration was real.

choices.label: Claim the repair was yours
choices.outcome_text: You mention it casually at the briefing — 'I was up all night with the recycler.' People clap. Ise looks at you from across the room. She doesn't contradict you. She doesn't speak at all. After that, she fixes things in the dark, and you keep getting the credit. She stops meeting your eyes.
choices.epitaph: Took credit for Ise's work. She never contradicted me. She just stopped meeting my eyes.

choices.label: Use the knowledge to recruit Ise as an ally
choices.outcome_text: You find Ise privately. 'I know what you did,' you say. She waits. 'I won't tell anyone — if you help me with the next project. And the one after that.' She understands the transaction. Her skills, your platform. She nods once. The alliance is sealed in silence.
choices.epitaph: Made Ise an offer she couldn't refuse. Her skills, my platform. Sealed in silence.

choices.label: Say nothing and let the mystery stand
choices.outcome_text: Nobody knows who fixed it. The water runs. People are grateful to the anonymous ghost in the machine room. Ise catches your eye once and looks away. She suspects you know. You'll never discuss it.
choices.epitaph: Said nothing. The water runs. The ghost in the machine room stays anonymous.

quests.trigger: A rival for leadership is popular and well-liked. Tools go missing from storage. You know who could take the fall.
quests.discovery: The storage inventory is short: two wrenches, a coil of wire, a half-tank of fuel. Nobody took them — they were requisitioned for the perimeter repair and the paperwork wasn't filed. But the ledger is ambiguous, and Kessler's name is on the sign-out sheet from last week. Kessler is running against you for the supply committee. He's well-liked. He doesn't know about the paperwork gap yet.

choices.label: File the correct paperwork and clear the record
choices.outcome_text: You fill out the requisition form, date it properly, and slide it into the ledger. The gap closes. Kessler never knows he was almost accused of something he didn't do. The election goes to a split vote. You lose by two ballots.
choices.epitaph: Filed the paperwork. Closed the gap. Lost the election by two votes. Slept soundly.

choices.label: Plant the missing tools in Kessler's storage
choices.outcome_text: You move the wrenches and wire to the shelf under Kessler's name during the night shift. In the morning, the inventory audit finds them. Kessler's face goes white. 'I didn't take these,' he says, but his name is right there. The committee suspends him. He leaves the shelter within the week. You win the election unopposed.
choices.epitaph: Planted the tools under his name. His name was right there. He left within the week.

choices.label: Anonymously report the discrepancy
choices.outcome_text: You slip a note under the committee door: 'Check Kessler's sign-outs.' The audit begins. Kessler scrambles to explain the paperwork gap he didn't know existed. He's not expelled, but the shadow follows him. His campaign stalls. You win, and your hands are technically clean.
choices.epitaph: Slipped the note. Let them find it themselves. My hands were technically clean.

choices.label: Tell Kessler privately so he can explain
choices.outcome_text: You find Kessler at the water station. 'There's a ledger gap and your name's on it.' He goes pale, then grateful. He files the correction himself. The election is honest. You lose. He shakes your hand afterward and means it.
choices.epitaph: Told Kessler. He filed the correction. I lost the election. He shook my hand and meant it.

quests.trigger: Two groups both trust you as a neutral mediator. You can sell each side's position to the other.
quests.discovery: The water station and the knowledge keeper's camp both want the same thing: the seed bank in the abandoned homesteads to the south. Both send you as their intermediary — both because you're trusted, both because they think you favor them. The water station offers trade goods for intelligence on the camp's negotiation limits. The knowledge keepers offer the same. You could play both sides, or play them straight.

choices.label: Negotiate an honest split between both groups
choices.outcome_text: You lay the maps on the table. The water station takes the upper fields; the knowledge keepers take the root cellars. Both sides grumble. Neither side is satisfied. But the seed bank is divided without blood, and you walk away with a reputation for fairness that will open doors for months.
choices.epitaph: Negotiated the split. Both sides grumbled. No blood. Fairness opens doors.

choices.label: Sell each side's limits to the other and profit from both
choices.outcome_text: You tell the water station the keepers will accept less. You tell the keepers the station is desperate. Both deals close in your favor — you take a mediator's cut from each side that nobody else would have approved. The seed bank is divided, but both groups leave feeling cheated. They don't know it was you. Not yet.
choices.epitaph: Sold both sides to each other. Took a cut from each. They both left feeling cheated.

choices.label: Sabotage the talks so you can take the seed bank alone
choices.outcome_text: You arrange for the talks to collapse — a leaked insult, a missed deadline, a forged message. Both groups retreat, furious at each other. You go to the abandoned homesteads alone at dawn and take the entire seed bank. It's a king's ransom in calories. The two groups don't speak to each other for months. They don't speak to you either.
choices.epitaph: Burned the talks. Took the seed bank alone. A king's ransom in calories. Two alliances in ashes.

choices.label: Withdraw from mediation entirely
choices.outcome_text: You tell both groups you can't serve two masters. They find other intermediaries. The talks drag on for weeks and produce a worse deal for everyone. But your name isn't on any of it. Sometimes the smartest play is not playing.
choices.epitaph: Walked away from both. The talks dragged on. My name wasn't on any of it.

quests.trigger: You've acquired compromised medical supplies. Someone who trusts you needs medicine badly.
quests.discovery: The crate from the military outpost was sealed but water-damaged. Half the antibiotics inside have degraded — you can tell by the color shift. They'll look fine to anyone who doesn't know what to check. Tagret's camp has an infection spreading. He asked you specifically for medical help. You have the compromised crate in your storage, and you have three doses of the good stuff you've been saving.

choices.label: Give Tagret the good medicine from your own supply
choices.outcome_text: You carry the three good doses yourself. Tagret's medic checks the batch numbers and nods. The infection slows. You're three doses poorer and your own people will go without if someone falls sick this month. Tagret remembers. He always remembers a debt.
choices.epitaph: Gave Tagret my own supply. Three doses poorer. He remembers every debt.

choices.label: Deliver the compromised crate and say nothing
choices.outcome_text: You haul the crate to Tagret's camp. He's grateful — genuinely grateful, which makes it worse. Two days later, the degraded antibiotics fail. Two of his people die of sepsis. Tagret doesn't blame you. He blames the wasteland. You let him.
choices.epitaph: Delivered the bad medicine. Two of his people died. He blamed the wasteland. I let him.

choices.label: Warn Tagret about the compromised batch
choices.outcome_text: You find Tagret and tell him about the water damage. He inspects the crate and curses. You've saved his people from false medicine and earned a debt that can't be repaid with goods. The compromised crate is destroyed. Tagret owes you, and he knows it.
choices.epitaph: Warned Tagret. Destroyed the bad batch. He owes me something that can't be repaid with goods.

choices.label: Mix the good and bad — dilute the risk
choices.outcome_text: You combine the three good doses with six degraded ones, hoping the good will compensate for the bad. It's a gamble with other people's biology. Some of his people recover. Some don't. The ones who don't — their families will remember the batch that half-worked.
choices.epitaph: Mixed the good with the bad. A gamble with biology. Some recovered. Some didn't.

quests.trigger: You intercept a radio broadcast about a supply convoy. Others are counting on your silence.
quests.discovery: The radio crackles at 0300. A convoy — unmarked, heading north through sector seven — carrying medical supplies and MREs. The frequency is supposed to be secure. Only three people in the shelter know you monitor it. The peacekeeper outpost would pay well for this intelligence. The knowledge keepers would trade knowledge. Your own people are hungry. The convoy passes in eighteen hours.

choices.label: Share the intelligence with the whole shelter
choices.outcome_text: You call a meeting and play the recording. The shelter mobilizes — a team rides out at dawn and intercepts the convoy peacefully, trading labor for a share of the medical supplies. Everyone eats better that week. But the frequency is now known to more people, and next time, the convoy might not be so cooperative.
choices.epitaph: Shared the frequency with everyone. We traded labor for medicine. But the secret is shared now.

choices.label: Sell the intelligence to the highest bidder
choices.outcome_text: The peacekeeper outpost pays in fuel and ammunition. The knowledge keepers offer a map of underground cisterns. You take both payments. The convoy is hit by a raider party within the hour — tipped off by someone else who was listening. Nobody from your shelter was involved. The radio goes silent after that. No more broadcasts on that frequency.
choices.epitaph: Sold to both sides. The convoy was hit by raiders within the hour. The frequency went dead.

choices.label: Use the information for your shelter alone
choices.outcome_text: You assemble a small team — people you trust, people who owe you. The convoy is intercepted at the narrow pass. You trade tools for a crate of MREs. Your shelter eats well for a week. Nobody else knows. The radio operator at the other end wonders who was listening.
choices.epitaph: Took a small team. Traded tools for MREs. Our shelter ate well. Nobody else knew.

choices.label: Ignore it — some things aren't worth the risk
choices.outcome_text: You turn off the radio and go back to sleep. The convoy passes. Someone else intercepts it — you hear the distant engines, then silence. You'll never know what was in those trucks. Some doors are better left closed.
choices.epitaph: Turned off the radio. Heard the engines pass. Some doors are better left closed.

quests.trigger: You discover a respected leader's private stockpile — proof of hypocrisy that could destroy them.
quests.discovery: While repairing the east wall, you find a false panel in the rubble. Behind it: forty cans of food, a water purification unit, a sealed first aid kit. All hidden. All unreported. The name scratched into the crate wood is Voss — the shelter's moral authority, the woman who lectures everyone about shared sacrifice. She preaches equality at every meeting while sitting on a month of private reserves.

choices.label: Confront Voss privately and demand she share
choices.outcome_text: You find Voss at dawn. 'I found your cache.' Her face cycles through fear, shame, and then a cold calculation you haven't seen before. She agrees to share — publicly. But she looks at you differently now. Not with gratitude. With the measured gaze of someone who knows you hold her leash.
choices.epitaph: Confronted Voss. She shared — publicly. But she looks at me like I hold her leash.

choices.label: Expose her publicly at the next meeting
choices.outcome_text: You wait until the full assembly. You describe the cache, the crate, the name. Voss stands very still while the room turns against her. She's stripped of her committee seat by sunset. Her influence evaporates. The shelter gains forty cans and loses its conscience. People eat better. They also trust less.
choices.epitaph: Exposed Voss in front of everyone. She lost her seat. We gained forty cans and lost our conscience.

choices.label: Use the knowledge to quietly control her votes
choices.outcome_text: You mention the cache in passing, just to Voss, just once. 'I hope we can agree on the supply allocation.' She understands. She always votes your way after that. The shelter thinks she's come around to your position. Only you know it's a hostage situation.
choices.epitaph: One mention. She understood. She votes my way now. The shelter thinks she changed her mind.

choices.label: Seal the panel and walk away
choices.outcome_text: You put the panel back. The rubble looks undisturbed. Voss gives her speech about shared sacrifice that evening. You listen. You say nothing. The knowledge sits behind your teeth like a loose filling. Someday you might use it. Not today.
choices.epitaph: Sealed the panel. Walked away. The knowledge sits behind my teeth. Someday, maybe.

quests.trigger: Someone keeps breaking curfew. The shelter needs discipline. You can make an example — or show mercy.
quests.discovery: Bray has broken curfew three times this week. She says she's checking on her brother's grave outside the perimeter. The curfew exists because of the night raids — two people died last month walking after dark. The shelter is watching. They want to see what you do. Mercy looks like weakness. Severity looks like strength. The truth is somewhere in the middle and nobody wants the truth.

choices.label: Escort Bray to her brother's grave yourself
choices.outcome_text: You go with her at first light. The grave is small — a child's drawing weighted down with stones. You stand there while she cries. On the walk back, you talk about the curfew. She understands. The shelter sees you came back with her, alive, and the rule holds. But the humanity holds too.
choices.epitaph: Walked her to the grave. A child's drawing under stones. The rule held. So did she.

choices.label: Expel Bray from the shelter
choices.outcome_text: You announce the expulsion at the morning briefing. Bray doesn't argue. She picks up her pack — it's light, almost empty — and walks through the gate. Nobody follows. The curfew holds perfectly after that. The shelter is quiet in a way that isn't peace. It's the quiet of a held breath.
choices.epitaph: Expelled Bray. Her pack was almost empty. The curfew held perfectly after that.

choices.label: Publicly demote Bray and assign her the worst duties
choices.outcome_text: You strip Bray of her ration priority and assign her to the latrine detail. She works in silence. The others watch. The message is clear: break the rules, suffer publicly. Bray's brother's grave goes unvisited. She stops asking. The shelter is disciplined. The shelter is afraid.
choices.epitaph: Demoted Bray publicly. Latrine duty. She stopped asking about her brother's grave.

choices.label: Make an exception — let Bray visit with an armed escort
choices.outcome_text: You assign a guard to accompany Bray to the grave each evening. It costs a person from the night watch. Other families hear about the arrangement and want the same. Exceptions breed exceptions. But Bray sleeps better, and the guard reports the eastern road is clear.
choices.epitaph: Made an exception. Cost a guard each evening. Exceptions breed exceptions.

quests.trigger: A small allied group has a leader you could undermine. Their people are already restless.
quests.discovery: The burn zone camp has twelve members. Their leader, Cade, is competent but cold. You've noticed the restiveness — side conversations during meetings, eyes that drift when he speaks, a woman named Pell who challenges him at every turn. Cade asks you to speak with the dissenters. Pell asks you to listen. Both think you're neutral. Neither is right.

choices.label: Support Cade and help him hold the camp together
choices.outcome_text: You tell Cade what you've heard. He nods slowly — he already knew, but your confirmation matters. You stand with him at the next meeting. The dissenters quiet. The camp holds. Cade owes you, and the alliance between your shelters deepens. Stability has a price, but someone else is paying it.
choices.epitaph: Stood with Cade. The camp held. Stability has a price. Someone else paid it.

choices.label: Quietly encourage Pell to take over
choices.outcome_text: You meet Pell at the water point. You don't say 'overthrow Cade.' You say things like 'the camp seems frustrated' and 'leadership should reflect the group.' Pell does the rest. The coup is bloodless. Cade leaves quietly. Pell is grateful — and dependent. The camp is yours now, through a proxy who thinks she's free.
choices.epitaph: Never said the word. Pell did the rest. The camp is mine through a proxy who thinks she's free.

choices.label: Play both sides until both depend on you
choices.outcome_text: You tell Cade you'll help him manage Pell. You tell Pell you'll help her manage Cade. Both pour their confidence into you. When the inevitable confrontation comes, you're the only person either side trusts to mediate. The compromise leaves both weakened and you indispensable. It's the most elegant thing you've ever done.
choices.epitaph: Played both sides. Both weakened. Both dependent. The most elegant thing I've ever done.

choices.label: Stay out of it — their politics aren't your problem
choices.outcome_text: You tell both Cade and Pell it's not your place. The camp fractures within a week. Cade leaves with three loyalists. Pell takes over and immediately makes three decisions you disagree with. But it's her camp, her mistakes. Your hands are clean.
choices.epitaph: Stayed out. The camp fractured. Her mistakes, her camp. My hands were clean.

quests.trigger: The water pump fails. People are desperate. You know how to fix it — but timing the fix is worth more than the fix itself.
quests.discovery: The main water pump dies at noon. By evening, the tanks are below a quarter. People are rationing spit. You know what's wrong — the impeller gasket. You've been meaning to mention it for weeks. You could fix it in an hour. But an hour of crisis is also an hour of leverage. The shelter committee is already arguing about who's to blame. Nobody has asked you yet.

choices.label: Fix it immediately and ask for nothing
choices.outcome_text: You walk to the pump house, pull the gasket, replace it with the spare you've been carrying. Water flows within the hour. People cheer. You wave it off. The committee never knows how close the gasket was to failing completely. You've saved them and asked for nothing. The debt is invisible and infinite.
choices.epitaph: Fixed it in an hour. Asked for nothing. The debt is invisible and infinite.

choices.label: Wait until the crisis peaks, then fix it — and name your price
choices.outcome_text: You wait. The tanks drop to ten percent. Fights break out at the tap. At the darkest hour, you stand up and say: 'I can fix it. But I want the supply committee chair.' They look at you. They look at their children. They agree. You fix the pump in forty minutes. The silence while you worked was the loudest thing you've ever heard.
choices.epitaph: Waited until the tanks hit ten percent. Named my price. They agreed. The silence while I waited was the loudest thing I've ever heard.

choices.label: Tell the committee you know the problem but need resources
choices.outcome_text: You describe the gasket issue and request two people and four hours. The committee grants it. You fix the pump with an audience. Everyone sees the work. Everyone knows your name. It's not as clean as doing it quietly, but it's not as cruel as waiting. A transaction, not a tragedy.
choices.epitaph: Described the problem. Fixed it with an audience. A transaction, not a tragedy.

choices.label: Share what you know so anyone can fix it
choices.outcome_text: You write down the repair procedure — gasket location, replacement steps, torque specifications — and post it at the pump house. The shelter's mechanic follows your instructions and has the water running by morning. You've made yourself unnecessary. There's a cost to that, but the water runs.
choices.epitaph: Wrote down the repair steps. Made myself unnecessary. The water runs.

quests.trigger: Someone you betrayed long ago returns — scarred, hungry, and asking for help. They don't recognize you at first.
quests.discovery: The stranger at the gate has a burn scar across the left side of their face. They ask for water and a night's rest. You recognize them — Corin.
