Six months ago, you sold their location to the raiders to buy safe passage for your group. You told yourself it was strategic. Corin survived the raid, barely. They don't recognize you. Not yet. The scar changed their face. But their eyes are the same.

choices.label: Reveal yourself and accept whatever comes
choices.outcome_text: You say their name. Corin freezes. The water cup stops halfway to their mouth. You tell them the truth — all of it. The silence afterward is the longest of your life. Corin sets the cup down, stands, and walks out the gate. They don't look back. But they don't come back with raiders either. Some debts are paid in restraint.
choices.epitaph: Said their name. Told them everything. They walked out. Didn't come back with raiders.

choices.label: Give them shelter but never reveal who you are
choices.outcome_text: You give the stranger water, a corner to sleep in, a ration. They thank you with the easy gratitude of someone who expects nothing. You watch them eat and wonder if this is mercy or the longest con you've ever played. They leave at dawn. You never say the name.
choices.epitaph: Gave the stranger water and a corner. They thanked me. I never said the name.

choices.label: Turn them away before they recognize you
choices.outcome_text: You tell them the shelter is full. It isn't. You watch them walk down the road, the scar catching the light. If they turn around, if they remember, if they talk — you'll have to deal with it. But they don't turn around. The road swallows them. You lock the gate and check it twice.
choices.epitaph: Turned them away. The scar caught the light. They didn't turn around. I checked the gate twice.

choices.label: Recruit them — they're useful, history aside
choices.outcome_text: You offer Corin a place. Steady work, a bunk, food. They accept. Over the following weeks, they prove competent — strong, reliable, good with their hands. You never mention the past. They never suspect. It's the most efficient betrayal: making the betrayed work for the betrayer and calling it opportunity.
choices.epitaph: Hired them. They're strong, reliable. They never suspect. The most efficient kind of betrayal.

quests.trigger: The person you betrayed most is now the only one who can save you. The debt will own you.
quests.discovery: Your patrol is pinned down near the flooded area — three raiders with rifles, your people behind a concrete barrier. Ammo is low. The radio reaches one group close enough to help: Doran's camp. Doran, whose cache you stole months ago. Doran, who lost everything because of you. His voice on the radio is calm. 'I can send people. But you'll owe me.'

choices.label: Accept the debt and survive
choices.outcome_text: You say the word. Doran's people arrive within the hour — flanking, suppressive, professional. The raiders scatter. Your people are alive because the man you robbed chose mercy, or strategy, or something you can't name. The debt is structural now. Doran will call it in, and you'll have to answer.
choices.epitaph: Accepted the debt. Doran's people saved us. He'll call it in. I'll have to answer.

choices.label: Find another way out — even if it costs more
choices.outcome_text: You cut through the drainage pipe instead. It takes four hours, costs two boxes of ammunition, and everyone comes out scraped and half-drowned. But you don't owe Doran anything. The cost was high and measurable. Debts are neither.
choices.epitaph: Cut through the drainage pipe. Four hours, two boxes of ammo. But I owe Doran nothing.

choices.label: Offer Doran something specific — trade, not debt
choices.outcome_text: You radio back: 'Name a price. Fixed terms. No open debts.' There's a pause. 'The fuel reserves from the eastern run.' It's steep. You agree. Doran's people arrive. The fuel changes hands. The transaction is clean. But clean transactions with the people you've betrayed still feel like something else.
choices.epitaph: Named a fixed price. Paid it. Clean transactions with the betrayed still feel dirty.

choices.label: Refuse all help — your people can handle it
choices.outcome_text: You tell your people to conserve ammo and wait for a gap. You run it yourself — a sprint across open ground that draws fire while the others fall back. You take a graze wound to the shoulder. Two people don't make it. But the ones who do are free. They know the cost. You know it more.
choices.epitaph: Ran across open ground. Took a graze wound. Two didn't make it. The rest are free.

quests.trigger: A young survivor is using your exact tactics — manipulation, leverage, betrayal. They're good at it. Too good.
quests.discovery: You recognize the pattern because you invented it. The new arrival — Sable, twenty years old, sharp-eyed — has already turned two shelter members against the food committee, acquired a private stash through 'trades' that weren't, and positioned herself as indispensable to the radio operator. She's building power the way you build power: one quiet betrayal at a time. She looks at you with something like admiration. Or recognition.

choices.label: Confront Sable and force her to stop
choices.outcome_text: You corner her at the water station. 'I know what you're doing. Stop.' She doesn't deny it. 'You did the same thing,' she says. 'I watched. I learned.' She's right, and the accusation lands because it's true. She stops. But she also stops trusting anyone, because she now knows the only person who could mentor her chose to cage her instead.
choices.epitaph: Told her to stop. She said she learned from me. She was right. She stopped. She also stopped trusting.

choices.label: Eliminate Sable before she becomes a rival
choices.outcome_text: You fabricate a safety violation — unauthorized perimeter breach, endangered the group. The committee expels Sable without a hearing. She looks at you as she leaves. Not angry. Disappointed. She saw you as a teacher. You just proved the lesson: the person on top doesn't share the method.
choices.epitaph: Fabricated a violation. Expelled her. She looked disappointed, not angry. I proved the lesson.

choices.label: Recruit Sable as your apprentice
choices.outcome_text: You find Sable and say: 'You're good. But you're sloppy in three places.' She listens. You teach her the places. In return, she works for you — quietly, efficiently, without the mess of open alliance. It's the partnership you always wanted. It's also the partnership that will eventually eat you alive. You both know it.
choices.epitaph: Took her on. Taught her the sloppy places. She'll eat me alive eventually. We both know it.

choices.label: Ignore her — what does it matter?
choices.outcome_text: You watch Sable work and feel something you haven't felt in a while: professional respect. She's building her own power base. Let her. The shelter can hold two architects of manipulation. Or it can't. Either way, it's not your problem today.
choices.epitaph: Let her build. Professional respect. The shelter can hold two architects. Or it can't.

quests.trigger: A dying person has information that could save many lives — but extracting it means breaking a confidence they trusted you with.
quests.discovery: Old Fen is dying of the long cough. Everyone knows it. What not everyone knows is that Fen kept a ledger — names, locations, supply caches, safe routes — accumulated over thirty years of wasteland survival. Fen gives you the ledger on the condition you share it with 'those who need it, not those who want it.' The ledger is worth a fortune. The peacekeepers would pay in weapons. Your shelter needs weapons.

choices.label: Honor Fen's wishes — share only with those in need
choices.outcome_text: You distribute the ledger's contents carefully — safe routes to the flooded area refugees, cache locations to the hunger-stricken families. It takes weeks. The information saves lives in small, quiet ways. The peacekeepers hear about the ledger and offer less next time. You've spent a fortune in intelligence on gratitude.
choices.epitaph: Shared it with those who needed it. The information saved lives. Gratitude doesn't buy ammunition.

choices.label: Sell the ledger to the peacekeepers for weapons
choices.outcome_text: The outpost commander counts the pages and nods. The weapons are good — military grade, well-maintained. Your shelter is the most heavily armed group in the sector. Fen's thirty years of survival knowledge become bullets and blades. The people who needed it get nothing. Fen would be disappointed, but Fen is dead.
choices.epitaph: Sold Fen's thirty years for military-grade weapons. He'd be disappointed. Fen is dead.

choices.label: Use the information yourself and destroy the ledger
choices.outcome_text: You memorize the key entries — the ones that matter for your routes, your trade, your advantage. Then you burn the ledger in the shelter stove. The flames curl the pages black. Nobody else will ever have this information. You are the sole heir to thirty years of survival, and you intend to spend the inheritance.
choices.epitaph: Memorized the key entries. Burned the rest. Sole heir to thirty years of survival.

choices.label: Copy it — share a redacted version, keep the full version
choices.outcome_text: You spend three nights copying the ledger. The redacted version goes to the shelter — safe routes, basic cache locations. The full version stays in your personal lockbox. You've honored the spirit of Fen's wish while keeping the letter for yourself. It's the kind of compromise that lets you sleep and wake at the same time.
choices.epitaph: Copied it. Shared the safe version. Kept the full one. A compromise that lets me sleep and wake.

quests.trigger: You've captured a rival's family member. The leverage is immense. The moral cost is absolute.
quests.discovery: The patrol brought back a girl — sixteen, maybe seventeen. She was scavenging near the burn zone, alone. She's also Pell's daughter. Pell, who broke away from the burn zone camp and has been raiding your supply lines for weeks. Pell doesn't know you have her daughter. The girl is frightened but unhurt. She's also the most valuable piece of leverage you've ever held.

choices.label: Release the girl unconditionally
choices.outcome_text: You send the girl back with a message: 'Tell your mother the raids stop, or we talk. No conditions.' Pell's raids stop within two days. She doesn't come to talk. But she doesn't raid either. The girl's safety purchased a ceasefire. You could have purchased more. You chose less.
choices.epitaph: Sent her back. No conditions. The raids stopped. I could have purchased more. I chose less.

choices.label: Use the girl to force Pell's surrender
choices.outcome_text: You send a message to Pell: 'Stop the raids and turn yourself in, or your daughter stays with us indefinitely.' Pell surrenders that evening. She doesn't see her daughter. The girl is unharmed but silent. She doesn't cry. She stares at you with an expression that isn't fear. It's something worse. It's understanding.
choices.epitaph: Forced Pell's surrender through her daughter. The girl didn't cry. She understood. That was worse.

choices.label: Trade the girl for specific resources — a clean transaction
choices.outcome_text: You contact Pell through an intermediary. 'Your daughter for the fuel cache and the water filter parts.' Pell agrees without hesitation. The exchange happens at the eastern road. The girl runs to her mother. Pell counts the fuel cans. Both sides got what they wanted. Neither side will forget how it was obtained.
choices.epitaph: Traded the girl for fuel and filter parts. Both sides got what they wanted. Neither will forget.

choices.label: Keep the girl as a ward — 'for her safety'
choices.outcome_text: You tell Pell the girl is safer with you. 'Until things settle down,' you say. Pell has no choice. The girl becomes a permanent guest — which is to say a permanent hostage. She eats your food, sleeps in your shelter, and watches you with the patient vigilance of a trapped animal. You tell yourself it's temporary. You both know better.
choices.epitaph: Kept her 'for safety.' A permanent guest. A permanent hostage. She watches me like a trapped animal.

quests.trigger: A former ally has become a liability. They know too much and talk too freely. The shelter wants answers.
quests.discovery: Greer knows everything — your supply routes, your negotiation positions, the location of your emergency cache. Greer also drinks too much and talks too freely. Last night at the common fire, Greer nearly revealed the eastern route to a group of newcomers. Nobody caught it. You did. Greer is loyal but loose. The shelter's security depends on information control, and Greer has become a leak.

choices.label: Talk to Greer privately and set boundaries
choices.outcome_text: You find Greer sober — which takes two mornings of trying. You explain the risk without accusation. Greer's face goes pale. 'I didn't realize,' they say. They mean it. You set rules: no fire-circle conversations about operations, ever. Greer complies. The leak is sealed with honesty, and Greer becomes more careful than anyone.
choices.epitaph: Talked to Greer sober. They didn't realize. They meant it. The leak sealed with honesty.

choices.label: Exile Greer — quietly, permanently
choices.outcome_text: You arrange for Greer to be assigned to a distant supply run. When the team returns, Greer isn't with them. 'They decided to stay at the waystation,' you tell the shelter. Nobody questions it. Greer is alive, somewhere, with knowledge that slowly becomes outdated. The leak is sealed with distance and a lie.
choices.epitaph: Exiled Greer quietly. 'They stayed at the waystation.' Nobody questioned it. The leak sealed with a lie.

choices.label: Spread false information through Greer deliberately
choices.outcome_text: You feed Greer a fabricated supply route — one that leads to a dead end and a trap. If raiders follow the 'leak,' they'll walk into an ambush. Greer talks at the fire that night, exactly as predicted. The false route spreads. You wait. Two weeks later, three raiders are found dead in the dead-end pass. Greer never knows they were used as bait.
choices.epitaph: Fed Greer false information. Three raiders walked into the trap. Greer never knew they were bait.

choices.label: Accept the risk — Greer's loyalty matters more
choices.outcome_text: You decide the leak is tolerable. Greer is loyal, skilled, and has saved your life twice. One loose tongue at the fire circle is the price of keeping a good person. You start watching what you say around Greer. It's an inconvenience, not a crisis. Some problems are managed, not solved.
choices.epitaph: Kept Greer. Accepted the risk. Some problems are managed, not solved.

quests.trigger: Your oldest ally offers a partnership that could secure everything — if you're willing to cut them out instead.
quests.discovery: Renna has been your ally since the first winter. She brought you through the flood season, shared her medical training, vouched for you when nobody else would. Now she proposes a merger — combining your shelters into one unified command. It would make you the strongest power in the sector. But you realize that as co-commanders, you'd have to share. And if Renna were... unavailable... the merger would put you in sole command of everything she's built.

choices.label: Accept the partnership as equals
choices.outcome_text: You shake Renna's hand. The merger goes through — two shelters, one command, shared authority. It's messy. You disagree on supply allocation, on patrol routes, on everything. But the combined shelter is stronger than either alone, and Renna catches your blind spots. Partnership is harder than dominion. It's also less lonely.
choices.epitaph: Shook her hand. Two shelters, one command. Partnership is harder than dominion. Less lonely.

choices.label: Sabotage the merger and take Renna's resources by force
choices.outcome_text: You arrange for the merger talks to collapse — then move on Renna's shelter while her people are confused and leaderless. It takes one night. Renna surrenders to avoid bloodshed. She looks at you across the room where you've known each other for two years. 'I trusted you,' she says. You have everything you wanted. The sentence echoes.
choices.epitaph: Collapsed the talks. Moved in one night. 'I trusted you,' she said. I have everything I wanted.

choices.label: Negotiate from within — gain control through the fine print
choices.outcome_text: You agree to the merger but insist on controlling the supply chain and the radio. Renna agrees — she doesn't care about logistics. Within three months, every decision flows through your hands. Renna is still the figurehead, but you hold the machinery. She realizes it eventually. By then, it's too late for her to do anything about it.
choices.epitaph: Agreed to the merger. Controlled the supply chain and radio. She's the figurehead. I hold the machinery.

choices.label: Decline the merger — some alliances work better at a distance
choices.outcome_text: You tell Renna you value the alliance but not the amalgamation. She's hurt but understanding. The shelters remain separate, cooperative, independent. It's less efficient. It's also more honest. Renna toasts to 'the alliance that survived the conversation.' You drink to it and mean it, mostly.
choices.epitaph: Declined the merger. 'The alliance that survived the conversation,' she toasted. I meant it. Mostly.

quests.trigger: You're strong enough to demand tribute. A smaller camp has something you need — and no way to refuse.
quests.discovery: The knowledge keeper camp has the last functioning printing press in the sector. You need it — not for knowledge, but for the paper. Paper burns, paper insulates, paper trades. The keepers are scholars. They use the press for broadsheets nobody reads anymore. They won't sell it. But they can't defend it either. Your patrol could take it in an hour. All you have to do is ask — or take.

choices.label: Trade fairly for the press — offer something of equal value
choices.outcome_text: You offer three crates of medical supplies and a month's fuel ration. The keepers deliberate for two days. They accept. The press changes hands in a ceremony with speeches you don't entirely believe. But the transaction is honest, and the keepers remain willing partners for future trade. Fair dealing has a compound interest all its own.
choices.epitaph: Traded fairly. Medical supplies and fuel for the press. The keepers remain partners. Fair dealing compounds.

choices.label: Demand the press as tribute — they can't refuse
choices.outcome_text: You send four armed people to 'request' the press. The keepers look at the weapons, look at each other, and wheel the press out to the road. The eldest keeper — Maren, no relation to the Maren from years ago — spits at your deputy's feet. The press is yours. The keepers' loyalty to anyone but themselves is broken. You've gained a machine and made enemies of every person who values knowledge.
choices.epitaph: Sent four armed people. The eldest keeper spat at my deputy's feet. The press is mine. The enmity is permanent.

choices.label: Propose a shared arrangement — you protect it, they use it
choices.outcome_text: You offer protection in exchange for priority access to the paper output. The keepers agree cautiously. The press stays in their camp; your people get first claim on broadsheets and blank sheets. It's not ownership. It's a lease. Less than you could take, more than you'd get by trading. The keepers sleep with one eye open regardless.
choices.epitaph: Proposed sharing. Protection for priority access. Not ownership. A lease. They sleep with one eye open.

choices.label: Let the keepers keep it — paper isn't worth the cost
choices.outcome_text: You look at the press, look at the keepers' defiant faces, and walk away. Paper is paper. The cost of taking it isn't the effort — it's what taking it says about you. You find other insulation. The keepers remember that you chose not to. That memory is worth more than paper, eventually.
choices.epitaph: Walked away. Paper is paper. The cost of taking it was what it said about me. They remembered.

quests.trigger: You demand absolute loyalty. One person refuses to kneel. The shelter watches.
quests.discovery: You've built enough power that loyalty is expected. Most people comply. Hale doesn't. At the morning briefing, in front of forty people, Hale says: 'I'll work with you. I won't work for you.' The room goes silent. Everyone is watching. This isn't about Hale — it's about whether your authority has limits. Hale is skilled, well-liked, and has never done anything wrong. That's what makes the refusal dangerous.

choices.label: Accept Hale's terms — work with, not for
choices.outcome_text: You pause. The room holds its breath. 'Fine,' you say. 'Work with.' Hale nods. The tension breaks. Some people are relieved. Others are recalculating — if Hale can refuse, maybe they can too. You've kept a good worker and shown a crack in the wall. Both consequences are real.
choices.epitaph: Said fine. Work with. Hale nodded. Some were relieved. Others were recalculating.

choices.label: Expel Hale — make the example public
choices.outcome_text: You give Hale until sundown. The shelter watches Hale pack — methodical, unhurried, dignified in a way that makes the punishment look worse than the crime. At the gate, Hale turns: 'You'll run out of people who kneel. That's how this ends.' The shelter is quiet for three days. Nobody refuses again. Nobody trusts you again either.
choices.epitaph: Expelled Hale. 'You'll run out of people who kneel,' they said. Nobody refuses again. Nobody trusts again.

choices.label: Assign Hale the most dangerous task — let the wasteland decide
choices.outcome_text: You assign Hale to the radiation survey in the burn zone — the most dangerous run in the sector. It's technically a fair assignment. Everyone rotates through dangerous tasks. But Hale knows, and you know, that the assignment is punishment wearing the mask of duty. Hale goes. Hale comes back, irradiated but alive. The mask stays in place. Barely.
choices.epitaph: Assigned the radiation survey. Punishment wearing duty's mask. Hale came back irradiated but alive. Barely.

choices.label: Break Hale psychologically — isolate until they comply
choices.outcome_text: You don't expel Hale. You isolate them. Reassigned to solo duties. Meals alone. No one speaks to Hale because no one wants to be associated with defiance. It takes eleven days. On the twelfth, Hale stands at the briefing and says: 'I work for you.' The room exhales. You've won. The victory tastes like ash and old metal.
choices.epitaph: Isolated Hale for eleven days. On the twelfth: 'I work for you.' I won. It tastes like ash.

quests.trigger: The last neutral camp refuses to submit. Destroying them sends a message. Sparing them shows weakness.
quests.discovery: The flooded area camp is the last independent settlement in the sector. Thirty people, mostly families, growing food in raised beds above the waterline. They refuse your tribute demand. Their leader — a former schoolteacher named Anika — sent back your messenger with the message: 'We want no trouble. We will not kneel.' The camp is defensible but not strong. You could take it in a day. Or you could let the last sanctuary stand.

choices.label: Let the sanctuary stand — some things matter more than control
choices.outcome_text: You pull the patrol back. Anika's camp continues, small and defiant and free. Your advisors call it weakness. Your people whisper. But the flooded area camp becomes a story — proof that not everything submits. Years from now, when the math of power has changed, that story will matter. You choose to believe that.
choices.epitaph: Pulled back. Let the sanctuary stand. My advisors called it weakness. I chose to believe it mattered.

choices.label: Destroy the camp and send a message
choices.outcome_text: The assault takes four hours. Anika's people fight with the desperation of the cornered. When it's over, the raised beds are trampled, the food stores burned, the families scattered into the water. You leave a marker: 'This is what refusal costs.' The sector goes quiet. It's the quiet of a held breath that will never exhale.
choices.epitaph: Destroyed the camp. Burned the beds. 'This is what refusal costs.' The sector went quiet. Permanently.

choices.label: Offer one last negotiation — submit symbolically, keep autonomy
choices.outcome_text: You send a new offer: fly the banner, acknowledge the authority, pay a token tribute. Anika considers for three days. She accepts. It's a face-saving compromise — you get the symbolism, she keeps the substance. Both sides pretend it's enough. The sanctuary stands, technically independent, practically yours. The fiction holds because both sides need it to.
choices.epitaph: Offered a compromise. She accepted. The fiction holds because both sides need it to.

choices.label: Undermine the camp from within — turn their people
choices.outcome_text: You send agents to the flooded area camp — not with weapons, with offers. Better rations. Protection. A future. One by one, families leave Anika's camp and join yours. Anika watches her sanctuary dissolve not through violence but through attrition. Within a month, the camp is empty. Anika leaves alone. You didn't destroy the sanctuary. You made it unnecessary.
choices.epitaph: Didn't destroy the sanctuary. Made it unnecessary. Anika watched her people leave one by one.

quests.trigger: A dangerous mission requires people. Your own loyal followers are the obvious choice. They trust you.
quests.discovery: The military outpost has intelligence you need — a map of every fortified position in the sector. Getting it requires sending a team through the burn zone during a radiation storm. Survival odds are thirty percent. Your most loyal people — the ones who've been with you since the beginning, who'd follow you anywhere — are the obvious choice. They'll go because you'll ask. They know it might be a one-way trip. You know it too.

choices.label: Go yourself — you can't ask this of anyone
choices.outcome_text: You assemble a volunteer team — nobody ordered, nobody pressured. You lead it yourself. The radiation storm hits during the return. Two people don't make it. You carry the map back with blistered hands and a dose that will shorten your life by years. The shelter sees you walk in first, map in hand, bleeding. Loyalty like that can't be bought. It can only be earned this way.
choices.epitaph: Led the team myself. Two didn't make it. The map cost me years. Loyalty can't be bought.

choices.label: Send your loyal people — they won't question it
choices.outcome_text: You call five names. They nod. They don't ask about survival odds because you haven't told them, and they trust you enough not to. Three come back. They bring the map. They also bring radiation sickness. You treat them as best you can. They don't mention the odds they later learned about. Trust, once broken by the math of survival, doesn't complain. It just stops.
choices.epitaph: Sent five. Three came back. They brought the map and radiation sickness. Trust doesn't complain. It just stops.

choices.label: Ask for volunteers — let them choose
choices.outcome_text: You describe the mission honestly — the odds, the risks, the reward. The room is quiet. Then three people stand. Not your loyalists — strangers, people you've barely spoken to. They go because they choose to, not because you asked. Two survive. The map is yours. The volunteers are changed. But they chose, and that choice matters.
choices.epitaph: Asked for volunteers honestly. Three strangers stood. Two survived. They chose. That mattered.

choices.label: Send the newcomers — they're more expendable
choices.outcome_text: The newest arrivals haven't earned their place yet. That's the logic you use. Five newcomers, poorly equipped, sent into the storm. They don't know the terrain, don't know the risks, don't know that your loyalists were the first choice. Two make it back. The map is incomplete — they couldn't carry everything. You got what you needed. The newcomers who survived will never trust anyone.
choices.epitaph: Sent the newcomers. Expendable, I called them. Two survived with an incomplete map. They'll never trust.

quests.trigger: You've reached the top. Every rival is gone, every ally indebted, every threat neutralized. Now what?
quests.discovery: The shelter is yours. Completely, totally, without challenge. The last rival left yesterday. The last ally who questioned you is silent. The food stores are full because you control the distribution. The weapons are locked where only you have the key. You sit in the meeting room alone and realize there's nobody left to talk to. The silence is absolute. This is what victory looks like.

choices.label: Open the doors — share power before it hollows you
choices.outcome_text: You call a meeting. A real one — not for announcements, for discussion. You propose a council. You propose term limits. You propose transparency. The room stares. They've forgotten what shared governance looks like. It takes months to build. Some of what you built gets dismantled. But the silence in the meeting room is replaced by voices — messy, argumentative, alive.
choices.epitaph: Called a real meeting. Proposed a council. The silence was replaced by voices. Messy. Argumentative. Alive.

choices.label: Consolidate further — power must be maintained, not shared
choices.outcome_text: You formalize the control. Written rules, enforced compliance, a hierarchy with you at the apex. The shelter runs efficiently. The food is distributed. The threats are managed. People eat, sleep, work, repeat. It's not happiness. It's not misery. It's a machine with you as the central gear. The machine works. The machine doesn't dream.
choices.epitaph: Formalized the control. The shelter runs efficiently. A machine with me as the central gear. It doesn't dream.

choices.label: Find someone to replace you — then remove them when they falter
choices.outcome_text: You install a figurehead — someone competent enough to manage, not competent enough to threaten. You govern from behind. When the figurehead makes mistakes — and they always do — you correct them quietly. The shelter thinks they have a leader. You know the leader is the shadow. It's the most comfortable prison you've ever built.
choices.epitaph: Installed a figurehead. Govern from behind. The shelter thinks they have a leader. I am the shadow.

choices.label: Walk away — leave it all behind
choices.outcome_text: You pack a bag at dawn. You leave the key to the supply room on the table, the radio codes written on a slip of paper, the map of every alliance and debt pinned to the wall. You walk through the gate without saying goodbye. Behind you, the shelter will figure itself out or fall apart. Neither is your problem anymore. The road is empty. The sky is grey. You've never felt lighter.
choices.epitaph: Left the key on the table. Walked out at dawn. The road was empty. I've never felt lighter.

quests.trigger: Your 'allies' are terrified of you. The shelter runs on fear. You can feel the difference — can you?
quests.discovery: People move when you enter a room. Not out of respect — out of the flinch reflex. Conversations stop. Eyes drop. The food is distributed on time. The work gets done. The perimeter holds. Everything works, and everything is silent. A child laughs in the corridor and her mother pulls her close, apologetic, as if joy is a breach of protocol. You built this. Every flinch is a brick in your wall.

choices.label: Try to rebuild trust — start with small gestures
choices.outcome_text: You start eating in the common room. You ask questions and wait for answers. You laugh at a joke — a real laugh, surprised and human. The room doesn't relax. Not yet. But one person — just one — laughs back. It's a start. Trust rebuilds at the speed of consistency, and you have a very long way to go.
choices.epitaph: Ate in the common room. Asked questions. One person laughed back. Trust rebuilds slowly.

choices.label: Accept the fear — it's more reliable than loyalty
choices.outcome_text: Fear is predictable. Fear doesn't disappoint. You tighten the protocols, formalize the hierarchy, make the consequences clear. The shelter runs like a clock. Nobody laughs in the corridors anymore. The work gets done. The perimeter holds. You sit alone in the meeting room and the silence is total. This is what reliability costs.
choices.epitaph: Tightened the protocols. Nobody laughs anymore. The silence is total. This is what reliability costs.

choices.label: Find the one person who isn't afraid — and understand why
choices.outcome_text: There's one person who still meets your eyes. Old Fen's apprentice, a quiet woman who catalogues the supply room. You ask her why she isn't afraid. She thinks. 'Because you can't take anything I have left,' she says. She has nothing. She's free. You sit with that for a long time.
choices.epitaph: Asked the one unafraid person why. 'You can't take what I don't have,' she said. She has nothing. She's free.

choices.label: Double down — fear should have a structure, a system
choices.outcome_text: You build the apparatus. Informants in every work crew. A reward system for reporting dissent. A punishment ladder, graduated and 'fair.' The shelter becomes a panopticon. People perform loyalty the way they perform breathing — automatically, without thinking. You've built a perfect system. It runs whether you're awake or asleep. You're not sure you could dismantle it if you wanted to.
choices.epitaph: Built the apparatus. Informants, rewards, punishments. A perfect system. I'm not sure I could dismantle it.

quests.trigger: The final accounting. Everything you built on betrayal stands or falls. The wasteland delivers its verdict.
quests.discovery: It's morning. You stand at the shelter gate and look out at the sector you've shaped through twenty-four acts of calculated self-interest. The alliances are broken. The rivals are gone. The sanctuary is ashes or submission. The people inside the shelter are fed, housed, and utterly dependent on your continued dominance. You have won. The wasteland has given you exactly what you asked for. The question is whether you can live with the answer.

choices.label: Open the gate. Share everything. Begin again.
choices.outcome_text: You unlock the supply room. You broadcast the radio frequencies. You tear down the informant network and burn the ledger of debts. People stare like you've lost your mind. Maybe you have. By evening, the shelter is in chaos — beautiful, terrifying chaos. People arguing, sharing, deciding things without your permission. It's the most alive the shelter has been since before you took control. You sit in the noise and feel something you haven't felt in a long time. Relief.
choices.epitaph: Opened the gate. Burned the ledger. The chaos was beautiful. I felt something I hadn't felt in years. Relief.

choices.label: Seal the gate. Rule what you've built. This is the answer.
choices.outcome_text: You lock the gate and pocket the key. The shelter is yours — a closed system, perfectly controlled, running on the momentum of your will. Nobody challenges you. Nobody needs to. The machine runs. You are the machine. At night, in the silence you've built, you hear nothing. Not peace. Not quiet. Nothing. The wasteland's answer is the sound of your own breathing in an empty room.
choices.epitaph: Sealed the gate. The machine runs. At night I hear nothing. Not peace. The wasteland's answer is my own breathing.

choices.label: Walk through the gate alone. Leave it all.
choices.outcome_text: You take a pack, a knife, three days of rations. You write a note — not an apology, just a record of what happened and why. You leave it on the table with the key. The gate closes behind you with a sound like a period at the end of a sentence. The road stretches out, grey and featureless. You don't look back. You don't know where you're going. For the first time in a long time, that's enough.
choices.epitaph: Left a note and a key. Walked through the gate. The road is grey. I don't look back. That's enough.

choices.label: Stand at the gate. Neither open nor close. Just stand.
choices.outcome_text: You stand at the gate as the sun crosses the sky. People pass behind you — going to work, going to eat, going about the life you've built and broken and built again. Nobody speaks to you. Nobody needs to. The gate is neither open nor closed. You are neither ruler nor exile. You are the pause between one story and the next. The wasteland doesn't judge. It just waits.
choices.epitaph: Stood at the gate all day. Neither open nor closed. The wasteland doesn't judge. It just waits.
